This run resolves the one major remaining uncertainty with a plausible chance of a new best. If it helps, the last two experiments can exploit singleprofile variants. Expected cost is lower than the multiprofile multimodal runs (roughly 2–3 GPU hours versus about 4.5), because there is no multiprofile transformer aggregation.

1) Evidence: imagenet_vit_l is the dominant factor. Every strong run uses it, and the best result so far is config_030 (scvi_n200 + vit_l, multiprofile transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. Swapping in scgpt or resnet50, or using weighted fusion or avgpool, clearly hurts. Image-only multiprofile (config_049, 0.713 accuracy, 1.44 GPU hours) nearly matches the best and has the highest F1 (0.695). Single-profile multimodal (config_040, 0.715 accuracy, 0.62 GPU hours) is also close at a fraction of the cost. So the RNA branch and the multiprofile aggregation each seem to add little on top of vit_l. 2) This run tests image-only vit_l in single-profile mode, the simplest untested variant of the strong backbone. It isolates whether RNA fusion and profile aggregation matter at all, and it could match or exceed the top accuracy without either. 3) Why now: the remaining multimodal variants mostly re-use settings already shown to hurt (weighted fusion, avgpool, pca or scgpt encoders), so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This run is the cheapest in the space (expected about 0.3–0.6 GPU hours, below config_040). It resolves a key design question cheaply and keeps the final experiment free for the best follow-up.

1. Evidence: the best result is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy. The single-profile version, config_040, nearly matches it (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) at about one-seventh of the cost. Image-only single-profile reaches only 0.494, so the RNA modality carries most of the signal at single-profile level. Concat fusion clearly beat weighted (by about 0.09) and transformer beat avgpool (by about 0.09), so options using weighted fusion or avgpool look unlikely to win. PCA_n2000 was only modestly behind scVI in the multiprofile setting (0.688 vs 0.725), and scGPT was poor. 2. Test: this run asks whether the richer pca_n2000 RNA representation beats scVI in the single-profile ViT-L concat setup. Without multiprofile aggregation, raw gene-level variance may matter more, so it could exceed 0.725. 3. Why this run: as the final experiment, it keeps every component that has worked well (ViT-L, concat fusion, the strong single-profile multimodal setup) and varies only the remaining plausible lever. The alternatives depend on choices already shown to underperform. Expected cost is low, about 0.6–0.8 GPU hours, similar to config_040 and far below the roughly 4–5 GPU hours of the multiprofile runs.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating multiple profiles per sample usually helps, but this is untested here. 2) Test: config_010 is a strong, representative multimodal multiprofile baseline. It uses scVI (n200) for RNA, ResNet50 for images, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It tells us whether the full multimodal, multiprofile pipeline reaches high accuracy, and it serves as an anchor. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA), image encoder (ViT-L), or dropping to a single modality. 3) Why now: the likely winner sits in this region of the space, so a mid-cost representative is the most informative first step. It avoids the most expensive combinations (ViT-L image encoder plus scGPT RNA encoder) while still testing the key hypothesis. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high. Multiprofile transformer aggregation with two modalities makes it costlier than single-profile or unimodal configs, but the compact scVI and ResNet50 encoders make it notably cheaper than the ViT-L or scGPT multimodal variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI-200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation and concat fusion reached 0.579 accuracy (F1 0.563) for 5.16 GPU hours. With a single data point, we cannot yet tell which design axes drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_029 keeps every setting fixed except the image encoder, which changes from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Any accuracy change can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. The image representation is likely one of the highest-impact choices in the space, and ViT-L features are often stronger. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: if ViT-L helps, it points to the strongest branch of the search (ViT-L variants across RNA encoders and fusion types) for the remaining 8 experiments. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 and use the remaining runs on aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. Expected relative cost: higher than config_010, roughly 1.5 to 2 times its 5.16 GPU hours, because of the larger ViT-L image representation. The large potential gain justifies that cost.

1) Evidence so far: with scVI RNA, transformer aggregation and concat fusion fixed, ResNet50 (0.579 acc / 0.563 F1) beat ViT-L (0.540 / 0.524). Both accuracy and F1 agree, so ResNet50 is the provisional image encoder, though this rests on one comparison. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (config_010) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether the learned multiprofile aggregator is worth its cost, which is a major untested design choice. 3) It is the best next use of the budget for two reasons. It sits next to the current best, so it has a realistic chance of matching or beating it. Its result also decides the aggregation default for the remaining runs. If avgpool comes out comparable, later tests of RNA encoder and fusion can use the cheaper backbone. Expected cost: lower than config_010's 5.16 GPU hours because avgpool replaces the transformer, likely around 4 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.540 with the transformer and scVI held fixed). Avgpool is slightly ahead of the transformer (0.591 vs 0.579). That gap is small and comes from a single comparison, so it may not be reliable. Every run so far used scVI RNA embeddings and concat fusion, so the RNA encoder and fusion type are still completely unexplored. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves accuracy. 3) The RNA encoder has two untested options and could plausibly shift accuracy more than the fusion choice. Testing it first on the best backbone is therefore the most informative next step, while still having a real chance of beating 0.591. The weighted-fusion test (config_003) can follow. Expected cost is similar to config_031, about 7 GPU hours, and possibly a bit more depending on scGPT's embedding size.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scVI for scGPT, with resnet50, avgpool and concat held fixed, raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.653 (F1 0.573 to 0.628). resnet50 beat imagenet_vit_l (0.579 vs 0.540), and avgpool slightly beat transformer (0.591 vs 0.579). These are single runs, so small gaps are uncertain. Fusion is the one design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: this experiment keeps the best configuration (scGPT, resnet50, multiprofile avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest base. 3) Why now: it exploits the clear scGPT gain while answering an open question that applies across the remaining search. Expected cost is similar to config_033 (about 4–5 GPU hours), since weighted fusion adds little compute and avgpool with resnet50 was the cheapest setup so far. If weighted fusion helps, later runs can build on it; if not, concat is confirmed and the budget can move to the pca_n2000 RNA encoder or single-profile alternatives.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the most influential choice tested so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt in the resnet50/avgpool/concat setting raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.653, with F1 rising alongside it. Concat fusion clearly beats weighted fusion (0.653 vs 0.421). resnet50 has outperformed vit_l, and avgpool is slightly ahead of the transformer. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, has never been tested, so the most impactful dimension is still only partly explored. 2. Test: config_009 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_033. It tells us whether scgpt is truly the best encoder or whether a high-dimensional PCA input can match or beat it. 3. Why now: Fusion and image encoder appear settled for the moment. Aggregation and modality ablations, such as scgpt with a transformer or RNA-only, are smaller refinements I can run with the remaining 3 experiments. Resolving the RNA encoder question now ensures later exploitation builds on the right encoder. Expected cost: moderate, about 4 to 7 GPU hours, similar to the other resnet50/avgpool multimodal runs. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slightly to cost, but it avoids the extra expense of a transformer or ViT.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Switching it moved accuracy from 0.59 (scvi) to 0.65 (scgpt) to 0.715 (pca_n2000, config_009, the current best). Concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.65 vs 0.42). ResNet50 beats ViT-L, and avgpool slightly beats transformer. The main untested question is whether the image branch helps at all, since no unimodal baseline has been run. 2) This experiment tests the PCA-2000 RNA-only multiprofile model with avgpool, which is config_009 without the image branch. If it matches or beats 0.715, imaging is adding little or even noise, and the last two runs should focus on RNA-only variants. If it falls clearly below, imaging contributes, and the remaining budget should go to PCA plus ResNet50 concat variants such as transformer aggregation or singleprofile. 3) It answers an important open design choice while staying close to the best region, so it has a real chance of becoming the new best. Expected cost: it drops image processing, so it should be well below config_009's 36 GPU hours. It is likely moderate, though the large 2000-dimensional PCA input may still make it costlier than the 4–7 hour scvi and scgpt runs.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is the RNA-only pca_n2000 avgpool multiprofile model (config_024: 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). It cost only 1.34 GPU hours. The multimodal pca_n2000 version with resnet50 (config_009) scored slightly lower at 0.715, despite costing 36.42 GPU hours. So the images do not appear to help, and pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested. Aggregation is the main design choice not yet tested in this setting. With scvi multimodal, transformer and avgpool were close (0.579 vs 0.591), which is a single, small comparison and not conclusive for the much stronger pca features. 2) Test: config_051 changes only the aggregation of the current best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether attention-based multiprofile aggregation can extract more from the 2000-dimensional PCA features. 3) Why now: It directly exploits the leading direction while settling an open design choice. It is expected to be cheap, roughly 1.5–3 GPU hours, which is far below any multimodal pca run. That keeps total compute low and leaves two experiments for follow-up, such as single-profile RNA-only.

1. Evidence: The pca_n2000 RNA encoder is clearly the strongest. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_024) gives 0.725 accuracy for 1.34 GPU h. Adding ResNet50 images (config_009) did not help, scoring 0.715 for 36 GPU h. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool, and weighted fusion was clearly worse than concat. Image modality and alternative fusion choices therefore look unpromising. Profile setting is the one major design axis that remains completely untested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. Test: config_017 runs the best known encoder (pca_n2000, RNA-only) in the single-profile setting. This checks whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed, or whether a simpler single-profile model matches or beats 0.725. 3. Why this experiment: It is the most informative remaining test that still has a real chance of beating the current best. It is also very cheap, expected around 1 GPU h or less, since it has no aggregation and no image branch. That cost is far below the expensive multimodal alternatives such as pca with imagenet_vit_l, which the evidence suggests add little accuracy. It leaves budget for one final exploitation step.

1) Evidence: pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, reaching 0.715 to 0.725, versus at most 0.653 for scgpt and 0.591 for scvi. Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by a wide margin (0.653 vs 0.421). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.540), and avgpool or no aggregation beats transformer aggregation. Single-profile RNA-only (0.721 at 0.04 GPU hours) nearly matches multiprofile RNA-only (0.725). Multiprofile multimodal pca+ResNet50+concat reached 0.715 but cost 36 GPU hours. 2) Test: config_032 combines the best components (pca_n2000, ResNet50, concat) in the cheaper single-profile setting. It checks whether adding image features without multiprofile aggregation can push past the 0.725 RNA-only best. 3) Why this choice for the last run: every other option includes a component already shown to be weaker (weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, ViT-L, or a non-pca encoder). This makes config_032 the best remaining chance at a new top score. Expected cost is low to moderate: far below the 36 GPU hours of multiprofile multimodal, likely a few GPU hours at most.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so the main uncertainty is whether combining RNA and image data (multimodal) and pooling several profiles per sample (multiprofile) actually help. Domain priors suggest both should beat RNA-only, image-only and single-profile setups. 2) Test: this run sets a central, mid-cost anchor in the region most likely to score well: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scVI 200-dimensional RNA embedding, the ResNet50 image encoder, simple average pooling and concatenation fusion. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it: switching to the transformer aggregator, to weighted fusion, to the larger ViT-L image encoder, to the scGPT or PCA-2000 RNA encoders, or dropping to a single modality. 3) Why now: starting at the most plausible region while avoiding the most expensive components (transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT) gives a dependable baseline at moderate GPU cost. If the expensive upgrades help, the remaining 9 runs leave room to escalate to them. Expected relative cost: moderate. Multiprofile multimodal processing adds cost, but the low-dimensional scVI input, the lighter ResNet50 and average pooling keep it well below the ViT-L or transformer-based variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_033 is identical except that avgpool aggregation is replaced by transformer aggregation. Aggregation is the main way a multiprofile model combines its profiles, and learned attention over profiles could plausibly beat simple averaging. Because only one factor changes, any difference in accuracy can be attributed to it. 3. Why it is the best next use: Settling aggregation early tells us whether later experiments, such as trying ViT-L image features, scGPT RNA features or weighted fusion, should build on transformer or avgpool. That makes the remaining 8 experiments more efficient. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_013, perhaps around 8 to 10 GPU hours, because of the attention layers. That is still cheaper than switching to the larger ViT-L image encoder.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) clearly beat avgpool (0.530 accuracy, 0.515 F1). Transformer was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours), so it is the anchor to keep. 2. Test: this run keeps the best configuration (config_033) and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. That isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone adds accuracy on top of transformer aggregation. The image encoder is probably a larger lever than fusion type, which is a smaller tweak left for later. 3. Why now: we have 7 experiments left, and settling the image encoder early tells us which backbone to use for the later RNA-encoder (scgpt vs pca) and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_033, roughly 6 to 9 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. That is justified because the image backbone could plausibly decide which configuration ends up best.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 accuracy, with the same scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat setup), and the F1 scores agree. ResNet50 slightly beat ViT-L under the transformer (0.650 vs 0.618), but that is a modest single comparison. The RNA encoder is the main untested axis: only scvi_n200 has been tried, and it has three options, so it could plausibly move accuracy more than fusion type. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, resnet50, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It is a clean one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) It explores a high-impact axis while staying in the best-performing region, and the result will tell me whether to test PCA next or move on to weighted fusion (config_003, or its scGPT counterpart config_026). Expected cost is similar to config_033 (about 5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger. That is still well below the 7.27-hour avgpool run.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 with scvi_n200 + resnet50). ResNet50 slightly beats ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). scGPT and scVI are essentially tied (0.653 vs 0.650), but scGPT costs much more (9.06 vs 5.16 GPU hours). Fusion is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the strong, cheap setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer) and changes only fusion to weighted. Compared with config_033, this isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: it reduces uncertainty on an important unexplored dimension with a single controlled change, on the cheaper of two near-equal RNA encoders. If weighted fusion helps, I can then try it with scGPT (config_026). Expected cost is moderate, about 5 GPU hours, similar to config_033 and roughly half of an scGPT run.

1) Evidence: three design choices look clear so far. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 12 points (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by about 11 points (0.650 vs 0.535). ResNet50 edges out ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). Among RNA encoders, scGPT and scVI are nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650, with similar F1), but scGPT cost about 75% more GPU time. The one major design choice still untested is the PCA_n2000 RNA encoder. 2) Test: config_010 places PCA_n2000 inside the best-performing setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, concat). This tells us whether a simpler, high-dimensional linear RNA representation matches or beats the learned encoders. 3) Why now: it fills the last important gap in the RNA-encoder dimension inside the strongest region of the search space. It therefore has a real chance of setting a new best, and it informs how the remaining 4 experiments are spent. Expected cost: moderate, likely similar to or slightly above the scVI transformer run (about 5–7 GPU hours) and below the scGPT run (about 9 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.650 vs 0.535). PCA is a poor RNA encoder (0.435). scGPT and scVI are about equal (0.653 vs 0.650), and ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 0.03 with scVI. The one important untested choice is the modality setting: no unimodal baseline has been run, so we do not know whether the image branch adds signal or mostly noise. 2. This experiment runs the RNA-only model with the strongest setup found so far (scGPT encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). It shows how much the image modality contributes and whether dropping it could match or beat the current best of 0.653. 3. Why now: the only untested multimodal concat+transformer option without PCA is config_005 (scGPT + ViT-L). Since ViT-L has underperformed ResNet50, it is unlikely to beat 0.653. The modality ablation is more informative and could reveal a better and cheaper direction, which would guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is moderate: lower than the multimodal scGPT run (9.06 GPU hours) because there is no image encoder, likely around 5–7 GPU hours.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530), and concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.650 vs 0.535). The two best runs are scGPT/ResNet50 (0.653) and scVI/ResNet50 (0.650), so the RNA encoder choice between these two matters little, while PCA is poor. The main remaining uncertainty inside the winning recipe (multiprofile, transformer, concat) is the image encoder for scGPT. With scVI, ViT-L scored about 3 points below ResNet50 (0.619 vs 0.650), but that is a single comparison and may not transfer to scGPT features. Test: config_005 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer, concat) is the only untested combination of the top-performing aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. It checks whether pairing ViT-L with scGPT can match or beat the current best. Why now: alternatives such as weighted fusion, avgpool, PCA or single-profile models have strong evidence against them or are unlikely to exceed 0.65. This is the highest-upside test with 2 experiments left. Expected cost: moderate-to-high, roughly 5-9 GPU hours. That is similar to config_032, since scGPT runs were the most expensive and the ViT-L run was slightly cheaper than ResNet50.

1) Evidence: The best design so far is multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation with concat fusion and a ResNet50 image encoder. Two runs reach this level: scGPT in config_032 (0.653 acc, 0.628 F1) and scVI in config_033 (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). One-factor changes from that design consistently hurt. Avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.530, weighted fusion to 0.535, PCA to 0.435, and ViT-L lowered it by about 0.02-0.03. RNA-only scGPT reached only 0.512. The remaining untested multiprofile neighbours of the best config therefore change factors already shown to hurt, such as weighted fusion (config_026) or avgpool (config_040). 2) Question: The largest open design choice is single-profile versus multiprofile input. Config_001 keeps the best components (scGPT, ResNet50, concat) but uses single profiles with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is truly needed or whether simpler per-profile training does as well or better. 3) Why now: Re-running close variants of the best config is unlikely to give a meaningful gain. Testing the one unexplored axis has the best chance of revealing a new optimum and still leaves one experiment to exploit the answer. Expected cost is low to moderate. With no multiprofile aggregation it should cost well below the 9.06 GPU hours of config_032, probably around 2-4 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_001 (singleprofile, scGPT, ResNet50, concat) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It is also the cheapest multimodal run at 1.16 GPU hours, and it beats every multiprofile variant. The other patterns are consistent. ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 0.02 to 0.03 accuracy. Concat clearly beats weighted fusion (0.650 vs 0.535). scVI and scGPT are nearly tied (0.650 vs 0.653), with scVI costing much less. PCA is clearly worse. 2. This experiment keeps the winning singleprofile, ResNet50, concat setup and swaps the RNA encoder to scVI. It tests whether scVI's near-tie with scGPT carries over to the singleprofile setting and could edge out the current best. 3. On the final run, the other options look weaker. ViT-L variants and weighted fusion are both expected to score lower, so this is the most plausible way to beat 0.678. If it falls short, nothing is lost because config_001 is already recorded. Expected cost is low, about 1 GPU hour or less: no multiprofile aggregation, and scVI was cheaper than scGPT in the multiprofile runs.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. Prior expectations are that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation are likely to give the highest accuracy, but their benefit over simpler settings is uncertain. 2) This experiment tests a strong, representative multimodal multiprofile configuration: scVI-200 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. It sets an upper-region baseline. Later experiments can then vary one factor at a time against it: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, concat vs. weighted fusion, encoder choices, and single-modality ablations. 3) Starting with a likely high performer gives a good best-so-far result early in the 10-experiment budget. Using avgpool instead of a transformer and the compact scVI embedding keeps cost moderate compared with the transformer variants. Expected relative cost is medium-high: multimodal multiprofile processing with ViT-L features costs more than single-modality or single-profile runs, but avgpool makes it cheaper than the transformer-aggregation options.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_012 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1 for 4.82 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_007 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates whether learned attention across multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. Aggregation is a key structural choice that affects every multiprofile configuration in the search space, so the answer will guide many later picks. 3) Why now: it is a one-variable change to the current best, so the result is easy to interpret, and it is a plausible way to raise accuracy directly. Encoder and fusion variations can follow once the aggregation question is settled. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_012, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 6–8 GPU hours), because transformer aggregation adds compute over multiple profiles. I judge that worthwhile given its potential to be the strongest setup.

1) Evidence: with the same scVI + ViT-L + weighted setup, avgpool aggregation reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Transformer aggregation reached only 0.208, so avgpool is the stronger aggregation choice for this setup. This is one pair of runs, but the gap is large enough to act on. 2) Test: keep the winning avgpool + ViT-L + weighted setup and change only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. The RNA representation is the biggest untested design choice and could plausibly drive most of the remaining accuracy gains. This isolates whether a richer foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) Why now: it exploits the clearest signal so far (avgpool) while reducing uncertainty about a high-impact factor. The result will guide the remaining 7 experiments: either fine-tune fusion and image encoder around scGPT, or revert to scVI or try PCA. Expected cost is similar to config_012 (about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours), since it is still multiprofile multimodal with ViT-L; scGPT embeddings may add slightly more.

1) Evidence: avgpool aggregation clearly beats transformer (about 0.52 vs 0.21 with an otherwise identical setup). scVI and scGPT RNA encoders perform about the same with ViT-L, weighted fusion and avgpool (0.520 vs 0.514 accuracy). scGPT has the better F1 (0.498 vs 0.479) and was cheaper (2.94 vs 4.82 GPU hours). Fusion type is still completely untested, as are the ResNet50 image encoder and the PCA RNA encoder. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) and switches fusion from weighted to concat on the cheaper scGPT backbone. That isolates the effect of fusion in a direct comparison with config_035. 3) Fusion is a key design choice that affects every multimodal configuration, so learning it early narrows the remaining 6 experiments. Using scGPT rather than scVI tests this at lower cost with similar expected accuracy. Expected cost is moderate, about 3 GPU hours, similar to config_035 and cheaper than the scVI equivalent.

1. Evidence: Four multimodal multiprofile runs suggest that avgpool aggregation beats transformer by a wide margin (0.520 vs 0.208). Weighted fusion beats concat (0.514 vs 0.427 with scGPT). The RNA encoder matters little: scVI scored 0.520 and scGPT 0.514, though scGPT had higher F1. All four runs used imagenet_vit_l, so the image encoder choice is completely untested. 2. Test: config_046 keeps the best recipe (scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates the effect of the image encoder, the largest remaining uncertainty among the major design choices. 3. Why now: Running pca_n2000 would only refine an axis that already looks flat. The image encoder axis could shift the result in either direction and will guide the remaining 5 experiments. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the 4.82 GPU hours of config_012, because ResNet50 features are smaller than ViT-L features and avgpool with weighted fusion is the cheaper aggregation and fusion pairing.

1) Evidence: switching the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50 gave the largest gain so far, from 0.520 to 0.688 accuracy (config_012 vs config_046). Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.520 vs 0.208), and weighted fusion beat concat (0.514 vs 0.427). With the ViT-L encoder, scGPT matched scVI on accuracy (0.514 vs 0.520), had higher F1 (0.498 vs 0.479) and trained faster (2.94 vs 4.82 GPU hours). 2) Test: config_008 keeps the best known setup (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This shows whether the RNA encoder matters once the stronger image backbone is used, and whether scGPT's F1 edge turns into higher accuracy. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor change from the current best, so it exploits strong evidence while resolving a key remaining choice. Expected cost is similar to or slightly below config_046's 5.90 GPU hours, since scGPT runs were cheaper than scVI under weighted fusion. That is moderate and avoids the costly concat and transformer variants.

1. Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor. With avgpool and weighted fusion, ResNet50 beats ViT-L by roughly 0.17 to 0.21 accuracy. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.208 vs 0.520), and weighted fusion beats concat (0.514 vs 0.427). The best result so far is config_008 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The scVI version (config_046) reached 0.688, so the RNA encoder matters, but less than the image encoder. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tried in this strong setting. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the winning setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps in PCA-2000 RNA features. Expected cost: moderate, about 6 to 8 GPU hours. That should be similar to or a little above the scvi/resnet50 transformer run (6.2 h) and well below the scGPT run (12.3 h).

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_010 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_010 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). The other factors are fairly settled. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, val acc 0.706, F1 0.667). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. 1) Evidence so far: the best result is scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion (0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). scGPT beat scVI by about 4 points under matched settings. Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation with scVI (0.494 vs 0.328), so avgpool looks like the right aggregation. Fusion type is still completely untested, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and switches only weighted fusion to concat. That cleanly isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest RNA/image/aggregation setup. 3) Why this is the best next use: fusion is the main untested design choice on the leading branch, and concat could plausibly add accuracy. The result also tells us which fusion to carry into the remaining runs (for example, a ResNet50 image-encoder swap or unimodal baselines). Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 3 GPU hours, because concat fusion adds negligible overhead. That makes it cheaper than the scVI ViT-L avgpool run at about 4.8 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: Every run so far used the imagenet_vit_l image encoder. Within that setting, avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328), weighted fusion beat concat (0.537 vs 0.260), and scGPT beat scVI (0.537 vs 0.494). Each of these rests on a single comparison, but together they point to scgpt + avgpool + weighted as the current best (config_025, 0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). The image encoder is still a completely untested design choice. 2. Test: config_007 keeps the best configuration unchanged except for swapping the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates the effect of the image backbone and tells us whether a better configuration exists around the current best. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest region found so far while reducing uncertainty about an important axis that has not been explored. The result will guide the remaining 5 experiments, for example whether to try pca_n2000 or single-profile variants with resnet50 or vit_l. Expected cost: about 3 GPU hours or less, similar to or cheaper than config_025, since resnet50 features are smaller than ViT-L's and avgpool with weighted fusion was the cheapest setup observed.

1) Evidence so far: every run has been multiprofile. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.537 vs 0.260). Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328 with scVI). scGPT beats scVI (0.537 vs 0.494), and ViT-L edges out ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). The best so far is config_025 (scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, 0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). The biggest open question is the profile setting, since single-profile has never been tested. 2) This run keeps the strongest components (scGPT, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to single-profile. It is the closest controlled comparison to config_025 and shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually helping. 3) If single-profile matches or beats multiprofile, it opens a cheaper and possibly better branch for the remaining 3 experiments. If it loses, it confirms that multiprofile is worth its cost, and the remaining runs can test the PCA encoder or RNA-only variants. Expected cost is relatively low, likely below config_025's 2.94 GPU hours, because there is no multiprofile aggregation step.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is clearly better than concat (0.537 vs 0.260 with scGPT/ViT-L). avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328 with scVI). scGPT beats scVI (0.537 vs 0.494). ViT-L is slightly better than ResNet50. Single-profile scGPT/ViT-L/weighted (0.523) came close to the multiprofile best (0.537) at about 1/4 of the cost (0.67 vs 2.94 GPU hours). The main untested design choice is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, which is often a strong baseline. 2) Test: config_008 checks pca_n2000 with the best known settings (ViT-L, weighted fusion) in the cheap single-profile setting. It compares directly with config_021 to rank PCA against scGPT. 3) Why now: it is a low-cost screen, expected at about 0.7 GPU hours versus roughly 3-5 for a multiprofile run. If PCA matches or beats scGPT, I can use a remaining experiment on its multiprofile avgpool weighted counterpart (config_036). If not, I can put the remaining budget into refining the scGPT branch.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.537 vs 0.260 for scGPT/ViT-L multiprofile avgpool). Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.327 for scVI). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). Multiprofile avgpool gives a modest gain over single-profile for scGPT (0.537 vs 0.523). Among RNA encoders, PCA-2000 nearly matched scGPT in the single-profile setting (0.520 vs 0.523), while scVI was weaker. The main open question is whether PCA-2000 can match or beat scGPT once it is placed in the best known setup. 2) This experiment tests PCA-2000 with ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion, keeping every other design choice at its best value. It isolates the RNA-encoder choice in the top-performing setup and could beat the current best of 0.537. 3) It is the most promising untested extension of the strongest evidence, and its result will guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3–5 GPU hours, similar to other multiprofile avgpool weighted runs. That is higher than single-profile runs but justified by its higher expected accuracy.

1. Evidence: the multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted setup with the imagenet_vit_l encoder is the best family so far: pca 0.540 and scgpt 0.537. Concat fusion was much worse (0.26). Transformer aggregation was much worse (0.33 vs 0.49 with scvi). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). The choice of RNA encoder mattered little between pca and scgpt, and the remaining untested multimodal variants (ResNet50, scvi, transformer, concat) all contain components that look worse. The main open question is whether the RNA branch helps at all, since no unimodal baseline has been tested.
2. This experiment: image-only, multiprofile, avgpool with the ViT-L encoder isolates the image branch inside the best-performing structure. Weighted fusion may already be leaning heavily on the image modality, so an image-only model could match or beat the multimodal ones by avoiding RNA noise.
3. Why now: it is the highest-information remaining option that still has a real chance of a new best, and it tells us whether the final experiment should refine multimodal or unimodal. Expected cost is moderate: likely lower than config_036 (7.0 GPU h) and roughly similar to or below config_025 (2.9 GPU h), because there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (pca_n2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. The image-only ViT-L avgpool model (config_038) nearly matches it at 0.536. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation and weighted fusion clearly beats concat, so those choices are settled. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 lowered accuracy with scGPT (0.514 vs 0.537), so config_030 (the ResNet50 version of the best setup) would likely land near 0.51. 2) Uncertainty: The RNA-only branch has never been tested. Because image-only nearly equals multimodal, it is unclear whether RNA contributes much under weighted fusion. Its standalone strength is the largest unexplored question. config_031 tests the RNA encoder that did best in multimodal runs (pca_n2000) with the best aggregation (multiprofile avgpool). 3) Why this last slot: Only the best accuracy counts, and the remaining multimodal variants are predictably at or below the current best. The higher-variance untested branch gives the best, though still uncertain, chance of exceeding 0.540, and RNA-only may well score lower. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely well below config_036's 7 GPU hours, since no image backbone features are processed.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter. My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models are most likely to give the highest accuracy, but this has not been confirmed. 2) What it tests: config_024 is multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. It is a strong but moderately priced baseline. Cheaper parts (avgpool, ResNet50, a compact 200-dimensional scVI representation, simple concat) let me check whether combining modalities across multiple profiles works before paying for transformer aggregation, ViT-L or scGPT. 3) Why now: A central, well-performing anchor is the best start under a 10-experiment budget. Later runs can change one factor at a time from it (aggregation, image encoder, RNA encoder, fusion) or compare against unimodal and single-profile variants. Expected cost: moderate, more than single-profile or unimodal runs but clearly cheaper than ViT-L, transformer-aggregation or scGPT multimodal configurations.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_022 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates whether learned attention-based pooling across multiple profiles beats simple averaging. In multiprofile set-based models, aggregation is plausibly one of the strongest levers on accuracy. 3. Why it is the best next step: a single-factor comparison against the baseline gives a clean answer on a key design axis. It does this without paying for a ViT-L image encoder or scGPT, both of which would raise cost and add confounds. If the transformer helps, later experiments can build on it, for example by swapping the image or RNA encoder. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_024, roughly 1.2 to 1.5 times or about 9 to 11 GPU hours, because transformer aggregation adds overhead. It should still be cheaper than ViT-L-based configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Both completed runs use the multimodal, multiprofile setting with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion. They differ only in aggregation. Avgpool reached 0.520 accuracy and transformer reached 0.514. That gap is small, the transformer had higher F1 (0.498 vs 0.479), and it was cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h). So aggregation looks roughly neutral so far. The bigger unknowns are the image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion type. 2. What this tests: config_036 keeps the cheaper transformer aggregation, scvi_n200 and concat fixed, and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of a stronger, larger image representation, which is plausibly the largest untested lever. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: A clean single-factor comparison of the image encoder reduces uncertainty about a major design choice. It also has real upside for top accuracy. Later experiments can then test the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca) and weighted fusion on the better image backbone. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_022, perhaps around 6–8 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger.

1) Evidence: switching the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l gave a large jump, from about 0.51 to 0.715 accuracy (config_036), with F1 rising alongside it. With resnet50, the aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) made only a small difference. The transformer was cheaper and had better F1. The RNA encoder is the main design choice not yet explored: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding adds accuracy on top of the strong image features. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder could plausibly shift accuracy as much as the image encoder did. Settling it early tells the remaining 6 runs which RNA encoder to use for fusion and aggregation fine-tuning. Expected cost is similar to config_036 (about 5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher due to the larger scGPT embeddings. That is moderate relative to the 17 GPU hours used so far.

1. Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. imagenet_vit_l configs reached about 0.715–0.721 accuracy, while resnet50 configs reached about 0.51–0.52. The RNA encoder matters much less: scgpt (0.721) and scvi_n200 (0.715) are within noise. Fusion has never been varied, since every run used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_007: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer, multiprofile) and changes only the fusion to weighted. That isolates the effect of the one remaining untested design choice on the strongest backbone. 3. A gain here would directly raise the best accuracy found. A loss would settle concat as the fusion choice and free the remaining budget for checking aggregation (avgpool) or an image-only vit_l baseline. Expected cost is similar to config_007 and config_036, roughly 4–5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds little compute over concat. That is moderate and cheaper than the resnet50 runs.

1) Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor so far. imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and concat fusion reached about 0.715-0.721 accuracy, versus about 0.51-0.52 for resnet50. Concat fusion clearly beats weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.537 with scgpt + ViT-L + transformer). scgpt and scvi_n200 perform about the same. The main open question within the strong ViT-L + concat region is aggregation: avgpool has only been tested with resnet50, where it was slightly ahead of transformer (0.520 vs 0.514) and within noise. 2) This experiment holds the best configuration (config_007: scgpt, ViT-L, concat) fixed and swaps transformer for avgpool. It is a direct one-variable test of whether avgpool can push accuracy above 0.72. 3) Aggregation is the main design choice not yet tested in the high-performing region. The result decides where to exploit in the remaining 3 experiments, for example the pca_n2000 RNA encoder or an image-only ViT-L baseline. Expected cost is moderate, roughly similar to or somewhat higher than config_007's 3.95 GPU hours. The avgpool resnet50 run took the longest so far (7.27 GPU hours), so an upper bound near 7 GPU hours is possible.

1) Evidence: one combination clearly wins. ImageNet ViT-L with a transformer aggregator and concat fusion reached about 0.72 with both scGPT (0.721) and scVI (0.715). Each single change from that recipe dropped accuracy to about 0.51-0.54: switching to ResNet50, switching to avgpool aggregation, or switching to weighted fusion. Validation F1 follows the same pattern. The RNA encoder made little difference within the best recipe, so the image encoder and aggregator appear to drive performance. 2) This experiment completes the RNA-encoder comparison inside the winning recipe by testing the one untested option, pca_n2000. It shows whether a simpler RNA representation matches or beats the learned ones. 3) It is the most direct exploitation step, keeping every component already shown to matter. Weighted fusion, avgpool and ResNet50 variants are strongly indicated to underperform, so testing them would likely waste budget. Expected cost is moderate, about 4-5 GPU hours, similar to config_036 and config_007 since transformer aggregation has been the cheaper option. The 2000-dim PCA input may add slightly to that. An image-only ViT-L transformer run (config_043) remains a cheaper follow-up to check whether RNA contributes at all.

1) Evidence: the best results all share imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. config_007 (scGPT) reached 0.721 and config_036 (scVI) reached 0.715. Swapping in resnet50, avgpool or weighted fusion consistently dropped accuracy to about 0.51-0.54. scGPT and scVI score almost the same, while PCA reaches 0.59, so the image branch looks like the main driver. It is still unclear whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image signal. 2) Test: an image-only run with the same strong backbone (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). This isolates how much the RNA modality contributes. If it matches or beats 0.72, the best direction is simpler models. If it falls clearly below, multimodal concat is confirmed and the last experiment can refine the RNA encoder or profile setting. 3) Why now: it stays within the best-performing region, so it has a real chance of matching the top result while resolving a key design question for the final experiment. Expected cost is moderate to low, likely below the 4-5 GPU hours of the multimodal transformer runs, because the RNA branch and fusion step are removed.

1) Evidence: Within multiprofile runs, ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion form the best combination. config_007 (scGPT) reached 0.721 and config_036 (scVI) reached 0.715. Swapping in avgpool (0.53) or weighted fusion (0.54) dropped accuracy sharply. PCA (0.59) and ResNet50 (about 0.52) were clearly worse. Image-only ViT-L scored 0.639, so adding RNA helps. The profile setting is the one major axis not yet tested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the winning RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion (scGPT + ViT-L + concat) and switches to singleprofile, which removes aggregation. It tests whether singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile. 3) The remaining near-best multiprofile variants all change a component that has already hurt accuracy, so they are unlikely to beat 0.721. This run explores the last untested key design choice at low risk and gives a basis for the final experiment. Expected cost is low, likely below the best multiprofile run (about 4 GPU hours), probably around 1–3 GPU hours, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: The strong region is multiprofile + ViT-L + transformer + concat. scGPT reached 0.721 and scVI reached 0.715, while PCA reached 0.591. All three RNA encoders are now tested in that setup, so no untested near-copy of the best remains. Both alternatives to the best setup scored much lower with scGPT: avgpool fell to 0.532 and weighted fusion fell to 0.537. However, the weighted-fusion drop is a single data point and could depend on the encoder. 2) This experiment tests whether weighted fusion works better with the scVI ViT-L transformer setup, the second-best configuration. If the scGPT result was encoder-specific, this could beat 0.721. 3) With one run left, any choice is a long shot, but this is a one-factor change from a top configuration. The other one-step option, scVI with avgpool (config_018), changes a factor that hurt consistently and costs about 7 GPU hours. Image-only and RNA-only options are unlikely to beat multimodal. Expected cost is low, roughly 3 GPU hours, similar to the 2.86 hours of config_014.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so I am relying on priors. For multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA and image signals and pooling information across multiple profiles usually gives the highest accuracy. Strong pretrained image features (ViT-L) and a compact, well-regularized RNA latent space (scVI with 200 dimensions) are reasonable defaults. Learned weighted fusion and transformer aggregation tend to match or beat concatenation and average pooling. 2. What it tests: config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is my best prior guess for a top-performing setup. It sets a high-performing anchor that later runs can be compared against, one factor at a time. Likely follow-ups are avgpool vs. transformer (config_011), ResNet50 vs. ViT-L (config_010), and modality ablations to check whether the extra cost is justified. 3. Why now: Only the best accuracy within the budget counts, so securing a strong result early lowers risk and makes later cheaper ablations easy to interpret. Expected relative cost: high, among the most expensive options, because it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation, multimodal processing and ViT-L features. I accept that cost because this configuration is plausibly the best one.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The full multimodal setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1 at 3.6 GPU hours. We do not know which part of this expensive setup drives the score. The most important and most cost-relevant unknown is whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. It keeps the same RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion, so the comparison isolates the value of multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: the answer determines where the remaining 8 experiments go. If single-profile comes close to 0.619, later searches over encoders and fusion can use cheap single-profile runs. If it drops clearly, we can focus on multiprofile variants such as aggregation type and RNA encoder with confidence. Expected cost is substantially lower than config_043, roughly 30-50% of its 3.6 GPU hours, since no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 + ViT-L weighted-fusion backbone held fixed, the multiprofile transformer reached 0.619 accuracy (F1 0.610). The single-profile version reached 0.573. That is a solid gain of about 4.6 points, but it cost about 7x more (3.60 vs 0.53 GPU h). It is still unclear whether the gain comes from aggregating multiple profiles at all or from the transformer aggregator specifically. 2) Test: config_011 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, so it isolates that choice. If avgpool matches or beats the transformer, the remaining budget can explore encoders and fusion on a cheaper multiprofile base. If it clearly loses, that supports keeping the transformer for the final exploitation steps. 3) Why now: aggregation is a high-impact choice that we have not yet tested, and the answer shapes both accuracy and cost for the other 6 experiments. Expected cost is moderate: still multiprofile and multimodal with ViT-L, but probably somewhat cheaper than the 3.6 GPU h transformer run, around 2.5-3 GPU h.

Evidence: across three runs, multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_043, 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1) clearly beats singleprofile (0.573) and avgpool aggregation (0.422). So transformer-based multiprofile aggregation is the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type have each been tested at only one value (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted). Test: config_005 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scGPT, as a clean one-factor comparison. Why now: the RNA representation is plausibly the largest remaining lever on accuracy. Exploiting the best architecture while varying one key factor balances exploitation with reducing uncertainty, leaving five later runs to probe fusion (e.g., config_047) or a cheaper ResNet50 encoder (config_010). Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_043, about 3.5–4.5 GPU hours, since it is still multiprofile multimodal with transformer aggregation and scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy. Two design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.619 vs 0.422 with everything else the same). scVI beats scGPT (0.619 vs 0.520). Multiprofile with transformer also beats singleprofile (0.573). Fusion has not been varied at all, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_047 changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat, on the best configuration. This cleanly tells us whether concat fusion helps the leading setup. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the largest untested design gap. Changing just one factor makes the result easy to interpret. The answer tells us which fusion to use in later tests of PCA RNA features and the ResNet50 image encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 3.5–4 GPU hours, since it uses the same multiprofile transformer and ViT-L setup. That is moderately expensive, but justified because it is the most likely candidate to improve on the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Changing a single component from that setup gave clear drops. Transformer beat avgpool (0.62 vs 0.42), weighted fusion beat concat (0.62 vs 0.21), and scVI beat scGPT (0.62 vs 0.52). The large gap between RNA encoders shows this choice matters a lot, yet the PCA_n2000 encoder is still untested. 2. This experiment keeps the winning backbone (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. It tests whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation can beat scVI, and it completes the RNA-encoder comparison within the best architecture. 3. Since the RNA encoder has shown the largest single-swap effect apart from fusion and aggregation, which are now settled, this is the most likely route to a new best within the remaining budget. Swapping the image encoder to ResNet50 can follow later as a cheaper check. Expected cost is moderate-to-high, about 3–4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_043, because it uses multiprofile transformer aggregation with ViT-L. PCA's larger 2000-dimensional input may add slightly to that.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1. Each one-factor change from it has scored worse: avgpool (0.42), concat (0.21), scGPT (0.52) and PCA (0.52). Single-profile was also lower (0.57). So scVI, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion look well supported. The image encoder has never been varied, though; every run used ViT-L. 2) Test: config_010 keeps all of config_043's settings and only swaps ViT-L for ResNet50. It shows whether the image backbone is a bottleneck or an untapped gain. 3) Why now: this is the last major untested axis next to the best configuration, so it has the best chance of beating 0.619 while also reducing uncertainty. With 3 experiments left, the answer narrows the remaining search. Expected cost is about the same as or a bit below config_043 (~3–4 GPU hours), since ResNet50 embeddings are smaller than ViT-L's.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Changing any single component from it made results worse. scGPT and PCA encoders gave about 0.52, ResNet50 gave 0.53, avgpool gave 0.42, concat fusion gave 0.21, and single-profile gave 0.57. The one design axis still untested is the modality setting, so we do not know whether the image branch adds accuracy or adds noise. 2. Test: config_027 keeps the strongest components (scVI n200 encoder and transformer multiprofile aggregation) but removes the image modality. This directly measures how much the image branch contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.619, the last experiments can shift toward unimodal or RNA-centric variants. If it falls well short, that confirms config_043 as the near-optimal design. 3. Why now: Every other single-factor change from the best setup has been ruled out, so this is the most informative remaining ablation. It also has a realistic chance of a new best, since weighted fusion beating concat suggests the model benefits from down-weighting one modality. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the 3.6 GPU hours of config_043 because no large ViT-L image features need to be processed.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is the cheap RNA-only scVI multiprofile transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc, 0.40 GPU h). The best multimodal run (config_043, 0.619) scored slightly lower on accuracy, slightly higher on F1 (0.610 vs 0.599), and cost 9x more. So adding images has not clearly helped. Two design choices look settled: transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin, and weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin. The RNA encoder is the main open lever. In multimodal runs scVI beat PCA (0.523) and scGPT (0.520), but those comparisons are confounded by the image branch and fusion. 2) Test: config_022 swaps scVI for PCA-2000 inside the winning RNA-only multiprofile transformer setup. It checks whether a higher-dimensional linear RNA representation does better once image fusion is removed, and so whether the encoder ranking holds in the RNA-only setting. 3) Why now: of the remaining options, the RNA-only multiprofile transformer variants (PCA or scGPT) are the most plausible way to beat 0.629. PCA was marginally ahead of scGPT in the multimodal comparison and avoids foundation-model embedding overhead. Expected cost is low, about 0.4-0.6 GPU h, similar to config_027 and far below multimodal runs, which keeps the total budget small. One experiment will still remain to exploit the answer.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with a transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc), slightly ahead of its multimodal weighted counterpart (0.619). The image branch seems to add little. Several factors look clearly harmful: avgpool cost about 0.20 accuracy, scgpt about 0.10, pca about 0.10 to 0.20, and concat fusion was catastrophic. The mildest penalty seen was singleprofile versus multiprofile in the multimodal setting, about 0.046. 2) This experiment tests whether the strongest RNA-only setup (scvi_n200) works as well or better without multiprofile aggregation. Without the image branch and aggregation noise, a simpler model could match or exceed config_027. 3) Since this is the final experiment, the other candidates near the best are weak bets. scgpt RNA-only, scvi avgpool and image-only all have direct evidence of larger drops. Among them, this option has the smallest expected gap to the current best, so it has the best chance of setting a new best. It should also be the cheapest option, likely under 0.4 GPU hours, comparable to or below config_027.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence on any axis: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. Priors from multimodal profiling suggest that combining RNA and image modalities, and aggregating over multiple profiles, both tend to improve accuracy. 2) config_004 tests that prior with a mid-range setup: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder, the strong imagenet_vit_l image encoder, cheap avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. It avoids the costliest components (scgpt, transformer aggregation) while keeping the likely highest-value ones. 3) It is a strong anchor result early in the budget. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, scgpt or PCA vs. scVI, weighted vs. concat fusion, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. Expected cost is moderate to high: multiprofile multimodal training with ViT-L features costs more than unimodal or single-profile runs, but avgpool and the 200-dim scVI input keep it below the transformer or scgpt variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool and concat reached 0.635 validation accuracy and 0.618 F1, at 4.49 GPU hours. Nothing else has been measured yet. 2) Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps every other setting the same. This gives a clean test of whether learned attention across profiles beats mean pooling. Aggregation is a major design choice and likely has a large effect on accuracy in multiprofile settings. 3) Why now: of the single-factor changes available, this one has the best chance of improving on the current best. Whatever the result, it tells us which aggregation to carry forward into later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_004, roughly 1.2 to 1.5 times or about 5.5 to 7 GPU hours, because transformer aggregation adds overhead. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. 1. Evidence: the best result is config_016 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Several single changes away from it did worse. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 gave 0.653. Using a single profile gave 0.632. Transformer aggregation gave 0.507. Weaker RNA encoders also did worse: scvi gave 0.635 and scgpt gave 0.422. The one design choice not yet tested on the best backbone is fusion type. Concat hurt scvi (0.635 to 0.421), but that is a single observation and the effect may depend on the encoder. 2. Test: config_040 keeps everything from config_016 and changes only weighted fusion to concat. This checks whether the stronger, higher-dimensional PCA features benefit from concat, and whether the concat penalty holds across encoders. 3. Why this is the best final experiment: with one run left, the realistic way to beat 0.721 is a one-factor change from the best configuration. The alternatives seem less likely to win. Image-only runs look weak given that scgpt+ViT with weighted fusion reached only 0.42, and transformer, ResNet50 and single-profile variants have already underperformed. The chance of beating 0.721 is modest given the scvi concat result, but it is the best remaining shot. Expected cost is about the same as config_016, roughly 7 GPU hours: mid-to-high for this study and cheaper than the ResNet50 multiprofile run.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion. The prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models should do best, because they combine complementary RNA and image signals across several profiles. 2) This run sets a strong baseline using choices that are usually reliable: scVI (200-dimensional) RNA embeddings, ImageNet ViT-L image features, simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Later runs can then vary one factor at a time against it: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, weighted vs. concat fusion, the RNA encoder, or dropping a modality. 3) It is likely close to the top-performing region, so it supports exploitation, and it also works as a reference point for exploration. Expected cost is moderate to high: multimodal multiprofile with the large ViT-L features, but cheaper than the transformer-aggregation versions because avgpool is used.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_029 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1 at 4.49 GPU hours. One point says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_023 keeps everything the same except the aggregation, which changes from avgpool to transformer. This is a clean single-variable test of how the multiple profiles are combined. Learned attention over profiles is a plausible large lever over simple mean pooling. 3) Why it is the best next step: it builds on the only known working setup while settling a key structural choice. That choice will then guide the later encoder, fusion and modality comparisons across the remaining 8 experiments. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_029 because transformer aggregation adds compute, roughly 5–6 GPU hours.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The two completed runs differ only in aggregation. Transformer aggregation (config_023) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Avgpool (config_029) reached 0.208 accuracy. This is strong evidence that transformer aggregation over multiple profiles matters most, so later runs should keep it. What we do not know is how much the image branch (ViT-L) adds on top of the scVI RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_004 keeps the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation, but drops the image modality. This isolates the image's contribution. If RNA-only comes close to 0.52, the remaining budget can focus on RNA encoders and transformer variants at lower cost. If it drops clearly, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important, and later runs can tune fusion and the image and RNA encoders within the multimodal transformer family. 3. Why this is the best next use: it settles a fundamental design question with a single controlled change. Expected cost is lower than the ~4.6 GPU-hour multimodal ViT-L runs, likely around 2–3 GPU hours, because there is no large image encoder to process.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 for the same multimodal scVI + ViT-L concat setup). The cheap RNA-only scVI transformer model (0.532 accuracy, 0.516 F1, 0.40 GPU h) matches or slightly beats the multimodal concat version (0.520, 4.65 GPU h), so the image branch with concat fusion adds no measurable value so far. The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored, and it seems to drive most of the signal. 2) Test: config_039 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for scGPT embeddings. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Rationale: It probes an important untested design choice at very low cost (about 0.4-0.6 GPU h, roughly a tenth of a multimodal ViT-L run). The result will tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later, more expensive multimodal experiments, for example with weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 in the otherwise identical multimodal pair). The cheap RNA-only scVI transformer model (0.532 accuracy, 0.516 F1, 0.40 GPU h) currently matches or slightly beats the far costlier multimodal ViT-L version (0.520, 4.65 GPU h). So the RNA encoder looks like the main lever. scGPT does poorly (0.332), but pca_n2000 is untested. 2) This experiment holds the best cheap setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. That isolates the RNA encoder choice, which has the largest observed effect so far. 3) It should be cheap, about 0.4–0.6 GPU h, roughly 10x less than a multimodal run. If PCA beats scVI, it becomes the base for the remaining multimodal and fusion runs, such as the PCA multimodal transformer configs. If it does not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fusion type and image encoder choices (weighted fusion, ResNet50) with scVI.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 for the same multimodal setup). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.532, versus 0.471 for PCA and 0.332 for scGPT). The current best is rna_only scVI with a transformer (0.532). The matching multimodal concat model, using ViT-L, scored slightly lower (0.520, F1 0.479 vs 0.516). This suggests that concat fusion fails to benefit from the image modality and may add noise. The key open question is whether weighted fusion lets the model down-weight or properly calibrate the image stream and push multimodal performance above RNA-only. This experiment changes only the fusion method relative to config_023 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer), so the comparison is clean. If weighted fusion helps, the remaining budget can exploit it, for example by trying the cheaper ResNet50 image encoder with weighted fusion. If it does not help, we can stop spending on expensive multimodal runs and refine RNA-only setups. Expected cost is high, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_023. It is justified because it is the most likely route to beating the current best.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation is critical, since avgpool reached 0.21 while transformer reached about 0.52 under the same multimodal setup. scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.532 vs 0.471 for PCA and 0.332 for scGPT). Adding ImageNet ViT-L images has not beaten RNA-only scVI (0.520 vs 0.532), though weighted fusion gave a slightly better F1 than concat (0.498 vs 0.479). Untested: whether a different image encoder makes the image branch useful. 2) Test: this keeps the best components (scVI, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps ViT-L for ResNet50. It checks whether ResNet50 image features add information on top of RNA and can beat the RNA-only best. 3) Why now: no other single change is as likely to beat 0.532, and it resolves the main open question, which image encoder to use. Expected cost: moderate, likely somewhat below the ViT-L multimodal runs (about 3–4 GPU hours) since ResNet50 features are smaller, but well above the RNA-only runs (about 0.4 GPU hours).

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_044 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1. Switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 gave a gain of about 0.08. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.52 vs 0.21). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.53 vs 0.47 for PCA and 0.33 for scGPT in RNA-only runs). With ViT-L, concat and weighted fusion gave the same accuracy (0.520 each), so fusion choice is unresolved and could matter for ResNet50. 2) Test: config_026 keeps every winning component (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the fusion to concat. This is a clean single-variable check of whether concat can beat weighted fusion with ResNet50. 3) Why now: it is the most plausible untested configuration to exceed 0.599, since the alternatives swap in weaker components (PCA or scGPT encoders, avgpool, or dropping the RNA modality). It also leaves 2 experiments for follow-up. Expected cost is relatively high, similar to config_044 at about 6 GPU hours, because it is a multiprofile multimodal transformer run. That cost is justified because it is the likeliest candidate for the best result.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Two choices look settled. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by a wide margin (0.52 vs 0.21 with ViT-L), and ResNet50 beats ViT-L in multimodal runs (0.60–0.71 vs 0.52). Concat beat weighted fusion with ResNet50, though that rests on one pair of runs. scGPT is clearly weak (0.33 RNA-only). The main open question near the optimum is the RNA encoder. PCA trailed scVI in the RNA-only setting (0.47 vs 0.53), but that gap is modest and has never been tested alongside the strong ResNet50 image features. The gap could shrink, or PCA's richer 2000-dim input could complement the image features under concat fusion. Test: config_027 keeps the winning backbone (ResNet50, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This is a clean one-factor comparison against the best configuration. Why now: it has the highest plausible chance of matching or beating 0.706. The alternatives look worse. Single-profile removes the aggregation step that has proven critical. Image-only drops the RNA modality, which likely contributes. Avgpool and scGPT variants are clearly inferior. Expected cost: high, about 5–6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_026 or slightly more because of the larger PCA input. This is justified because it is a credible candidate for the best configuration, and the result will tell us what to run with the final experiment.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Several design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation strongly beats avgpool (0.52 vs 0.21). scVI is the best RNA encoder, and scGPT and PCA trail it. ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L, because ViT-L multimodal runs only matched RNA-only (about 0.52), while adding ResNet50 lifted accuracy to 0.60-0.71. The open question is how much of the gain comes from ResNet50 image features alone, since no image-only run has been tested. Test: config_028 (image-only, ResNet50, transformer) isolates the image contribution under the best aggregation setting. If the image signal dominates, it could match or beat the multimodal result. If not, it confirms that fusion with scVI is needed and that config_026 is the final best. Why this run: other variants of the best configuration are poor bets. scGPT, PCA, avgpool and weighted fusion have each already underperformed, so no single-change variant has a strong expected upside. config_028 offers a plausible though modest chance of improvement while answering a key design question. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-5 GPU hours, cheaper than the 5-7 GPU hour multimodal ResNet50 runs because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no information yet about modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. Prior expectation is that combining RNA and image data and aggregating several profiles per sample should do best, but this is unverified. 2. What it tests: this run sets a strong, representative baseline for the most promising region (multimodal, multiprofile). It uses moderate components: scVI-200 RNA embeddings, ResNet50 image features, average-pool aggregation and concat fusion. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it, such as ViT-L versus ResNet50, transformer versus avgpool aggregation, weighted versus concat fusion, or a different RNA encoder. Single-modality or single-profile runs can also be compared against it. 3. Why now: it targets the likely best area while keeping cost moderate. Multiprofile aggregation and multimodal input add training time, but compact scVI embeddings, ResNet50 and simple avgpool avoid the extra cost of ViT-L features or transformer aggregation. This gives an informative, cost-efficient anchor for the remaining 9 experiments. Expected relative cost: medium, below the ViT-L and transformer multiprofile variants and above the single-modality and single-profile runs.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. That gives a solid baseline, but we know nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. That makes it a clean one-factor comparison. The image encoder is one of the choices most likely to move accuracy, because stronger pretrained visual representations often help with morphological profiling. 3. Why now: whichever encoder wins can be fixed for the rest of the search, which shrinks the remaining space roughly in half. Later experiments can then test aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted) and the RNA encoder. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 7.27 GPU-hour baseline, likely about 1.2–1.5x, because of the larger ViT-L representations. That is justified by the potential gain and by how much it clarifies the search.
