1) Evidence: the two runs differ only in image encoder. ResNet50 reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1, while ImageNet ViT-L reached only 0.422 and 0.405. That is a large gap, so ResNet50 is the clear image-encoder choice for now. The other design choices (aggregation, fusion, RNA encoder) remain untested. 2) Test: config_012 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ResNet50, concat fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention across profiles improves on simple averaging. Aggregation is likely one of the most influential remaining choices for multiprofile models. 3) Why now: it exploits the strong ResNet50 result while settling an important open design question with a clean one-variable comparison. Fusion and RNA-encoder variants can follow in later runs. Expected cost: somewhat higher than config_022's 7.27 GPU hours, roughly 8-10 GPU hours, because transformer aggregation adds overhead. That is justified since this is a plausible route to the top accuracy.

1) Evidence: Three runs all used the scVI RNA encoder. Within those runs, ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L (0.72 vs 0.42), and avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.72 vs 0.54), with F1 tracking accuracy each time. The best so far is config_022 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat, 0.721). The RNA encoder is the largest untested axis that could still give a substantial gain. 2) Test: config_031 keeps the winning ResNet50, avgpool and concat choices and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. A pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding may carry richer signal than the 200-dim scVI latent. 3) Why now: Fusion type (weighted vs concat) is likely a smaller tweak, so I will test it afterwards on whichever RNA encoder wins. Settling the encoder question first lets the remaining 5 experiments exploit the better encoder (e.g., scGPT or PCA with weighted fusion). Expected cost: similar to config_022, about 6–8 GPU hours, since it uses the same multiprofile avgpool ResNet50 pipeline and only a different precomputed RNA embedding.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_022 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Swapping single components hurt it clearly. The transformer aggregator gave 0.537, the ViT-L image encoder gave 0.422, and scGPT in place of scVI gave 0.632. Fusion type is the one important design axis with no data at all, since every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_040 is config_022 with only concat replaced by weighted fusion. This cleanly measures the effect of fusion on the strongest base, and it could improve on 0.721 directly. 3. Why now: a one-factor exploitation step on the best configuration is the most efficient way to resolve a key open design choice. Swapping in the PCA RNA encoder (config_011) is the natural follow-up. Expected cost: similar to config_022, roughly 5-7 GPU hours, since it uses the same multiprofile multimodal architecture with only a light fusion change.

1) Evidence: config_022 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat, multiprofile) leads at 0.721 acc and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it lowered accuracy: scGPT gave 0.632, ViT-L gave 0.422, transformer aggregation gave 0.537 and weighted fusion gave 0.518. So resnet50, avgpool and concat look like the right choices. The main untested axis is the third RNA encoder, pca_n2000. The scvi-to-scGPT drop of about 9 points shows the RNA encoder strongly affects accuracy. 2) This run keeps the best backbone and swaps only scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. It tests whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation can beat scVI. 3) It is the most direct remaining path to exceed 0.72, and the one-factor change keeps the result easy to interpret. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 5–7.5 GPU hours, similar to config_022. The 2000-dim input adds little next to the resnet50 multiprofile pipeline, and it avoids the expensive ViT-L or transformer variants that have already underperformed.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-axis change from it lowered accuracy. Switching to the ViT-L image encoder gave 0.422, transformer aggregation gave 0.537, weighted fusion gave 0.518, scGPT gave 0.632 and PCA gave 0.688 (at 36 GPU hours). Encoder, aggregation and fusion choices are now fairly well mapped around this optimum. The main untested question is the model setting: does the image branch actually add value, or does it add noise? The large swings when only the image side or the fusion changed hint that image features may sometimes hurt. 2. Test: config_036 is the same multiprofile scVI avgpool pipeline with RNA only. It directly measures how much the ResNet50 image modality contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.72, the remaining runs should focus on RNA-only variants. If it falls clearly short, multimodal is confirmed, and the last runs can test single-profile versus multi-profile around config_022. 3. Why now: it resolves the largest remaining design uncertainty at low cost. Dropping the image encoder should make it among the cheapest runs, likely about 2–4 GPU hours, well below config_022's 7.3.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. The rest of the history narrows the choices. scVI beat both scGPT and PCA. ResNet50 beat ViT-L. Avgpool beat the transformer. Concat beat weighted fusion. RNA-only scVI nearly matched the best at 0.713, with slightly higher F1. The only major design choice never tested is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. Test: config_005 keeps the best-performing components (scVI, ResNet50, concat) and switches to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether per-profile modeling does better. Why now: the other choices already lean toward weaker options, so this has the best chance of beating 0.721 while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty. It also tells us how to spend the last two runs, either on a singleprofile follow-up such as RNA-only or weighted fusion, or by returning to multiprofile variants. Expected cost: moderate and likely below config_022's 7.3 GPU hours, since it skips multiprofile aggregation, though above RNA-only runs. It should be far cheaper than the PCA-based runs, which cost about 36 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat (0.7207). RNA-only scVI with avgpool is close behind (0.7131) and has higher F1 (0.695 vs 0.681), at only 0.10 GPU hours. So the image branch adds little, and the RNA representation looks like the main driver. Among multimodal runs, PCA-2000 came second (0.688), ahead of scGPT (0.632). Transformer aggregation (0.537) and weighted fusion (0.518) clearly hurt, so those directions are poor bets. 2. Test: whether the higher-dimensional PCA-2000 RNA features, without image features possibly adding noise, can match or beat scVI in the strong RNA-only avgpool setup. This clarifies which RNA encoder is best when RNA carries most of the signal. 3. Why now: it is the most plausible untested route to a new best that does not rely on design choices already shown to hurt. RNA-only training is very cheap, likely around 0.1–1 GPU hours, far below any multimodal run such as the 36 GPU hours for multimodal PCA. It also informs the final experiment: if it does well, the last slot can try PCA RNA-only variants; if not, scVI remains the anchor.

1. Evidence: The best result is config_022 at 0.7207 accuracy (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat). RNA-only scvi_n200 with avgpool (config_036) is close behind at 0.7131 and has higher F1 (0.695 vs 0.681). So the scvi RNA representation drives most of the performance, and the image branch adds little. The other tested choices clearly underperformed: weighted fusion, ViT-L, single-profile input, and PCA or scGPT encoders. The transformer's large drop (0.537) was seen only in a multimodal setting, where it had to aggregate high-dimensional image features. 2. Test: This experiment checks whether transformer aggregation over low-dimensional scvi RNA profiles alone can capture cross-profile structure that avgpool misses, and so beat the current best. 3. Why this one: It is the final experiment, so only a possible new best matters. The incremental multimodal variants left mostly use components already shown to hurt. config_016 (RNA-only scGPT) is unlikely to win because scGPT trailed scvi by about 9 points in the multimodal comparison. The transformer remains the main uncertain design choice in the strong RNA-only branch, though its poor multimodal result means a gain is far from assured. Expected cost is very low, likely under 1 GPU hour, compared with 4–36 GPU hours for multimodal runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. These are modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. My prior is that multimodal multiprofile models with learned aggregation are the most likely to score highest, but this is unverified. 2) What it tests: config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA, resnet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a strong but moderately priced anchor in the likely-best region. Its results will serve as a reference point for later one-factor contrasts: concat vs. weighted fusion (config_002), avgpool vs. transformer aggregation (config_050), ViT-L vs. resnet50 image encoder (config_003), scGPT vs. scVI RNA encoder (config_047), and unimodal or single-profile ablations. 3) Why now: it puts the first run where the best accuracy is most likely to be found, while avoiding the heaviest option (scGPT + ViT-L). This leaves budget to test whether larger encoders are worth their cost. Expected relative cost: medium-high. Multiprofile multimodal training with transformer aggregation costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs, but the compact scVI and resnet50 encoders make it noticeably cheaper than the ViT-L or scGPT variants.

Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.537 accuracy and 0.518 F1, so nothing is known yet about which design choices matter. Test: config_003 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. The encoder is likely among the highest-impact choices, and a larger pretrained ViT often gives richer morphology features than ResNet50, so this has real upside for the best accuracy. Why now: it is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best and resolves a key uncertainty early, leaving 8 experiments to follow up on RNA encoder, fusion and aggregation. Expected cost: higher than config_004, roughly 1.3-2x its 6.22 GPU hours (about 8-12 GPU hours), because ViT-L is a larger image encoder. I accept that cost because the image backbone is plausibly decisive for the top configuration.

1) Evidence: In two runs that differed only in the image encoder (both scVI-200 RNA, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), ImageNet ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50. Accuracy was 0.599 vs 0.537 and F1 was 0.578 vs 0.518. ViT-L was also cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours). This is only one comparison, but the gap is large enough to treat ViT-L as the working image encoder. The biggest untested design choice is the RNA encoder. 2) Test: this run keeps the best configuration (config_003) fixed and swaps only the RNA encoder, from scVI-200 to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves multimodal accuracy. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder probably has a larger effect than fusion type or aggregation, so settling it early guides the remaining 7 runs. If scGPT wins, later runs can build on it. If not, scVI stays the base for fusion and aggregation tests. Expected cost is moderate, roughly similar to or slightly above config_003's 3.6 GPU hours, since scGPT embeddings are larger. That should still be well below the ResNet50 multiprofile run.

1) Evidence: With the other settings held fixed (multiprofile, transformer, weighted), imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 (0.599 vs 0.537 accuracy), and vit_l was also cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU hours). The RNA encoder had the largest effect seen so far: scvi_n200 reached 0.599 and scgpt only 0.411, with F1 following the same pattern. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, is still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (vit_l, transformer, weighted) and swaps scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. That isolates whether a different RNA representation can beat scvi on the factor with the biggest observed impact. 3) Settling the RNA encoder first matters because it is the dominant axis. Fusion (concat) and aggregation (avgpool) can be tuned in later experiments on top of the winning encoder. Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_003 at about 3 to 4 GPU hours. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add slight overhead, but it should stay well below the resnet50 run.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.599 vs 0.411 for scgpt and 0.208 for pca_n2000 with the ViT-L/transformer/weighted backbone). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 under scvi (0.599 vs 0.537), and it was also cheaper (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU h). The best configuration so far is config_003 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + weighted). Aggregation, fusion and profile setting have not been varied yet. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether multiprofile aggregation needs a learned transformer or whether simple pooling does as well or better. 3) Aggregation is a major untested design choice. Avgpool should cost less than transformer aggregation, roughly 3 GPU h or a bit under, compared with 3.60 for config_003. The result will decide whether the remaining budget should exploit transformer or avgpool when testing fusion (concat vs weighted) and single- vs multiprofile variants.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_003 (scVI-n200 + ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1. One-factor comparisons against it all lost. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 gave 0.537. Swapping scVI for scGPT gave 0.411, and swapping it for PCA gave 0.208. Swapping transformer for avgpool gave 0.512. Every experiment so far used weighted fusion, so fusion is the one design choice with no evidence at all. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the best setup and changes only weighted fusion to concat. This isolates the fusion effect and either beats the current best or confirms that weighted fusion should be kept. 3. Why now: It is the most direct way to improve on the top configuration and resolves the last unknown in its design. Expected cost is moderate, about 3.5–5 GPU hours. That is similar to config_003 (3.6 h) and far cheaper than the ResNet50 run (6.2 h). Concat fusion should add little overhead, which leaves budget for later image-only or single-profile checks.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_003 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.599 accuracy. Every single-factor change from it scored lower. Swapping the RNA encoder had the largest effect: scgpt dropped to 0.41 and pca_n2000 to 0.21, even with the strong ViT image encoder. Swapping the image encoder (resnet50, 0.54), aggregation (avgpool, 0.51) or fusion (concat, 0.57) mattered less. So the RNA representation appears to drive performance, but no unimodal baseline has been run. We therefore don't know whether the image branch adds signal or adds noise. 2) Test: config_018 is the RNA-only counterpart of the best setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer). It shows whether multimodal fusion gives a real gain or whether a simpler RNA-only model matches or beats 0.599. That result decides whether the last two experiments should refine fusion or drop the image branch. 3) Why now: model setting is the largest untested design choice, and this experiment resolves it while staying close to the best-known configuration. Expected cost is relatively low, probably about 2–3 GPU hours, since it skips image feature processing and fusion. That should be cheaper than the multimodal runs (about 2.9–6.2 GPU hours).

Evidence: the best result so far is the cheapest run, RNA-only scVI multiprofile transformer (config_018: 0.632 acc, 0.607 F1, 0.40 GPU h). Every multimodal variant did worse, so image fusion seems to add noise. Within multimodal runs, scVI was clearly the best RNA encoder over scGPT and PCA, and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.599 vs 0.512). The one major design choice never tested is profile setting: every run so far was multiprofile. This experiment tests RNA-only scVI with a single profile, which isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether a simpler model does better. It is the best use of the budget because it targets the main remaining uncertainty around the current best configuration, and it should be the cheapest run so far (likely under 0.4 GPU h, since there is no aggregation and no image branch). Either outcome guides the last two picks: if single profile wins, refine around it; if not, try other variants of the RNA multiprofile setup.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with the scvi_n200 encoder and transformer aggregation (config_018, 0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1), at only 0.40 GPU hours. Adding image encoders has consistently hurt accuracy (best multimodal 0.599), while also costing far more compute. Among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 clearly beats scgpt and pca_n2000. Multiprofile beats singleprofile for RNA-only (0.632 vs 0.586). 2) Test: config_016 is the only remaining scvi_n200 RNA-only multiprofile variant. It swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. In the multimodal runs avgpool did worse than transformer (0.512 vs 0.599), but that comparison may be confounded by the image branch. A simpler pooling step could generalize as well or better on the RNA-only pathway, so this run checks whether the aggregation choice still matters there. 3) Why now: it is the one remaining neighbor of the current best along a single design axis, so it tests the most promising region with the remaining budget. Multimodal and image-only options are unlikely to beat 0.632 given the evidence so far. Expected cost is very low, roughly 0.3–0.4 GPU hours, similar to or below config_018 and much cheaper than any multimodal run.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, for only 0.40 GPU hours. Adding images (0.599 to 0.537), switching to avgpool aggregation (0.42 to 0.51) or dropping to single-profile (0.586) all lowered accuracy. The one choice not yet tested in the winning RNA-only transformer setup is the RNA encoder. The only scGPT evidence comes from a multimodal run (0.41), where weighted fusion with images may have masked the encoder's own quality. 2. Test: config_030 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. This shows whether scGPT can beat scVI when it is not combined with images. 3. Why this is the best last experiment: No remaining option is likely to beat 0.632. Multimodal and single-profile variants have consistently underperformed RNA-only multiprofile, and PCA collapsed to 0.21. This is the cheapest remaining variant of the strongest design that is still plausible, so it is a low-cost final chance at improvement. Expected cost is similar to config_018 (about 0.4–0.6 GPU hours, possibly a little more for the larger scGPT embeddings). That is far cheaper than any multimodal option, which cost 3–6 GPU hours.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single- vs multi-profile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor in the search space. It uses both modalities, multiprofile input, the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat), a mid-range RNA encoder (scVI) and the generally stronger image backbone (ViT-L). It gives a reasonable estimate of achievable performance without committing to the more complex transformer or weighted-fusion options. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Every later experiment can change one factor from this anchor. Dropping a modality, switching to singleprofile, changing an encoder, or trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion would each attribute a performance change to a single design decision. This is more informative per experiment than starting from a corner of the space such as the simplest unimodal baseline.

Evidence: we have only one result. The multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. One run cannot tell us whether combining modalities helps or which modality drives performance. Test: config_005 is the RNA-only version of the same setup (same scvi_n200 encoder, multiprofile, avgpool). Changing only the modality isolates how much of the 0.332 comes from RNA alone and how much the image branch and fusion add. Why now: modality is the most basic design choice, and most of the remaining search space (36 of 51 configurations) is multimodal. Knowing early whether the image branch adds value tells us whether to keep spending budget on image encoders and fusion options or to focus on RNA encoders and aggregation.

Evidence: with the same scVI RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, adding ViT-L image features through concat fusion dropped validation accuracy from 0.635 (RNA-only, config_005) to 0.332 (config_036). F1 fell by a similar amount (0.618 to 0.315). The open question is whether images are uninformative or noisy, or whether naive concat lets the high-dimensional image embedding swamp the RNA signal. Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If accuracy recovers to or above the RNA-only level, fusion is the bottleneck and the weighted multimodal branch is worth exploiting. If it stays low, that points to the image modality or encoder as the problem, and the search can focus on RNA-only variants (encoder, transformer aggregation) or image-encoder checks. Why now: this single controlled change resolves the biggest design uncertainty so far, whether multimodality can help at all. That decides how much of the remaining budget belongs to the large multimodal half of the search space.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.635 accuracy (F1 0.618). Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features to the same setup lowered accuracy, to 0.540 with weighted fusion and 0.332 with concat fusion. So the image branch appears to hurt rather than help, and weighted fusion seems to reduce that damage, likely by down-weighting images. 2. Test: we have no image-only baseline, so we cannot tell whether the image features carry little useful signal or whether the fusion method is the problem. Image-only ViT-L with avgpool uses the same encoder and aggregation as the multimodal runs, so it isolates the image modality's standalone value. 3. Why now: multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. If image-only is near chance, we can drop most multimodal configurations and focus the budget on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it is reasonably strong, fusion design is the bottleneck, and further fusion and aggregation experiments are justified. Either result removes a lot of uncertainty about where to spend the remaining budget.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The single-modality models with avgpool score about 0.63 each (RNA 0.635, image 0.632). Multimodal fusion with avgpool falls well below them: 0.540 with weighted fusion and 0.332 with concat. So weighted fusion beats concat, but fusion as tested hurts rather than helps. It is unclear whether the bottleneck is avgpool aggregation of multiprofile inputs or fusion itself. 2. What this tests: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_037. It keeps scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l and the better weighted fusion fixed. This is a controlled test of whether a learned set aggregator lets multimodal models match or beat the single-modality baselines. 3. Why it is the best next use: Whether multimodal models can outperform single-modality ones at all is the central question of the study. This one experiment informs both the aggregation choice and whether further multimodal configurations are worth budget. If it improves substantially, transformer aggregation becomes the direction to exploit. If not, the problem points to fusion or encoders, which would redirect the next experiments.

1) Evidence: The two unimodal avgpool baselines are the strongest results so far (RNA-only scVI 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1, image-only ViT-L 0.632 / 0.607). Multimodal fusion has not beaten either one. Concat did badly (0.33), weighted did better (0.54), and switching avgpool to transformer aggregation raised weighted-fusion multimodal from 0.54 to 0.59, with F1 rising alongside it. 2) Test: config_006 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This shows whether the transformer gain carries over to a unimodal model or depends on the multimodal setting. 3) Value: it is a one-variable change from the current best result, so it is the most likely next step to set a new top accuracy. Either way, it tells us whether aggregation is a major design lever, which affects how we should prioritize the many remaining multimodal and image-only configurations.

1) Evidence so far: the best results come from unimodal avgpool models, RNA-only scVI at 0.635 and image-only ViT-L at 0.632. Every multimodal fusion tried with scVI plus ViT-L has done worse than either single modality: concat 0.33, weighted 0.54, weighted with transformer 0.59. For RNA, avgpool also beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.599). The biggest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder, since only scVI has been tested and pca_n2000 and scGPT are unexplored. 2) This experiment swaps scVI for scGPT and keeps everything else matched to the current best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Comparing it directly with config_005 shows whether the choice of RNA representation matters, and whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3) This is the best use of the next run because it isolates one high-impact, untested design choice inside a strong, well-understood baseline. More multimodal fusion runs look risky given their consistent underperformance. The result will also guide which RNA encoder to carry into any later multimodal or aggregation experiments.

1) Evidence: the best results so far are unimodal multiprofile models with avgpool: RNA-only scVI at 0.635 and image-only ViT-L at 0.632. Multimodal fusion has not beaten either. Weighted fusion beats concat, and transformer aggregation helped weighted fusion but slightly hurt RNA-only. scGPT was weaker than scVI. However, every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so we do not yet know whether multiprofile aggregation itself adds value. 2) This experiment runs RNA-only scVI in the singleprofile setting. It is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best, config_005, and shows how much the profile setting matters. 3) The profile setting is a major untested design axis that conditions how we read every aggregation and fusion result. A single controlled run on the strongest encoder resolves it efficiently. That is a better use of the budget than another small fusion or aggregation variant.

1. Evidence: The single-modality baselines are strong and similar: scVI RNA-only reaches 0.635 and ViT image-only reaches 0.632 (multiprofile, avgpool). Every multimodal run tested so far has done worse than either baseline: concat 0.33, weighted 0.54, transformer+weighted 0.59. These failures all used multiprofile aggregation. For RNA-only, single-profile (0.619) was close to multiprofile (0.635), so aggregation is not obviously needed. 2. Question: This run uses the best encoder pair (scVI + ViT-L) with the better fusion method (weighted) in the single-profile setting, with no aggregation. It tests whether the multimodal shortfall comes from fusion itself or from how fusion interacts with multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why now: This is the largest unresolved question in the study. If single-profile multimodal beats about 0.635, there is a clear new direction to exploit. If it also falls short, that points to fusion as the bottleneck, and remaining runs should go to single-modality refinements. Filling in config_038 (transformer+concat) would only refine a fusion method that already looks weak.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_035 (singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It beats every RNA-only and image-only run, so singleprofile multimodal with weighted fusion looks like the promising region. Two other questions already have some evidence. On fusion, weighted clearly beat concat in multiprofile (0.54 vs 0.33). On RNA encoder, scvi beat scgpt (0.635 vs 0.530). The image encoder, however, has never been varied: every image run so far used imagenet_vit_l, and resnet50 is completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_029 keeps the best setup and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This gives a clean one-factor comparison against config_035. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder choice affects about half of the remaining configurations, so resolving it is worth more than a fusion test (config_034), where the evidence already favours weighted. Because it stays in the best-performing region, it also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about whether combining RNA and image data helps, whether using multiple profiles helps, or which encoders and fusion methods work best. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-complexity multimodal anchor: scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input, average pooling and concat fusion. scVI is a common, efficient RNA representation, and avgpool and concat are the simplest choices for aggregation and fusion. It gives a reasonably strong first baseline whose result can later be compared one factor at a time with RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031) and other encoders. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Starting from a central point in the design space makes each later experiment a clean single-variable comparison. It also has a fair chance of performing well right away, which balances learning about the design space with finding a good configuration.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. We have no reference point yet, so we cannot tell whether the image branch adds value. 2. Test: config_005 removes only the image modality and keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This single-factor ablation directly measures how much the resnet50 image branch contributes. 3. Why now: Most of the search space is multimodal, so knowing early whether fusion beats RNA alone decides where the remaining budget should go. If multimodal clearly wins, later experiments can focus on image encoder, aggregation and fusion choices. If not, they should prioritise RNA encoder and aggregation.

1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion dropped accuracy sharply, from 0.650 (RNA-only) to 0.422. F1 fell by a similar amount (0.628 to 0.405). That is a large gap, not noise. It is still unclear whether the image modality is harmful in itself or whether naive concatenation lets weak or noisy image features swamp the RNA signal. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) and holds the RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. It therefore cleanly tests whether learned modality weighting can recover or exceed RNA-only performance. 3) Fusion is a key design axis across all 24 multimodal configurations remaining. Settling whether weighted fusion fixes the multimodal deficit tells us whether to keep investing in multimodal setups or pivot toward RNA-only variants, such as different encoders or transformer aggregation. A one-variable comparison against an existing result makes it the most informative use of the next run.

Evidence: with scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, concat fusion did poorly (0.422 acc), while weighted fusion reached 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1. That is only marginally better than RNA-only avgpool (0.650 / 0.628). So weighted fusion clearly beats concat, but the image branch adds little so far. Aggregation is a major untested structural choice: every multiprofile run used avgpool, and transformer aggregation has never been tried. Test: config_033 changes only aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to the current best (config_031). This isolates whether learned set aggregation over profiles improves on mean pooling. Why now: the answer applies to all multiprofile configurations, whichever encoders are used. It also exploits the best-known fusion choice, so it has good odds of a new best while resolving a key uncertainty. Encoder swaps (scGPT, ViT-L) remain good follow-ups once the aggregation choice is settled.

1) Evidence so far: with scVI RNA features, ResNet50 image features and multiprofile input, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.653 vs 0.422 accuracy). Avgpool aggregation also beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.653 vs 0.507). However, the best multimodal result is essentially tied with RNA-only (0.653/0.628 vs 0.650/0.628 accuracy/F1). So with ResNet50, the image branch adds almost nothing, and the value of the image encoder is the main open question. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and changes only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. That cleanly tests whether a stronger image representation lets multimodal fusion outperform RNA-only. 3) Changing one factor relative to the current best builds on the strongest evidence while resolving a key uncertainty. A gain would point the search toward ViT-L multimodal configurations. No gain would suggest the RNA encoder is the more important lever, and the next step would be comparing scGPT and PCA.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Every run so far has used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that setting, three patterns are fairly consistent. Weighted fusion strongly beats concat (0.653 vs 0.422). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.653 vs 0.507). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.653 vs 0.586). The best multimodal run (config_031) is only slightly better than RNA-only scVI (0.650), so the RNA representation appears to drive most of the performance. The RNA encoder choice is also the largest design axis we have not yet tested. 2) What this tests: Swapping scVI for scGPT while keeping the best-performing pipeline (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves accuracy and F1. 3) Why this is the best next run: It explores a major untested factor while exploiting the strongest known setup, so it could either produce a new best configuration or confirm that scVI is the right RNA encoder to keep for further refinement.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Within the multiprofile setting, several choices look settled for now. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.653 vs 0.422). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.653 vs 0.507). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.586). scVI is slightly ahead of scGPT (0.632). However, every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a major design choice we have not tested at all. 2) What this tests: config_029 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, where aggregation does not apply. Compared directly with config_031, it shows whether aggregating multiple profiles helps or whether a single profile does as well. 3) Why it is the best use of the next experiment: it is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best on a high-impact, completely unexplored dimension. Whichever way it comes out, it decides whether the rest of the budget should go to multiprofile aggregation variants or to the simpler singleprofile branch. It also keeps the strongest known components, so it has a reasonable chance of performing competitively.

1. Evidence: the best multimodal run, config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 accuracy), barely beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool, config_005 (0.650). This suggests the RNA representation carries most of the signal. Within this pipeline, the choices that have been varied each lowered performance: concat fusion (0.42), transformer aggregation (0.51), single-profile input (0.54) and ViT-L in place of ResNet50 (0.59). Swapping scVI for scGPT changed little (0.632). The PCA_n2000 RNA encoder has never been tested, so the RNA encoder is the least-explored design choice that seems to matter most. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best pipeline (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps in PCA_n2000. It is a one-variable comparison against config_031 (scVI) and config_043 (scGPT). It will show whether a simple high-dimensional PCA input matches or beats the learned embeddings, using accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: it fills the largest remaining gap on the most influential factor while staying inside the strongest known setup. That makes it both exploratory and plausibly competitive. The result will also tell us whether the remaining PCA-based configurations are worth spending budget on.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best multimodal result (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005; 0.650 / 0.628). Concat fusion collapsed to 0.422. Together this suggests weighted fusion may simply be down-weighting the image branch. No image-only baseline exists yet, so we do not know whether images carry useful signal at all. 2. What this tests: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (config_011) mirrors the best setup's image branch. It directly measures how much signal the image modality has on its own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: If image-only performance is weak, future experiments should focus on the RNA side (encoders such as scGPT vs scVI, and aggregation). If it is reasonably strong, the near-zero fusion gain means fusion design is the bottleneck and worth exploring. This one experiment resolves a key uncertainty that shapes the rest of the search, rather than adding another small variation to the multimodal grid.

1. Evidence: The best multimodal run (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005, 0.650 / 0.628). Image-only is weak (0.421). This suggests the image modality adds little, but that conclusion rests on a single paired comparison. scGPT is the second-strongest RNA encoder, at 0.632 in the weighted multimodal setting. 2. Test: Running scGPT RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool creates a second matched RNA-only vs multimodal pair (against config_043). It shows whether adding images helps, hurts or does nothing for a different RNA encoder. It also gives a clean scGPT vs scVI comparison in the RNA-only setting. 3. Why now: Whether the image branch matters is the most consequential open design question, since it decides whether the remaining budget should go to image and fusion variants or to RNA-side choices. This experiment checks that conclusion while staying close to the current best region, so it may also be competitive on accuracy.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about any design choice: modality, single vs. multi-profile, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is a central reference point. Each design choice can be isolated later by changing one factor at a time: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or a different encoder (config_018, config_036, config_042). 3) A plausible, mid-complexity configuration used as this hub makes every later experiment a clean one-factor comparison. That gets the most learning per experiment under the limited budget, while still having a reasonable chance of good accuracy.

1. Evidence: only one result exists. The multimodal model (scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell how much of that comes from the image branch versus the RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the same scVI encoder, the same multiprofile avgpool setup and the same aggregation, but removes images. It is a clean one-factor test of whether adding imaging improves accuracy. 3. Why now: modality is the highest-level design choice and decides how to spend the remaining budget. If RNA-only scores about the same, image encoder and fusion variants (ViT-L, weighted fusion) are unlikely to pay off, and effort should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it clearly drops, that confirms the multimodal direction and justifies exploring image encoders and fusion next.

Evidence: the multimodal scVI+ResNet50 avgpool concat model (0.435 acc, 0.423 F1) far outperforms the matched RNA-only model (0.208 acc). That gap suggests most of the signal may come from the image modality. What is still unknown is whether fusion adds anything beyond images alone. Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool completes a clean modality ablation, since every other setting matches the two runs already done. If it scores close to 0.435, the image encoder is the main driver, and the next budget should go to image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion type. If it scores clearly lower, RNA contributes complementary signal, and further searching over multimodal fusion and RNA encoders is justified. This single run decides where in the large multimodal grid the remaining budget is best spent.

1. Evidence: Image features carry most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.421 accuracy, while RNA-only (scVI) reached only 0.208. Multimodal concat improved slightly on image-only, to 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. This suggests RNA adds a small amount and the image representation is the main performance lever. Only ResNet50 has been tested, so the image encoder choice is the largest open question. 2. Test: This run changes one factor from the current best (config_030), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and concat stay fixed, so any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. 3. Why now: Because images dominate performance, the encoder choice is likely to matter most. This experiment both reduces uncertainty about an important design choice and could plausibly beat the current best. Aggregation, fusion and the RNA encoder are better tested after the image backbone is settled.

1. Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the same multimodal scVI/avgpool/concat setup raised accuracy from 0.435 to 0.725, with F1 rising in step from 0.423 to 0.685. RNA alone is weak (0.208), and adding it to ResNet50 gave only a small gain over image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). Aggregation has never been varied; every multiprofile run used avgpool. 2. Test: config_038 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging when the image features are strong. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a major untested design axis. Testing it on the strongest backbone is both informative and likely to perform well. Fusion type, RNA encoder choice and an image-only ViT-L ablation can follow once we know the better aggregator.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is a large jump over the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.435). But RNA-only scVI is weak (0.208), and with ResNet50, adding RNA barely beat image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). So it is unclear whether the gain comes from multimodal fusion or almost entirely from the ViT-L image encoder. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with avgpool differs from config_036 only by removing RNA. This isolates the RNA contribution when the image encoder is strong. 3) Why now: The answer decides how to spend the remaining budget. If ViT-L alone matches 0.725, RNA encoder and fusion choices matter little, and we should focus on image-side and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, RNA adds value, and exploring alternative RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and weighted fusion around config_036 becomes the priority. It is also a plausible high performer in its own right.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is far above image-only ViT-L (0.485) and the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.435), so the ViT-L multimodal avgpool direction looks strong. Transformer aggregation dropped accuracy sharply (0.332), so avgpool is the better choice for now. Fusion is the main gap: every multimodal run used concat, so we know nothing about weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_037 changes only concat to weighted on the best configuration. This isolates whether the fusion method matters, and it is a plausible way to improve on 0.725. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while settling a design choice that applies to every multimodal configuration. Whichever fusion wins can guide later RNA-encoder comparisons (scGPT, PCA) without confounding them with fusion.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. It clearly beats the image-only ViT-L run (0.485), which suggests the RNA signal helps once it is fused. Changing one factor at a time from config_036 lowered performance when aggregation became transformer (0.332) and when fusion became weighted (0.494). So avgpool plus concat looks like a strong backbone, though each comparison is still a single run. The main untested choice is the RNA encoder: every RNA run so far used scVI, and scVI alone was weak (0.208). Test: config_048 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only scVI for scGPT. This isolates the RNA encoder effect where it matters most. Why now: it is both a sensible exploitation step (scGPT is a pretrained foundation encoder that might improve on 0.725) and the best way to reduce uncertainty about a design axis with no data yet. That makes it a better use of budget than revisiting aggregation or fusion, which already have some evidence.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it all hurt badly: transformer aggregation (0.332), weighted fusion (0.494) and the scGPT encoder (0.227). Every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so the singleprofile option has never been tested. That makes profile setting the largest remaining uncertainty among the major design choices. Test: config_034 keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion method, and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether single-profile inputs do as well or better. The transformer-aggregation result hints that aggregation can hurt. Why now: it is a controlled one-factor comparison against the current best. Either it finds a better configuration or it confirms multiprofile+avgpool as the right choice and rules out half of the remaining search space. That is more informative per experiment than further fusion or encoder tweaks. Swapping in the PCA RNA encoder (config_024) is the natural next test after this.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it have each been tested and all lowered performance. Transformer aggregation gave 0.33, weighted fusion 0.49, the scGPT RNA encoder 0.23, and single-profile 0.52. The one main design axis still unexplored is the PCA (n2000) RNA encoder, which has never been tried in any setting. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the RNA encoder in config_036, from scVI to PCA. This shows whether scVI is specifically responsible for the strong multimodal gain, or whether any reasonable RNA representation combined with ViT-L, avgpool and concat works well. The large scGPT drop suggests the RNA encoder choice matters a lot. 3. Why now: This is a controlled one-factor comparison against the current best configuration. It closes the last untested RNA encoder option and has a real chance of matching or beating the best result. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than retesting axes that have already shown clear losses.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about which design choices matter. The open questions are whether multimodal fusion helps, which encoders are best, and whether multiprofile aggregation beats a single profile. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-range multimodal anchor using simple, commonly strong components: scvi_n200 for RNA, resnet50 for images, multiprofile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a baseline from which single factors can be changed in later runs (unimodal, encoder swaps, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, single profile). This gives clean ablations instead of scattered comparisons. 3. Why it is the best first run: It has reasonable odds of performing well, since it combines both modalities with multiple profiles using simple choices less likely to overfit. It also sits at the center of the design space, so each following experiment can isolate one decision. That makes it a sensible way to start under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists, config_030 (multimodal, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat). It reached 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1. One result gives no basis for judging which design choice drives performance. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes a single factor from that baseline by removing the image branch, keeping the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Comparing the two isolates how much the imaging modality adds over RNA alone. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion beats unimodal is the most important early question, because it decides whether much of the search space is worth pursuing. If RNA-only matches the baseline, later budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it drops clearly, the next experiments should go to image encoders and fusion strategies. This one-factor test reduces more uncertainty than tuning a secondary choice like aggregation or fusion type at this stage.

Evidence: with the same scVI encoder and avgpool aggregation, the concat multimodal model (config_030, accuracy 0.527, F1 0.510) scored below RNA-only (config_005, accuracy 0.573, F1 0.573). This suggests that naively adding ResNet50 image features may hurt, but one comparison is weak evidence. It is unclear whether the fault lies with the image modality itself or with the concat fusion strategy. Test: config_031 is identical to config_030 except it uses weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion closes the gap or beats RNA-only, the image modality is recoverable and fusion is the key lever. If it still underperforms, the image features themselves are likely the problem, which would point toward an image encoder or image-only check next. Why now: fusion is a design choice that affects half of all remaining multimodal configurations. A controlled one-variable comparison therefore reduces the most uncertainty per experiment while keeping a realistic chance of beating the current best.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.573 accuracy / 0.573 F1) clearly beats both multimodal scVI+ResNet50 runs (about 0.52-0.53). Concat and weighted fusion performed almost identically, so fusion type appears unimportant here. Adding ResNet50 image features seems to hurt rather than help. The RNA pathway is therefore the strongest lever so far, but only one RNA encoder (scVI) has been tested. 2) This run swaps scVI for scGPT and keeps everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). That isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Encoder choice is a major untested factor, and it will shape every later multimodal comparison. Testing it in the best-performing setting either improves the incumbent or shows that scVI is the right base. Either way it sharpens the search more than another fusion variant or a secondary aggregation tweak would.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (acc 0.573, F1 0.573). Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy to about 0.52–0.53 under both concat and weighted fusion, so the fusion method made little difference. scGPT was clearly weaker than scVI (0.512). Aggregation is the major design axis not yet tested: every run so far used avgpool. What this tests: config_006 keeps the strongest setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI) and changes only avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned aggregation across profiles adds value. Why it is the best next experiment: it builds directly on the current best configuration and could plausibly beat it. Either way, the result shows whether transformer aggregation is worth carrying into later multimodal or other-encoder experiments, which guides many of the remaining configurations.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.573, F1 0.573). Adding resnet50 images lowered accuracy to about 0.52-0.53 with either fusion. Switching to scGPT or to transformer aggregation also hurt. However, every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile-setting choice is completely untested. 2) What this tests: Running the same strong scvi_n200 RNA-only model with singleprofile changes only that one factor. It shows whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps, or whether a simpler single-profile model is as good or better. This matters because transformer aggregation already underperformed avgpool. 3) Why now: Profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, both unimodal and multimodal. Settling it with a clean comparison against the current best gives the most information per experiment. The other big untested factors, the pca_n2000 encoder and the ViT-L image encoder, can be tested next on top of the better profile setting.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool (config_005, 0.573 accuracy, 0.573 F1). The RNA encoder clearly matters: swapping in scGPT in the same setup dropped accuracy to 0.512. Adding ResNet50 images hurt with both fusion types (about 0.525). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. The PCA RNA encoder has never been tested, so the choice of encoder, which has the largest observed effect, is still unresolved. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the best pipeline (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to PCA. This gives a clean, controlled three-way comparison of scVI, scGPT and PCA. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest known setup while removing uncertainty on its most influential untested option. If PCA matches or beats scVI, that changes which RNA backbone should be used in all later multimodal tests, for example with ViT-L. That makes it the most useful next experiment before spending budget on the image-encoder axis.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only with scvi_n200, multiprofile and avgpool (0.573 acc, 0.573 F1). scvi beat both scGPT and PCA, and avgpool beat the transformer. Adding resnet50 images lowered performance under both concat (0.527) and weighted (0.523) fusion. So we cannot tell whether imaging is unhelpful in general or whether the resnet50 features are the weak part. Image encoders are the main untested design axis: imagenet_vit_l has never been tried. Test: config_036 keeps the best RNA setup and the fusion choice of config_030 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. Comparing the two isolates the image-encoder effect and shows whether a stronger image representation can make multimodal fusion beat RNA-only. Why now: this decides whether further budget should go to multimodal configurations, which make up most of the remaining space, or be focused on RNA-only refinements. It is both informative and has a realistic chance of producing a new best result.

1. Evidence: Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l in the scvi_n200 / multiprofile / avgpool / concat setup raised accuracy from 0.527 to 0.725 (F1 0.510 to 0.685). This is by far the largest effect seen so far. Multimodal resnet50 models scored below RNA-only scvi (0.573), which suggests resnet50 features added noise. It is unclear whether the 0.725 comes mostly from ViT-L image features or from a real complementary benefit of fusing them with RNA. Fusion type barely mattered with resnet50 (concat 0.527 vs weighted 0.523), so testing weighted fusion next is likely to be uninformative. 2. Test: Run ViT-L image-only under the same multiprofile avgpool setting. This isolates the image modality's contribution and, compared with config_036 and config_005, shows whether combining modalities adds value beyond ViT-L alone. 3. Why now: It answers the most consequential open question, whether to keep investing in multimodal combinations or focus on the image pathway, using a single run. Every later choice of RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion depends on that answer.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is far above the ResNet50 multimodal runs (about 0.52-0.53), so the image encoder is the dominant design choice. Concat versus weighted fusion made almost no difference with ResNet50 (0.527 vs 0.523). However, ResNet50 contributed little signal, so that comparison may not hold for a stronger encoder. Transformer aggregation and other RNA encoders looked worse in RNA-only runs, so those directions have weaker priors. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration and changes only the fusion method to weighted. It tests whether fusion matters once the image features are informative, which is a plausible interaction. 3) It is a low-risk extension in the most promising region of the space, with a real chance of beating 0.725. Either outcome helps decide whether fusion needs further exploration or can be fixed, before spending budget on profile setting or aggregation.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no data on whether multimodal fusion, multi-profile aggregation, or any encoder choice matters. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-complexity multimodal anchor. It uses scVI RNA features (a compact, widely used representation), a ResNet50 image encoder, multi-profile average-pool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a reference point that later single-factor changes can be compared against. Those changes include switching to single-profile or a transformer aggregator, weighted fusion, the ViT-L or scGPT encoders, and removing a modality to get unimodal ablations. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting from a central, likely-competitive setting keeps every follow-up experiment a one-variable comparison, which makes each later run interpretable. It also gives a reasonable chance of an early strong result. Starting at an extreme, either the simplest unimodal baseline or the most complex transformer setup, would tell us less about the main design axes.

1) Evidence: only one experiment is complete, the multimodal multiprofile scVI + ResNet50 model with avgpool and concat fusion (val acc 0.7207, F1 0.6815). So far there is no evidence about which design choices drive that result. 2) Test: config_005 removes only the image branch and keeps scVI, multiprofile and avgpool the same. This one-factor ablation measures how much the image modality adds over RNA alone. 3) Why now: whether imaging helps is the most consequential open question. If RNA-only performs about the same, later budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation rather than image encoders and fusion. If multimodal clearly wins, exploring image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and fusion variants is justified. Settling this early reduces uncertainty across most of the remaining search space.

1. Evidence: The multimodal scVI+ResNet50 avgpool/concat run reached 0.721 accuracy (F1 0.681). The matching RNA-only scVI avgpool run reached only 0.208 (F1 0.172). So the image branch likely carries most of the signal, but we cannot yet say whether RNA adds anything on top of images. 2. Test: config_011 is the image-only ResNet50 run with the same multiprofile avgpool setup. It completes the modality ablation with every other factor held fixed. If it scores close to 0.72, RNA adds little, and the remaining budget should go to image encoders (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) and aggregation. If it falls well below 0.72, fusion matters, and RNA encoder and fusion choices deserve more experiments. 3. Why now: Resolving which modality drives performance shapes how the rest of the limited budget is spent, so it is worth more than an incremental tweak to the current best configuration.

1. Evidence: Multimodal fusion (scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. That is well above image-only (0.519) and RNA-only (0.208). So combining modalities is strongly supported, and image features carry most of the single-modality signal. 2. What it tests: Because the image branch dominates, the image encoder is likely a high-impact choice that has not been tested yet. This experiment keeps the best configuration and changes only resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. 3. Why now: A one-factor change gives a clean answer on whether a stronger pretrained image backbone improves multimodal performance. It also has a real chance of beating the current best. Aggregation and fusion are lower priority until the backbone question is settled.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_030 (multimodal scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. That clearly beats image-only ResNet50 (0.519) and RNA-only scVI (0.208), so the two modalities add a lot together. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L dropped multimodal accuracy to 0.227, so ResNet50 looks like the right image encoder for now. Aggregation is a major untested choice: every multiprofile run so far used avgpool. 2) This experiment keeps the winning setup fixed (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple pooling. 3) It exploits the strongest region of the search space while resolving a high-impact structural question with one clean comparison. The answer will tell us which aggregation to use when we later vary fusion (weighted) and RNA encoder (PCA, scGPT), so it is a good use of the limited budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat (acc 0.721, F1 0.681). It clearly beats image-only (0.519) and RNA-only (0.208), so fusing the two modalities adds value. Switching to imagenet_vit_l collapsed performance (0.227), and transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.573). So resnet50 and avgpool look like the right choices for now. Fusion strategy is still completely untested; every run so far used concat. The RNA encoder is also unexplored. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps concat for weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the effect of the fusion method on the strongest backbone. 3. Why now: It combines exploitation and exploration. It has a good chance of matching or beating 0.72, and whatever the outcome, it settles a design axis that applies to every remaining multimodal configuration. That makes it a better use of the next run than varying a factor already shown to be weak. The RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) can then be tested on whichever fusion method wins.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Image-only ResNet50 (0.519) is much stronger than RNA-only scVI (0.208), yet fusing the two adds about 20 points, so the RNA branch clearly contributes. Swapping in ViT-L, using transformer aggregation, or using weighted fusion all hurt, so ResNet50, avgpool and concat look like the right local choices. The biggest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder: scVI is the only one tested, and its weak standalone result suggests better RNA features could raise multimodal accuracy further. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT, so any change in accuracy can be attributed to the encoder alone. It is the best use of budget because it resolves a major untested design axis while staying close to the strongest known setup. It also has a plausible chance of beating 0.721, and if it does not, PCA (config_018) or single-profile (config_028) remain clean follow-up tests.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: All seven completed runs used multiprofile, so the profile setting has never been tested. The best result so far is config_030 (scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Changing one part of that configuration has consistently hurt: weighted fusion (0.520), transformer aggregation (0.573), the ViT-L image encoder (0.227) and scGPT as RNA encoder (0.632). Image-only (0.519) and RNA-only (0.208) were both worse, so combining modalities helps. 2) What this tests: config_028 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile. This isolates whether profile-level aggregation is actually needed or whether simpler single-profile inputs do as well or better. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: profile setting is the largest design choice still unexamined. Because only one factor changes from the current best, the result can be read directly. A strong result would open a whole untested branch of the search space. A weak result would confirm multiprofile and let later runs focus on the remaining open question, the pca_n2000 RNA encoder (e.g., config_018).

1) Evidence so far: the best result is the multimodal multiprofile setup with resnet50, avgpool and concat fusion (config_030, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Changing any single factor away from it hurt: transformer aggregation gave 0.573, weighted fusion 0.520, the ViT-L image encoder 0.227 and single-profile 0.224. Two RNA encoders have been compared within this setup: scvi_n200 (0.721) beat scgpt (0.632). The third, pca_n2000, has not been tested in any configuration. 2) config_018 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps in pca_n2000. This completes the RNA-encoder comparison under the strongest known conditions. It shows whether the RNA representation matters and whether a simple 2000-dimensional PCA input can match or beat the learned encoders. That is plausible, since scvi RNA-only was weak (0.208), which suggests the scvi embedding may carry little signal. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it explores the one untested level of an important factor while staying in the high-performing region. It therefore has a real chance of a new best result and also settles the RNA-encoder choice before budget is spent on combinations of the remaining factors.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Every single-factor change from it has now been tested, and each one hurt: transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, the scGPT and PCA RNA encoders, and single-profile input. The most surprising result is the ImageNet ViT-L swap (config_036). It dropped accuracy to 0.227, about the level of RNA-only (0.208). This suggests the ViT-L image features added almost nothing, but it rests on one run. It could reflect a real weakness of ViT-L features or a fusion or training failure specific to that combination. 2. What this tests: Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool, compared directly with image-only ResNet50 (config_011, acc 0.519). If ViT-L alone also scores low, the image encoder is genuinely weak, and the 12 remaining ViT-L configurations can be deprioritized. If it scores reasonably well, the config_036 collapse came from the multimodal combination, and ViT-L multimodal variants deserve a closer look. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: The one-factor-at-a-time neighborhood around the best configuration is exhausted. This experiment isolates the image encoder without other modalities interfering, and its outcome decides whether a large part of the remaining search space is worth testing.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about any factor: modality, encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2. What it tests: config_018 is a central reference point for the multimodal search space. It is multimodal and multiprofile, and it uses the simplest, cheapest standard options: PCA RNA features, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a baseline. Later runs can each change one factor from it, such as unimodal ablations (config_002, config_011), single-profile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), or stronger encoders (scVI/scGPT, ViT-L), so each contrast cleanly isolates one design choice. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting from an extreme corner (the most complex or the most minimal setup) would make later comparisons harder to read. A simple multimodal anchor is a reasonable starting estimate of good performance and gives the most useful comparisons for the following experiments.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has run. config_018 (multimodal, PCA RNA plus ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. We have no reference point for whether the image branch adds anything over RNA alone. That question decides whether to spend budget on image encoders and fusion choices or on RNA encoders. 2. Test: config_002 removes only the image branch. RNA encoder (pca_n2000), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation stay the same. This is a clean single-factor ablation of the image modality. 3. Why now: With almost no evidence, reducing uncertainty about the most basic design choice is the best use of the next run. If RNA-only matches config_018, later runs should focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. If it is clearly worse, image encoders and fusion strategies are worth testing next.

Evidence: the multimodal model (config_018: PCA + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) reached 0.519 accuracy. The RNA-only model with the same PCA encoder, avgpool and multiprofile setting reached only 0.208 (F1 0.480 vs 0.172). So adding images helps a lot, but we cannot tell whether the multimodal model is truly combining both modalities or mostly relying on the image features. This experiment runs the matched image-only control: ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, with everything else held fixed. If image-only scores close to 0.52, the image branch drives performance, and the next budget should go to image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) and aggregation. If it scores well below 0.52, fusion adds real value, and RNA encoder and fusion choices are worth exploring. This clean ablation resolves the largest current uncertainty about where performance comes from, which makes it more useful than tuning a single factor of the multimodal model now.

1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool is clearly best so far (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). RNA-only PCA is weak (0.208), and concat fusion with PCA RNA drags performance down to 0.519. The image branch is therefore the main source of signal, yet its encoder choice is completely untested. 2) Test: Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L while keeping the same multiprofile avgpool setup isolates the effect of the image encoder against the current best baseline. 3) Why now: The image encoder is shared by about half of the remaining multimodal and image-only configurations. Settling this choice early will shape every later image or multimodal experiment, and it may also directly raise the best accuracy. It does both more than testing fusion or aggregation variants around a weak RNA branch.

1. Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). RNA-only with PCA is weak (0.208), and ImageNet ViT-L is poor (0.332). Adding PCA RNA to ResNet50 by concatenation dropped performance sharply (0.519 vs 0.713). We cannot yet tell whether this drop comes from the RNA signal itself or from naive concat fusion letting a weak, high-dimensional modality swamp the strong image features. 2. Test: config_019 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps everything else equal to config_018. This is a clean single-variable comparison. If weighted fusion recovers to or above image-only performance, multimodal fusion is still viable and fusion choice matters. If it stays well below, the weak PCA RNA features are the problem, and the search should turn to better RNA encoders (scVI/scGPT) or to image-only aggregation. 3. Why now: Fusion strategy decides the value of the whole multimodal half of the search space. Settling it early with one controlled run prevents spending budget on many multimodal configurations that may share the same flaw.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). ViT-L is much weaker (0.332), and RNA PCA is weak (0.208). Adding PCA RNA hurt performance under both concat (0.519) and weighted (0.427) fusion. Aggregation has only been tested as avgpool, so whether a learned transformer aggregator over multiple profiles helps or hurts is completely unknown. 2) What this tests: Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation on the strongest branch (image-only ResNet50, multiprofile) isolates the effect of aggregation, with every other factor held fixed. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It exploits the most promising direction while resolving a design choice that affects every multiprofile configuration, including all remaining multimodal ones. Exploring other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) remains a priority for later. However, RNA has so far only degraded results, so first refining and confirming the strongest pipeline is the more efficient use of the limited budget.

1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool is clearly best (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). PCA RNA alone is very weak (0.208). Adding PCA RNA to ResNet50 lowers accuracy with both concat fusion (0.519) and weighted fusion (0.427). The open question is whether RNA has little signal or whether PCA is simply a poor RNA encoder. 2) This experiment tests scVI RNA-only in the multiprofile avgpool setting, matched to config_002, so the only change is the RNA encoder. It shows whether a learned RNA representation gives a much stronger signal. 3) Best use of budget: most of the remaining space is multimodal configurations that depend on the RNA encoder. One cheap unimodal test tells us whether scVI-based fusion is worth exploring or whether search should focus on image-only variants such as single-profile ResNet50.

Evidence: the best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with avgpool (0.713 accuracy). PCA-based RNA alone is very weak (0.208), and fusing it with ResNet50 lowered performance (0.519 with concat, 0.427 with weighted). This suggests the weak RNA encoder may be hurting fusion. scVI RNA alone is much stronger (0.537 vs 0.208). Question: does pairing the best image setup (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) with the stronger scVI encoder, using concat fusion (the better of the two fusions tried), let multimodal models match or beat image-only? This changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_018, so the result is easy to interpret. It also tests whether multimodality itself is the problem or only the poor PCA features. That makes it the most decision-relevant use of the next experiment, balancing a plausible gain against learning which RNA encoder and modality choice matter.

1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). Every multimodal fusion tested has underperformed it (0.22–0.52). ViT-L and transformer aggregation both scored lower. One design axis has never been tested: profile setting. Every completed run used multiprofile, so we do not know whether multiprofile aggregation helps or hurts. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed (image-only, ResNet50) and switches only to singleprofile. It is a clean one-factor test of whether aggregating across profiles adds value. It also checks whether a simpler setup can match or beat the current best. 3) It resolves a major untested axis on the strongest branch, so either outcome is informative. It has a reasonable chance of improving accuracy, and its result will narrow down which of the many remaining singleprofile configurations are worth running.

1. Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool on multiprofile data is the clear leader (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Every multimodal run so far falls well below it (0.22–0.52). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scVI (0.537) far outperforms PCA (0.208). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has not been tested at all, so this is the biggest gap in what we know. The scVI multimodal result (0.224) is poor despite scVI working well alone, which suggests a fusion problem, but that cannot be untangled until we know which RNA representation is strongest.
2. Test: config_008 runs scGPT RNA-only under the best-performing protocol (multiprofile, avgpool). This gives a direct comparison against scVI and PCA under matched conditions and tells us whether scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder.
3. Why now: A single run closes the main remaining gap on the RNA encoder. The answer narrows all 12 untested scGPT multimodal configurations: if scGPT beats scVI, multimodal follow-ups should use it; if not, they can be deprioritized. This is a more informative use of budget than another multimodal run, whose low results are currently hard to interpret.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is unresolved.
