1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: an RNA-only, single-profile model with the compact scVI (n200) encoder. It is the simplest configuration and has no aggregation or fusion choices, so it gives a clean reference point. Later runs can each change one factor against it: switching to an image-only model (config_004/006), adding images with concat fusion (config_019/003), moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_012), or swapping the RNA encoder (config_026 PCA, config_005 scGPT). 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: starting with a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would mix many design choices, so its result could not be attributed to any one of them. A simple baseline sets the bar that more complex models must beat, rather than assuming they will win, and makes every later comparison easier to interpret.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only, single-profile scVI baseline (config_017: accuracy 0.507, F1 0.455). We know nothing yet about whether the image modality adds value, which is the most basic design question in this space. 2. Test: config_019 keeps everything from config_017 the same (single-profile, scVI RNA encoder) and only adds image features (ViT-L) with simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of going multimodal against the existing baseline. 3. Why now: Whether to include images affects most of the remaining configurations, so resolving it early guides the rest of the search. Using concat rather than weighted fusion, and staying single-profile, avoids changing several choices at once. ViT-L is a reasonable first image encoder to try; a gain or loss here tells us whether image or encoder comparisons are worth further budget.

1) Evidence so far: adding ImageNet ViT-L image features to scVI RNA (config_019, multimodal concat) gave 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1. RNA-only scVI (config_017) gave 0.507 and 0.455. We cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being more informative. 2) Image-only ViT-L single-profile completes the modality comparison with the same encoders. If it matches or beats 0.579, RNA adds little and later experiments should focus on image representations. If it scores clearly lower, fusing the two modalities adds real value, and it is worth tuning RNA encoders and fusion. 3) This is a single-factor control that resolves the most basic open design question, which is what drives performance. Answering it first should guide whether we spend the limited budget on multiprofile, aggregation, or fusion variants.

1. Evidence: Image-only with imagenet_vit_l is clearly the strongest result so far (acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Adding scvi_n200 RNA through concat fusion lowered performance to 0.579, and RNA-only reached just 0.507. This points to image features as the main source of signal, though each result is a single run. Profile setting is still completely untested. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (image_only, imagenet_vit_l) and changes only one factor: singleprofile becomes multiprofile, using the simpler avgpool aggregation. That isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. Avgpool keeps the change minimal before trying transformer aggregation. 3. It exploits the strongest direction while answering a key open design question. If multiprofile helps, it suggests a promising axis for later multimodal and aggregation comparisons. If it does not, we avoid spending budget on the many multiprofile configurations. Testing fusion variants such as weighted fusion (config_014) is a reasonable alternative, but it is less urgent because multimodal currently trails image-only by a wide margin.

Evidence: image-only single-profile ViT-L is clearly the best so far (0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA by concat lowered performance (0.579), and RNA-only was weak (0.507). Moving the same image model to multiprofile with avgpool collapsed performance to 0.421. The open question is whether that collapse comes from the multiprofile setting itself or from the avgpool aggregation, which may wash out informative profile-level signal. This experiment keeps the image-only ViT-L setup and multiprofile setting fixed and changes only the aggregation to a transformer, so it isolates that one factor. If it recovers or beats 0.725, multiprofile with learned aggregation becomes a strong direction to exploit, including for later multimodal runs. If it stays low, the evidence that multiprofile is harmful here gets much stronger, and the remaining budget can go to single-profile choices such as fusion type and encoders. Either result resolves a major design uncertainty, which makes it a better use of one run than another fusion or encoder variant.

Evidence: image-only single-profile ViT-L (config_006) is clearly best (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA by concatenation (config_019) dropped performance to 0.579. RNA-only scored 0.507. Multiprofile aggregation hurt image-only models with both avgpool and transformer. The key open question is whether RNA is inherently uninformative or whether naive concatenation lets the weaker modality degrade the image signal. Test: config_014 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) relative to config_019, keeping single-profile, scVI and ViT-L fixed. This isolates the effect of fusion. Why now: if weighted fusion recovers or beats image-only, the multimodal branch becomes worth exploiting. If it does not, that is fairly strong evidence to deprioritize multimodal configurations, which make up most of the remaining space. Either way, it prunes the search efficiently under a limited budget.

Evidence: the single-profile image-only ViT-L model (config_006) is clearly the best so far, at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Adding scVI RNA lowered performance with both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518). RNA-only with scVI is weak (0.507). Multiprofile image-only models with ViT-L degraded sharply under avgpool (0.421) and transformer aggregation (0.260). So the image branch in single-profile mode carries most of the signal, but the image encoder has been tested only with ViT-L. Test: config_004 is the same setup with ResNet50 as the image encoder. This changes one variable and isolates the effect of image representation within the best-performing setting. Why now: under a limited budget, this both exploits the strongest direction and resolves a key open design choice. If ResNet50 matches or beats ViT-L, it changes which backbone should anchor later fusion and multiprofile tests. If it is worse, it confirms ViT-L as the image encoder for future experiments.

Evidence: single-profile image-only ViT-L is clearly best (0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA lowered performance with both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518), and scVI RNA-only is weak (0.507). Multiprofile aggregation also hurt the image model badly. The main open question is whether RNA is inherently weak here or whether scVI is just a poor RNA representation, since scVI is the only RNA encoder tested so far. This experiment tests scGPT RNA-only in the same single-profile setting as config_017, so the RNA encoder is the only change. If scGPT is much stronger, retrying multimodal fusion with scGPT is justified. If it is also weak, the budget should go to image-centric configurations rather than more multimodal combinations. Under a limited budget, this one clean comparison tells us whether the large multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile image-only ViT-L (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA lowered performance under both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518). Multiprofile aggregation hurt image models badly, with avgpool at 0.421 and transformer at 0.260. RNA-only models are weak and close together (scVI 0.507, scGPT 0.519), and pca_n2000, the third RNA representation, has not been tested. One possible reason fusion hurts is that the RNA features are too weak or noisy. 2. Test: Single-profile RNA-only with pca_n2000 completes the RNA encoder comparison. It changes only the representation, against two existing baselines. 3. Why now: This is a cheap, cleanly isolated experiment that answers whether any RNA representation is strong enough for multimodal fusion to be worth more budget. If PCA clearly beats the others, PCA+ViT-L concat (config_002) becomes the logical next test. If it does not, the evidence favours concentrating on image-only single-profile models instead of spending runs on multimodal or multiprofile variants.

Evidence: The two best unimodal encoders are clearly identified. PCA_n2000 is the strongest RNA encoder (0.721 vs about 0.51 for scVI and scGPT), and ViT-L is the strongest image encoder (0.725 vs 0.471 for ResNet50). Multiprofile aggregation has done poorly for image-only models (avgpool 0.421, transformer 0.260 vs 0.725 singleprofile). Multimodal fusion so far has only used the weak scVI RNA encoder. With scVI, concat (0.579) beat weighted (0.518), but both fell below image-only ViT-L, so that gap may come from the weak RNA input rather than from fusion itself. Test: config_002 pairs the best RNA encoder (PCA) with the best image encoder (ViT-L), keeping singleprofile and the better-observed concat fusion. Compared with config_019, it changes only the RNA encoder. This shows whether fusion adds value once both modalities are strong. Why now: It is a controlled extension of the strongest evidence. It has the highest chance of beating the roughly 0.72 baseline. It also settles the key question of whether multimodality helps here, before spending budget on the multiprofile settings, which look unpromising.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which choices matter: modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_034 is the simplest available model. It uses RNA only, a single profile and a PCA encoder, with no aggregation or fusion to confound the result. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every more complex choice must beat to justify itself. 3. Why it is the best next step: Without a simple baseline, later gains from multiprofile aggregation, image features, fusion or learned encoders (scVI, scGPT) cannot be read clearly. Each can then be tested by changing one factor at a time from this anchor, such as config_045 or config_009 for multiprofile and config_030 or config_021 for the encoder. Starting here avoids assuming that more complex models are better.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479). We have no evidence yet on whether profile setting, encoder, aggregation, modality or fusion matter. 2. Test: config_045 keeps the RNA-only setting and the PCA encoder, and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with a learned transformer aggregator, a different encoder or image data. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major design axis that affects a large share of the remaining configurations. A clean one-variable comparison against the existing baseline gives the most interpretable information per experiment. It also sets up later tests of aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and of adding images.

1. Evidence: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Moving from singleprofile to multiprofile avgpool gave a small gain in accuracy (0.520 to 0.530) and a larger gain in F1 (0.479 to 0.515). We have no evidence about how much signal the image modality carries on its own. 2. This experiment tests an image-only model (ViT-L) using the same multiprofile avgpool setup as the current best, config_045. It differs from that run only in modality, so it gives a direct comparison of RNA versus image information. 3. Knowing the image-only baseline is needed to read any later multimodal result. Without it, a weak multimodal model could not be traced to uninformative images or to poor fusion. This single run reduces the largest open uncertainty, whether images are worth including, before spending budget on the many multimodal fusion and encoder combinations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (0.530 acc, 0.515 F1). It slightly beats single-profile PCA (0.520), with a clearer gain in F1. Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool is much weaker (0.411). The biggest open question is whether adding images helps or hurts an RNA model that is already better on its own. 2. Test: config_024 combines the two tested unimodal branches: PCA RNA plus ViT-L image, multiprofile, avgpool. It adds simple concat fusion. Everything else matches config_045 and config_047, so the comparison isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion pays off determines how the remaining budget should be spent. If it gains, later runs can tune fusion type and aggregation. If it does not, the budget should shift to RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT. Concat is the simplest baseline fusion, so it gives a clean reference before trying weighted fusion.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the multimodal, multiprofile model with PCA RNA, ViT-L image features, avgpool and concat (config_024). It reached 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1, well above RNA-only (0.530) and image-only (0.411). Adding multiple profiles helped RNA-only only slightly (0.520 to 0.530), though F1 rose more (0.479 to 0.515). Every multiprofile run has used avgpool, so we do not know whether a learned transformer aggregation adds value. 2. Test: config_048 keeps everything from config_024 except the aggregation, which switches from avgpool to transformer. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone, at the current best setting. 3. Why now: This both exploits the strongest direction and resolves an untested design axis that applies to every multiprofile configuration. The answer will tell us whether later multiprofile runs should use transformer or avgpool before we spend budget on secondary choices like fusion type or RNA and image encoders.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger single modality (about 0.52-0.53 versus 0.41 for image-only). Fusing both modalities with multiprofile input helps (0.635). Switching aggregation from avgpool to transformer gave a large further gain to 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1 in config_048. So far, every multimodal run has used pca_n2000 for RNA, so we do not yet know whether the RNA representation matters, even though RNA carries most of the signal. 2) What this tests: config_015 keeps the best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: representation of the dominant modality is likely to have a bigger effect than fusion type or image backbone. Testing it on top of the current best both exploits the strong transformer result and reduces uncertainty about a major untested design axis. The result will also tell us whether scGPT, or scVI by extension, is worth exploring further.

1. Evidence so far: multimodal multiprofile models clearly beat unimodal ones (about 0.64–0.72 versus 0.41–0.53). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 7 points with PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). scGPT edged out PCA under the transformer setup (0.725 vs 0.706), which is a modest gain. Fusion has never been varied: every multimodal run used concat, so it is the largest untested uncertainty among the core design choices. 2. config_002 keeps the current best setup (scGPT, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy. 3. It is a single-factor test on the strongest configuration. It answers whether fusion matters, and it may also improve on the best result. Testing ResNet50 or scVI next would be less useful, because fusion has no evidence at all, while encoders already have some.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal models clearly beat single-modality ones (0.64–0.72 vs at most 0.53). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 7 points with PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). Concat beat weighted fusion by a wide margin with scGPT (0.725 vs 0.586). scGPT was slightly better than PCA (0.725 vs 0.706; F1 0.685 vs 0.667), a small gap that should not be overread. The image encoder has never been varied: every image-based run used imagenet_vit_l. 2. What this tests: config_004 keeps the best configuration (config_015: scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50. This isolates the image representation choice in the strongest context. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder is the largest untested design axis. Fixing everything else makes the comparison clean. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best, so it balances exploration with exploitation. Testing scVI (config_039) is the natural follow-up.

Evidence: the strongest region is multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Within it, scGPT (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1) slightly beats PCA (0.706 acc, 0.667 F1). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool for PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). Concat clearly beat weighted fusion (0.725 vs 0.586). Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 collapsed performance (0.260). The one untested design choice in this best setting is the third RNA encoder, scVI. This experiment changes only the RNA encoder (scVI_n200) and keeps everything else fixed. It will show whether the RNA representation matters beyond the small scGPT-vs-PCA gap, and whether a compact probabilistic embedding can match or beat scGPT. It is the best use of the next run because it exploits the strongest evidence while isolating a single factor. It could also produce a new best result, and it completes the RNA-encoder comparison in the most relevant setting before spending budget on secondary questions such as single- vs multi-profile ablations.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_015 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Within the multiprofile multimodal setting, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.706 vs 0.635), concat beat weighted fusion, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by a wide margin. The profile setting is still the major untested axis for multimodal models. It has only been compared for RNA-only PCA, where multiprofile gave a small gain (0.530 vs 0.520). 2) Test: config_026 keeps the best encoders and fusion (scGPT + ViT-L, concat) and switches only to singleprofile, which by design removes aggregation. This shows whether the gains come from multiprofile context with learned aggregation, or whether a simpler single-profile multimodal model performs about as well. 3) Value: Profile setting is a core design choice that may change how later experiments are prioritized. A single controlled comparison against the current best settles it more directly than further fine-tuning of encoders or fusion that are already well supported.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which design choices matter. 2) config_027 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) is a mid-complexity anchor. It uses the simpler choices for aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat), paired with commonly strong encoders. 3) Most other design choices are one change away from it among the available configurations: weighted fusion (config_041), transformer aggregation (config_005), ResNet50 image encoder (config_008), scVI or scGPT RNA encoder (config_003, config_046), image-only (config_009) and RNA-only (config_042). That makes it the most efficient first experiment, because every later single-factor comparison against it can isolate the effect of one design choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image features. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) but removes the RNA modality. This is a clean one-factor ablation of multimodality. If image-only matches or beats 0.514, the next experiments should focus on image representation and aggregation. If it falls clearly below, RNA fusion is contributing and is worth refining (RNA encoder, fusion type). 3) Why now: Model setting (unimodal vs multimodal) is the most basic design choice and determines how to spend the rest of the budget. Settling it early with a controlled comparison is more informative than tuning secondary choices like fusion or aggregation around an unvalidated multimodal baseline.

1. Evidence: the multimodal model (PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L images, avgpool, concat; config_027) reached 0.5136 accuracy. The image-only counterpart (config_009) reached 0.5121. Fusion therefore adds almost no accuracy, though F1 rose about 0.02. This leaves it unclear whether RNA carries useful signal on its own or only slightly rebalances class predictions. 2. What it tests: config_042 is RNA-only with the same PCA-2000 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It completes a controlled three-way modality comparison where only the modality changes. It will show whether RNA alone is weak, comparable to images or complementary. 3. Why now: modality contribution is the most important open design question. Settling it first tells us where to spend the remaining budget, whether on RNA encoders and fusion strategies or on image-centric and aggregation variants, before tuning secondary choices like transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) clearly leads at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Multimodal concat (0.514) is about the same as image-only (0.512). This suggests concatenation lets the weaker image features swamp the stronger RNA signal. The key open question is whether that failure comes from the fusion method or from adding images at all. 2. config_041 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps PCA, ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This directly isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, multimodal is still worth exploring with better fusion. If it stays near 0.51, we can confidently focus the remaining budget on RNA-only encoders and aggregation. 3. This one-factor comparison settles whether the large multimodal branch of the search space is worth exploring, which makes it the most informative next experiment under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: The RNA-only model (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool; config_042) is clearly the best so far at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Adding images hurt. Concat fusion fell to about 0.514, weighted fusion fell to 0.260, and image-only (ViT-L) reached only 0.512. RNA therefore appears to carry most of the signal. However, we have tested only one RNA encoder (PCA), so how much the RNA representation matters is still unknown. 2. Test: config_034 swaps PCA for scVI and keeps everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder on the strongest branch found so far. 3. Why now: Encoder choice is a high-impact design decision, and this test changes only one variable. It exploits the promising RNA-only direction while reducing uncertainty that also bears on later multimodal and aggregation experiments. A better encoder would raise the performance ceiling. A worse one would make PCA the backbone to carry forward into tests of aggregation (e.g., config_031) and profile setting (e.g., config_036).

Evidence: the RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) multiprofile avgpool model is clearly the best so far (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). It beats scVI RNA-only (0.573), image-only (0.512) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.514, weighted 0.260). Every completed run used avgpool, so we have no evidence on whether transformer aggregation over profiles helps, even though aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration. Test: config_031 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer, which isolates the effect of aggregation. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while settling an important open design choice. If the transformer helps, it is a likely new best and points to which multiprofile variants to try next. If it hurts, avgpool is supported as the default and the budget can move to profile setting or RNA encoder comparisons.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models with pca_n2000 are clearly the strongest so far (0.639 with avgpool, 0.653 with transformer). Image-only (0.512) and multimodal fusion (concat 0.514, weighted 0.260) both underperform, so adding images has not helped yet. PCA beat scVI. All six experiments used the multiprofile setting, so the profile-setting choice is completely untested. 2. This run tests RNA-only pca_n2000 in the singleprofile setting. It changes only the profile setting relative to the best RNA-only runs. Aggregation becomes None, which follows necessarily from using a single profile. The result will show whether multiprofile aggregation gives a real gain over single-profile inputs. 3. Profile setting is a major design axis with no evidence yet. Testing it on the strongest and simplest model family gives a clean comparison and answers it with one experiment. A different RNA encoder could instead be tested with scgpt, but that would add less information about an unexplored design dimension.

1) Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile models are clearly strongest. PCA with transformer aggregation reached 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1, and PCA with avgpool reached 0.639. Multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.591), and PCA beat scVI under avgpool (0.639 vs 0.573). Multimodal fusion with ViT underperformed RNA-only, with concat at 0.514 and weighted fusion collapsing to 0.260. The RNA encoder appears to be the main lever, yet scGPT, the third encoder option, is completely untested. 2) Test: scGPT RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation differs from the current best (config_031) only in the RNA encoder. It therefore directly tells us whether a foundation-model embedding beats PCA within the best known setup. 3) Why now: this is a single-variable change on the strongest configuration. It covers the largest remaining uncertainty in the most influential design choice, and it has a real chance of becoming the new best. It is more useful than more multimodal variants, which current evidence suggests are hurt by the image modality.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with transformer aggregation (0.653 accuracy). Swapping avgpool for transformer improved RNA-only PCA modestly (0.639 to 0.653, with F1 also up). Multimodal PCA+ViT with avgpool and concat (0.514) did worse than RNA-only and about matched image-only, so image features may be diluting the RNA signal under simple pooling. Weighted fusion failed badly (0.260), so concat is the better fusion to keep. The open question is whether multimodal fusion is inherently unhelpful here or only limited by avgpool aggregation. Config_005 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_027, cleanly isolating that effect within the multimodal setting. If it approaches or beats 0.653, it is a strong exploitation candidate. If it stays near 0.51, that is solid evidence to stop investing in ViT-based multimodal models and focus on RNA-only refinements.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only pca_n2000 is the strongest direction so far. With transformer aggregation it reaches 0.653 accuracy, versus 0.639 with avgpool. The best multimodal run (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is lower at 0.599. Image-only vit_l is weak at 0.512, which suggests the image features may be adding noise rather than signal. However, every image run so far has used imagenet_vit_l, so the image-encoder choice is completely unexplored. 2. What this tests: it keeps the best multimodal setup fixed (multiprofile, pca_n2000, transformer, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates whether a different image representation can close or reverse the gap between multimodal and RNA-only. 3. Why it is the best next run: the open question with the most impact is whether multimodality can help at all, and this is a clean one-variable test of it. If resnet50 helps, multimodal becomes a viable path to beat 0.653. If it does not, we gain stronger evidence to focus the remaining budget on refining RNA-only models.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no baseline and no information about which design choices (modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, fusion) matter. 2. What this tests: config_050 is the simplest setup, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1 on this task. Every later configuration can be compared against it to see whether added complexity actually helps. Those additions include learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the image modality, multiprofile aggregation and fusion. 3. Why now: under a limited budget, starting from a well-defined minimal baseline is the most informative first step. It avoids the confounding that comes from starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model, where several design choices change at once. It also lets the next experiments vary one factor at a time from a known anchor, such as the RNA encoder (config_001 or config_034) or the modality (an image-only single-profile model).

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA baseline (config_050) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. Nothing is yet known about how profile setting, encoder, modality or fusion affect performance. 2) Test: config_016 keeps the modality (RNA only) and encoder (PCA) the same and switches to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, average pooling. That makes it a near single-factor test of whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. 3) Why now: profile setting divides much of the remaining search space, since most configurations are multiprofile. A clean answer here will narrow later choices more than changing several factors at once, such as jumping to a multimodal configuration. Average pooling is the minimal aggregation, so the profile effect is less confounded by aggregation complexity than it would be with a transformer.

1. Evidence: The two completed runs are both RNA-only with PCA. Single-profile (0.519 acc, 0.480 F1) and multiprofile with avgpool (0.518 acc, 0.484 F1) perform almost identically. So profile setting with simple averaging appears to matter little for RNA. The biggest open question is whether imaging adds anything, and we have no image evidence yet. 2. Test: config_012 keeps the single-profile PCA RNA baseline from config_050 and adds ViT-L image features through simple concat fusion. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed mainly to adding the image modality. 3. Why now: Modality is likely the highest-impact design choice. Comparing against an existing baseline gives an interpretable, low-confound answer. That answer will guide whether later budget goes to multimodal fusion and aggregation choices or back to RNA-encoder and aggregation exploration such as scVI, scGPT or transformer aggregation.

Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ViT-L concat model (0.527 acc, 0.510 F1) slightly beats RNA-only PCA (0.519 acc, 0.480 F1). The F1 gain (+0.03) is larger than the accuracy gain. Multiprofile avgpool gave no clear benefit for RNA-only PCA. The key open question is where the multimodal gain comes from, because the image modality has never been tested on its own. Test: an image-only ViT-L singleprofile run completes a clean modality ablation, alongside the single-profile RNA-only and multimodal runs. It shows whether ViT-L image features alone match or exceed the fused model, which would make the RNA contribution marginal, or are clearly weaker, which would support fusion as complementary. Why now: this one-variable comparison sets how to spend the remaining budget. It tells us whether to prioritize image-centric configurations, RNA encoder variants (scVI, scGPT), or fusion and aggregation choices, rather than guessing from a single multimodal result.

1. Evidence: RNA carries nearly all of the signal so far. RNA-only PCA reached about 0.519 accuracy, ViT image-only only about 0.208, and multimodal concat about 0.527. Multimodal concat gave a small accuracy gain but a clearer F1 gain (0.510 vs 0.480). Multiprofile avgpool did not help RNA-only (0.518 vs 0.519). Every run so far used the PCA RNA encoder, so the RNA representation is the biggest untested choice. 2. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest effect seen so far. pca_n2000 (0.519 accuracy) clearly beat scvi_n200 (0.427). Image-only ViT-L is weak (0.208). Experiment: config_045 (scGPT + ViT-L, singleprofile, concat) differs from the best run, config_034, only by adding the image modality. 1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only singleprofile (config_034) is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.586, F1 0.574). 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_009 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, transformer aggregation) at 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1. It beats single-profile scGPT (config_034) at 0.586. No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence on modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion, and no baseline. 2. config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) is a mid-complexity anchor. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI-n200 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. 1. Evidence: Within the multiprofile, avgpool, scvi_n200/resnet50 setting, RNA-only leads (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for RNA-only scVI (0.650 vs 0.435). 1) Evidence so far: the best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). 1. Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile avgpool models are the strongest so far (pca_n2000 0.653, scvi_n200 0.650 accuracy). 1) Evidence: The two best runs are RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool models with PCA (0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) and scVI (0.650 / 0.628), which are effectively tied. The alternatives look weaker. PCA with transformer aggregation or singleprofile would repeat choices that already hurt scVI, and the concat or ViT-L variants have poor priors.

1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters, and no reference point for judging gains. 2) config_014 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a baseline that later runs can each change one factor from: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), modality (image-only, multimodal), and profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer). 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable anchor lets every later experiment act as a clean one-factor comparison. Why it is the best next experiment: Whether to go multimodal is the most important branching decision, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. 1) Evidence so far: all three experiments use singleprofile with pca_n2000 and resnet50. Image-only (0.471 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.332). Concat fusion improved further to 0.518 accuracy and 0.484 F1. 1) Evidence so far: image-only (ResNet50, 0.471) clearly beats RNA-only (PCA, 0.332), so the image branch carries most of the signal. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA-only baseline, fusion was the problem and multimodal models remain viable. If it stays poor, the image features themselves are the likely problem, and image-only or ViT-L tests become the logical next step. 3) It is the best next use of the budget because it is a clean one-variable comparison of a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration, which is most of the remaining options. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, since a learned weighting can down-weight an uninformative modality.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features lowered accuracy, to 0.619 with weighted fusion and 0.227 with concat. The image modality has never been tested alone, so it is unclear whether the images carry little signal or whether the fusion methods are the problem. 2. Test: Image-only, single-profile, ResNet50 isolates how much signal ResNet50 image features carry, using the same image encoder and profile setting as the multimodal runs. 3. Why now: A weak result would suggest images are mostly noise, so the search should focus on RNA, especially aggregation (transformer beat avgpool). A moderate or strong result would support further work on fusion and image encoders (ViT-L). Either way, this one run settles a key uncertainty that affects a large share of the remaining configurations.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion lowered accuracy to 0.619, and concat fusion collapsed to 0.227. Multiprofile aggregation also hurt RNA, though transformer (0.635) beat avgpool (0.520). Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.535. The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has never been tested, yet it appears in about half of the remaining configurations, so the quality of the image representation is the largest unresolved design choice. 2) What this tests: config_046 is image-only, single-profile ViT-L, which differs from config_040 (image-only ResNet50) only in the image encoder. It therefore isolates whether ViT-L gives a stronger image representation, without fusion or aggregation effects mixed in. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, multimodal weighted fusion with scVI and ViT-L (config_011) becomes a credible way to surpass the RNA-only baseline. If it does not, most ViT-L multimodal configurations can be deprioritized, which saves budget either way.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the simplest model, scVI RNA-only single-profile (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). For multiprofile RNA, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.635 vs 0.520). For multimodal single-profile, weighted fusion far outperformed concat (0.619 vs 0.227), though it still trailed RNA-only. The two image encoders performed about the same on their own (0.535 vs 0.532). 2. Test: This configuration pairs the best-performing choices, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, in a multiprofile multimodal model with scVI and ResNet50. Compared with config_045, it adds multiprofile with transformer aggregation. Compared with config_002, it adds the image modality through weighted fusion. It is still a two-variable change against each anchor, so if it underperforms we cannot tell which addition caused it. 3. Why now: Whether multiprofile multimodal modeling can beat the simple RNA-only baseline is the main open question about the whole multimodal and multiprofile direction. Answering it is more valuable than swapping image encoders, which showed no difference on their own. It also stays within the configuration space the evidence favors.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest RNA-only single-profile model, using PCA (2000 components) with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point. Later runs can change one factor at a time against it: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), and adding images with fusion (concat, weighted). 3. Why now: With a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable baseline is the best first step. It shows whether added complexity actually helps, rather than assuming multimodal or multiprofile models win, and it makes each later single-factor comparison informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (2000 components), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.536 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.516. The two metrics are close, which loosely suggests performance is not heavily skewed across classes, but this is only an initial observation. No other experiments have been run, so it is unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or image fusion would improve on this, and the result should serve as the reference point for later single-factor comparisons rather than as evidence about which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.536, F1 0.516). Nothing yet tells us which design factor matters most. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor. It keeps RNA-only and PCA fixed and switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles per sample improves accuracy and F1 over the baseline. 3) Why now: profile setting is a structural choice that applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal models. Answering it early tells us whether most of the remaining configurations, which are multiprofile, are worth prioritizing. Using avgpool rather than the transformer avoids mixing the profile effect with aggregation complexity. A single-factor RNA-encoder swap (config_004) would also be informative, but resolving the profile question first prunes the search space more.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the llm_summary_001 baseline fixed (RNA-only, PCA encoder with 2000 components, no image encoder or fusion) and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average pooling. Validation accuracy rose from 0.536 to 0.688 (+0.152), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.659 (+0.143). Because only the profile setting and its required aggregation changed, this is reasonably direct evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the RNA-only PCA model, which makes multiprofile configurations a promising direction. However, the effect comes from a single run with no variance estimate, profile setting and avgpool cannot be separated, and it is unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal models, or more complex aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Moving the RNA-only PCA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.536 to 0.688, and F1 rose by a similar amount (0.516 to 0.659). This is the strongest signal so far. However, it comes from one run, and the multiprofile effect cannot yet be separated from the choice of avgpool as the aggregator. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000) and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether learned aggregation adds anything beyond simple pooling, or whether avgpool is enough. 3) Why now: It extends the most promising direction while changing just one factor. Its result also tells us which aggregator to use when we later test other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models and multimodal models. That avoids spreading the limited budget across both aggregator options in every later branch.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the best configuration so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA encoder with 2000 components, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool (llm_summary_002) to a transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.512 (-0.176), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.477 (-0.181). That puts it below even the single-profile baseline (0.536 / 0.516). Because aggregation was the only change, this is direct single-run evidence that in this setup the transformer aggregator underperforms simple average pooling, so avgpool is the stronger default for later branches (other RNA encoders, image-only, multimodal). However, there is no variance estimate. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects the transformer itself or untuned training or hyperparameters (e.g., overfitting or optimization issues on low-dimensional PCA inputs), and whether the result carries over to other encoders or modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (config_002, 0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). That run clearly beat the single-profile baseline (0.536) and the transformer aggregator (0.512), so multiprofile with avgpool is the current default. The largest untested question is whether the image modality adds any value. No image-only or multimodal run has been done, which leaves half of the design space unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_018 keeps config_002's multiprofile, PCA and avgpool settings fixed. It adds a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing it directly with config_002 isolates the effect of adding images to the best known setup, without mixing in a new RNA encoder or a different aggregator. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Whether to go multimodal determines whether the many remaining multimodal configurations are worth exploring. A gain would justify follow-ups on fusion type and image encoder. No gain or a loss would point the budget toward RNA encoder comparisons (e.g., config_005) and away from multimodal branches. Either result reduces uncertainty about a major design choice while staying close to the best configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far fixed (multiprofile, PCA encoder with 2000 components, avgpool aggregation; llm_summary_002) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.532 (-0.156), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.516 (-0.143), roughly matching the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.536 / 0.516). Because adding the image branch with concat was the only change, this is direct single-run evidence that this particular multimodal setup underperforms RNA-only in this setting, which argues for shifting budget toward RNA encoder comparisons rather than broad multimodal exploration. However, there is no variance estimate. The image branch and the concat fusion cannot be separated, and no image-only run exists to gauge how informative the image features are on their own. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects image features adding noise, scale or dimensional imbalance between the concatenated features, or untuned training. Alternative fusion methods or image encoders might therefore still behave differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Our best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Two changes from that configuration both hurt it by roughly 0.15 to 0.18. Swapping avgpool for a transformer aggregator was worse, and adding a ResNet50 branch with concat fusion was also worse. The RNA encoder is the main design choice we have not tested at all, since every run so far used PCA. 2) Test: Keep the best configuration fixed and change only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation improves on PCA in the multiprofile avgpool setting. If it does, scVI becomes the basis for later branches, including a fairer multimodal retest. 3) Why now: It is a clean single-factor comparison anchored to the strongest configuration. It has a real chance of beating the current best, and it tests whether the multiprofile gain holds beyond PCA. That makes better use of the limited budget than further multimodal or transformer variants, which have already underperformed in single runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion; llm_summary_002) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA with 2000 components to scVI with 200 latent dimensions. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.635 (-0.053), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.618 (-0.040). Because the encoder was the only change, this is single-run evidence that this scVI setting does not beat PCA here, so PCA remains the default. The drop is much smaller than the transformer (llm_summary_003) or ResNet50 concat (llm_summary_004) changes, and scVI still clearly exceeds the single-profile PCA baseline (0.536 / 0.516). That loosely suggests the multiprofile avgpool gain is not specific to PCA, though this has not been directly tested without a single-profile scVI run. There is no variance estimate, so the gap may partly reflect run-to-run noise. The encoder type cannot be separated from the large difference in dimensionality (200 vs 2000), and the scVI hyperparameters and training were not tuned, so other scVI latent sizes or other encoders (e.g., scGPT) remain open questions.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Three single-factor changes from it all did worse. A transformer aggregator gave 0.512. Adding ResNet50 with concat gave 0.532. Swapping PCA for scVI-200 gave 0.635, a moderate drop. The RNA encoder is the dimension still only partly explored: scGPT, a pretrained foundation-model representation, is untested, so we cannot yet say whether PCA's lead reflects encoder type in general or just this scVI setting. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. Comparing it with config_002 (PCA) and config_005 (scVI) completes a clean three-way encoder comparison under the strongest profile and aggregation settings. It also checks whether the multiprofile avgpool benefit holds across encoders. 3. Why now: This is a single-factor experiment on the most promising branch. It could either produce a new best result or confirm PCA as the RNA default before more budget goes to multimodal branches. Fixing the RNA encoder first matters because every multimodal configuration depends on it. Testing weighted fusion (config_019) or image-only baselines makes more sense once the RNA side is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion; llm_summary_002) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT, completing a three-way encoder comparison under these settings. Validation accuracy was 0.530 (-0.157 vs PCA's 0.688; -0.105 vs scVI-200's 0.635), and supporting F1 was 0.515 (vs 0.659 and 0.618). This puts scGPT roughly at the single-profile PCA baseline (0.536 / 0.516), so the encoder ranking here is PCA > scVI > scGPT, PCA remains the RNA default, and the multiprofile avgpool gain is not evident for scGPT, although no single-profile scGPT run exists to test this directly. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and it is unknown whether the drop reflects scGPT representations themselves or untested factors such as embedding dimensionality, the domain match of pretraining, whether scGPT was frozen or fine-tuned, or untuned training.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 with avgpool is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_018) dropped performance to 0.532 / 0.516. That run cannot tell us whether the image features are uninformative or whether naive concatenation hurt, for example through scale or dimensional imbalance swamping the RNA signal. The RNA encoder and aggregator comparisons have already settled on PCA and avgpool as defaults, so fusion is now the largest unresolved design question. 2. What this tests: config_019 keeps config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance, the concat result was a fusion failure and multimodal remains viable. If it still falls well short, the image branch itself is the likely problem, and an image-only run (config_011) becomes the logical next diagnostic. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: it is a clean single-factor comparison against an existing run. It resolves an important ambiguity before committing budget to the many remaining multimodal configurations. It also has real upside, because weighted fusion could learn to down-weight a noisy image branch and possibly beat the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept llm_summary_004 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted, which isolates the fusion choice. Validation accuracy rose from 0.532 to 0.650 (+0.118), and supporting F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.628 (+0.111). This is single-run evidence that concat fusion was a major part of the earlier multimodal drop, so multimodal remains viable. However, the result is still below the RNA-only PCA-2000 avgpool best (0.688 / 0.659; -0.038 accuracy), so adding images has not yet shown a net benefit. There are no variance estimates, and the gap to RNA-only may partly be run-to-run noise. The learned fusion weights were not reported, so it is unknown whether weighted fusion gains by making use of image information or by largely down-weighting the image branch. An image-only run and alternative fusion methods or image encoders remain the open diagnostics.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion hurt badly (0.532). Switching to weighted fusion recovered most of that loss (0.650) but still did not beat RNA-only. We do not know whether the ResNet50 image features carry useful signal, or whether weighted fusion recovered simply by down-weighting the image branch. 2. What this tests: an image-only, multiprofile, avgpool ResNet50 run uses the same profile setting and aggregation as the best configuration, with the modality as the only change. It measures how informative the images are on their own. Strong image-only accuracy would justify putting more budget into fusion and image-encoder variants (e.g., ViT-L with weighted fusion). Weak image-only accuracy would suggest focusing on RNA-only refinements. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: every multimodal branch depends on this answer, and the remaining untested configurations are mostly multimodal. One diagnostic run therefore lowers the risk of the remaining budget more than another single-factor multimodal tweak would.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a diagnostic run that used the same multiprofile avgpool setup as the best configuration (llm_summary_002) but with ResNet50 images only, to measure how informative the image features are on their own. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 and a supporting F1 of 0.519, well below RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.688 / 0.659; -0.152 accuracy) and multimodal weighted fusion (0.650 / 0.628). It roughly matches the single-profile RNA baseline (0.536) and the concat multimodal run (0.532). This is single-run evidence that ResNet50 image features are much weaker than PCA RNA features in this setup, which favors putting budget into RNA-only refinements over broad fusion exploration. However, the run does not show whether images add complementary signal in fusion, or whether weighted fusion recovered by down-weighting the image branch, since the fusion weights were not reported and there is no chance-level reference. There are also no variance estimates, and it is unknown whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or different ResNet50 training choices, such as frozen vs fine-tuned, would be more informative.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best so far (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_019) recovered most of the large concat drop but still trails RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.535 acc). So the main open question on the multimodal side is whether the image encoder is the bottleneck, and ViT-L has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps config_019 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the image representation in the best-performing fusion setup. A clear gain would show the image encoder is limiting multimodal performance and could let fusion surpass RNA-only. No gain would further support RNA-only as the main direction. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it is a single-factor change from the strongest multimodal configuration and tests the largest untested design axis (image encoder). It also has a plausible chance of beating the current best, unlike transformer aggregation or the weaker RNA encoders, which existing evidence already disfavors. An image-only ViT-L run would be informative but would not directly tell us whether fusion can beat RNA-only.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the strongest multimodal configuration fixed (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, isolating the image representation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.520 (-0.130), and supporting F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.479 (-0.148). That is well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 avgpool best (0.688 / 0.659), below the ResNet50 image-only run (0.535), and close to the weak transformer-aggregation run (0.512 / 0.477). This is single-run evidence that swapping in ViT-L does not relieve the multimodal shortfall in this setup and may hurt, which further supports RNA-only as the main direction. Uncertainties remain: there are no variance estimates, and no ViT-L image-only run exists to tell whether the ViT-L features are themselves weak or interact poorly with fusion. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects ViT-L representations or untested factors such as feature dimensionality or scale relative to PCA, frozen vs fine-tuned use, the domain mismatch of ImageNet pretraining, or training hyperparameters tuned for ResNet50. The learned fusion weights were again not reported.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 recovered most of the concat drop (0.650 / 0.628) but still trails RNA-only, and ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.535). So it is still unclear whether images add complementary signal or whether weighted fusion simply down-weights the image branch. One untested explanation is a scale or dimensional imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and the image features. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the multimodal ResNet50 avgpool weighted setup from config_019 and changes only the RNA encoder to the lower-dimensional scVI-200. It can be read against two existing runs. Against RNA-only scVI (config_005, 0.635), it shows whether images help when the RNA representation is weaker and more compact. Against config_019, it shows whether the RNA encoder ranking (PCA > scVI) holds under fusion. If accuracy exceeds 0.635, that is evidence of complementary image signal. If it does not, that strengthens the case for focusing the budget on RNA-only refinements. 3. Why this is the best next run: it changes a single factor, has a clean baseline on both comparison axes, and addresses the most important open question, whether multimodal fusion can ever add value here. The alternatives are less useful at this point: transformer variants have already failed, and a ViT-L image-only run would mostly confirm features that already look weak.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the multimodal ResNet50 avgpool weighted-fusion setup from llm_summary_007 and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It reached 0.713 validation accuracy and 0.695 supporting F1, the best run so far: +0.078 / +0.076 over RNA-only scVI-200 (llm_summary_005, 0.635), +0.063 over the same fusion setup with PCA-2000 (llm_summary_007, 0.650), and +0.025 over the previous best RNA-only PCA-2000 run (0.688 / 0.659). The comparison with llm_summary_005 isolates adding the ResNet50 branch with weighted fusion and gives the first single-run evidence that images can add complementary signal, at least alongside compact scVI features. The comparison with llm_summary_007 shows that the RNA ranking seen in RNA-only runs (PCA > scVI) reversed under fusion, which is consistent with, but does not prove, the hypothesized scale or dimensional imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and image features, because scVI-200 differs from PCA-2000 in both encoder type and dimensionality. Uncertainties remain: there are no variance estimates, so the small margin over RNA-only PCA may partly be noise; the learned fusion weights were not reported; and it is untested whether PCA reduced to around 200 dimensions, other scVI latent sizes, or concat fusion with scVI would behave similarly.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about how well individual modalities, encoders, profile settings, aggregation methods or fusion strategies perform. 2) config_001 is the simplest pipeline: RNA-only, single profile, PCA (2000) encoding, with no aggregation or fusion. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time. Natural next steps from here are swapping the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002), and adding the image modality. 3) With a limited budget, a cheap baseline is the most useful first experiment. It anchors every later comparison and shows whether added complexity (multimodal, multiprofile, foundation-model encoders) actually helps, rather than assuming it does.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest pipeline as a first baseline: RNA-only input, a single profile, a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.494 (the primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.453. The F1 below accuracy hints that performance may be uneven across classes, though this is not confirmed. Because no other experiments exist yet, this is only an initial reference point. It is still unknown how other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding the image modality would compare. The result comes from a single run, so its sensitivity to run-to-run variability is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: we have one result, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001): accuracy 0.494, F1 0.453. Every other design axis is untested: RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality and fusion. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile, using simple avgpool aggregation. All else stays fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000). Any difference can therefore be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself, which is a core design choice that applies across all modalities. 3) Why now: this is a clean one-variable comparison against the only reference point. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it tells us whether multiprofile helps at all before we pay for a transformer. The answer determines whether multiprofile configurations deserve priority in the rest of the budget. Swapping the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) is an equally clean next step, but the profile effect likely affects more of the remaining configurations. One run is not conclusive, so a small difference should be read cautiously and confirmed on another encoder or modality.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the llm_summary_001 baseline fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000 encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average-pooling aggregation, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.519 (vs. 0.494) and an F1 of 0.480 (vs. 0.453). This modest gain of about 2.5 points on both metrics is an initial signal that multiprofile input with avgpool may help, though the effect cannot be separated from the use of avgpool as the aggregator, and F1 remains below accuracy, consistent with possibly uneven per-class performance. Both results come from single runs with no estimate of run-to-run variance, so the difference may fall within noise. It is still unknown whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), with the image modality, or with stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Only RNA-only runs with pca_n2000 exist. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a small gain (0.494 to 0.519 accuracy, with F1 up by a similar amount). That is a single-run difference, so it may be noise. The largest open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all, and 42 of the 48 untested configurations depend on it. 2) Test: config_011 runs image-only with resnet50, keeping multiprofile and avgpool fixed. Only the input modality changes relative to config_002, so the comparison isolates how informative images are compared with RNA under the same profile and aggregation setup. 3) Why now: Under a limited budget, this result decides how to treat the large multimodal part of the search space. If images are weak, multimodal gains are doubtful and effort should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If images are strong, fusion experiments become a priority. Testing RNA encoders or transformer aggregation first would refine only the RNA-only branch and say nothing about the modality question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the first image-only pipeline: a resnet50 image encoder with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, matching llm_summary_002 except that resnet50 image features replaced pca_n2000 RNA features. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.421 (vs. 0.519 for llm_summary_002) and an F1 of 0.412 (vs. 0.480). This is an initial signal that, in this setup, resnet50 image features are less predictive alone than PCA RNA features, though the modality effect cannot be separated from the specific encoders, and the smaller accuracy–F1 gap may hint at more even per-class performance. All results are single runs with no variance estimate and no reported chance level, so it remains unknown whether images carry meaningful signal above chance, whether other image encoders or aggregators would do better, and whether image features add complementary information to RNA in fusion, which the image-only comparison cannot answer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the best result is RNA-only multiprofile pca_n2000 with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.519, F1 0.480). The matching image-only resnet50 setup (config_011) is weaker (acc 0.421, F1 0.412). However, image-only performance cannot tell us whether image features add complementary information to RNA. Whether fusion helps is the central untested design question in this multimodal study. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the config_002 setup fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds resnet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Both unimodal arms are already measured, so any change can be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: this is a clean one-factor comparison on the study's most important open question. Either outcome is informative. A gain would justify exploring encoders and fusion types within multimodal setups. No gain or a loss would suggest putting more budget into RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. With single runs, small differences should be read cautiously, and F1 will serve as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested whether image features add information beyond RNA. It kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_002: multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added resnet50 image features through simple concat fusion, making this a one-factor test of adding the image modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 (vs. 0.519 for RNA-only and 0.421 for image-only) and an F1 of 0.519 (vs. 0.480 and 0.412). This is an initial signal that the image features may carry some information complementary to RNA, with a modest accuracy gain of about 1.6 points, a larger F1 gain of about 3.9 points, and a narrower accuracy–F1 gap that may hint at more even per-class performance. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the accuracy gain in particular may fall within run-to-run noise. It is also unknown whether the benefit comes from complementary signal or simply from the larger concatenated feature space, and whether it holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, other aggregators, or fusion methods beyond concat.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. RNA is clearly the stronger single modality (0.519 vs 0.421 for image-only), so the RNA representation is probably a major driver of performance. Yet only PCA has been tested, and the choice of RNA encoder is the largest open uncertainty. 2. What this tests: config_042 keeps the current best setup fixed and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor test of whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA when images are also present. 3. Why it is the best next step: It targets the design choice most likely to matter, given that RNA carries most of the signal, while staying near the best-known region of the search space. Whether scGPT helps or hurts, the result will tell us whether to keep exploring alternative RNA encoders (scVI is the natural follow-up) or to shift effort to secondary choices such as aggregation, fusion and image encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was a one-factor test of the RNA encoder: it kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and swapped the pca_n2000 RNA encoder for pretrained scGPT embeddings. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 (vs. 0.535) and an F1 of 0.573 (vs. 0.519), the best result so far and the largest single-step gain in the search (about 5.5 points on both metrics), with a similar accuracy–F1 gap of about 1.8 points. Because only the encoder changed, this is a fairly direct initial signal that scGPT beats PCA as the RNA representation in this multimodal concat setting, though it may also reflect differences such as embedding dimensionality. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, and it remains unknown whether the gain holds RNA-only or with other aggregators and fusion methods, how scVI or other RNA encoders would compare, and whether image features still add complementary value on top of scGPT embeddings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In single runs, multiprofile input with avgpool beat single-profile (+2.5 pts), concat fusion of resnet50 with PCA beat RNA-only (+1.6 acc, +3.9 F1), and swapping PCA for scGPT gave the largest gain (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1, config_042). Aggregation is the main axis never varied: every multiprofile run used avgpool. The transformer aggregator, weighted fusion and the ViT-L image encoder are all still unexplored. 2. Test: config_044 keeps the best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, resnet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This is a one-factor test of whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles beats simple averaging on the strongest representation. 3. Why now: It explores a completely untested design choice while staying anchored to the best configuration, so it can both reveal a large improvement and isolate the aggregation effect. Ablations such as scGPT RNA-only (config_008) or weighted fusion (config_043) are valuable but can follow once the aggregation question is settled. Any small difference should be read cautiously given single runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 was a one-factor test of the aggregation method. It kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, concat fusion) and replaced avgpool with a learned transformer aggregator across profiles. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (vs. 0.591) and an F1 of 0.687 (vs. 0.573), the best result so far and by far the largest single-step gain in the search (about 12.4 accuracy and 11.5 F1 points), with a slightly wider accuracy–F1 gap of about 2.8 points. Because only the aggregator changed, this is a fairly direct but still initial signal that transformer pooling outperforms simple averaging in this configuration, though it may also partly reflect added model capacity rather than attention-based pooling specifically. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, and it remains unknown whether the gain holds with PCA or other RNA encoders, in RNA-only or image-only settings, with weighted fusion or ViT-L image features, and whether image features still add value on top of scGPT with transformer aggregation.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + resnet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat), with 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That result came from large one-factor gains for scGPT over PCA and for transformer over avgpool aggregation. The only evidence that images help is a modest gain (about 1.6 accuracy points) in the weaker PCA/avgpool setting, which may be within run-to-run noise. Image-only resnet50 was also clearly weaker than RNA. So it is unclear whether the image branch still adds anything once RNA uses scGPT with transformer aggregation. 2. What this tests: config_009 removes only the image modality from config_044 and keeps scGPT, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. This isolates the modality's contribution in the strongest setup. It also shows whether the transformer gain holds without images. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Future work could explore either image-side choices (ViT-L, weighted fusion) or RNA-side and aggregation choices. This ablation decides which direction deserves the remaining experiments. If RNA-only matches or beats config_044, image variants are a poor use of budget. If it drops clearly, that justifies next testing ViT-L (config_050) or weighted fusion (config_045).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor ablation of the image modality: it kept the best configuration (llm_summary_006: multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, transformer aggregation) fixed and removed the resnet50 image branch and concat fusion, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.471 (vs. 0.715) and an F1 of 0.442 (vs. 0.687), a drop of about 24 points on both metrics. Because only the modality changed, this is an initial signal that the image branch contributes substantially in the scGPT+transformer setup, which would favor image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion over RNA-only variants. However, the result is surprisingly low, falling below the simpler RNA-only PCA baselines (0.494 single-profile, 0.519 multiprofile avgpool). This raises the possibility that the scGPT+transformer pipeline underperforms or trains unstably without images, rather than images simply adding complementary signal; an interaction among modality, encoder and aggregator also cannot be ruled out. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so it remains unknown whether this gap is robust, and an RNA-only scGPT+avgpool run or a repeat run would help distinguish a genuine image contribution from an RNA-only training problem.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) comes from scGPT + resnet50 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Replacing avgpool with the transformer gave the largest single gain (+12.4 points). Removing the image branch dropped accuracy to 0.471, below even the PCA RNA-only baselines. So it is unclear whether the transformer's benefit comes mainly from aggregating image profiles, or whether this RNA-only run simply trained poorly. Image-only has only been tested with avgpool (0.421). 2) Test: config_012 changes only the aggregator relative to config_011 (image-only resnet50, avgpool to transformer). If image-only accuracy rises sharply, the transformer gain is largely image-driven, which would favour image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion. If it stays near 0.42, the gain likely needs both modalities together, or the RNA-only result reflects a training problem. In that case config_008 (RNA-only scGPT with avgpool) would be the natural next check. 3) Why now: This single one-factor run helps explain the main performance driver found so far. It also helps interpret the surprising RNA-only ablation, and it guides how to spend the remaining budget on image-encoder and fusion choices rather than guessing.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor test of the aggregator in the image-only setting. It kept llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile, resnet50, no RNA or fusion) and replaced avgpool with a transformer, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.629 (vs. 0.421) and an F1 of 0.599 (vs. 0.412), gains of about 20.7 and 18.7 points with an accuracy–F1 gap of about 2.9 points. This is an initial signal that much of the transformer benefit seen in llm_summary_006 is available from image profiles alone: this image-only run beats every RNA-only run (best 0.519) and all avgpool multimodal runs (best 0.591), though it remains about 8.6 points below the scGPT+resnet50 transformer concat model (0.715), suggesting RNA may still add complementary value. Whether the gain reflects attention-based pooling or simply added capacity is unresolved, and it remains unexplained why RNA-only scGPT with a transformer scored so low (0.471); an RNA-only scGPT+avgpool run would help tell an RNA-side training problem from an aggregator–modality interaction. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion look promising but are not yet established.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best model so far is config_044 (scGPT + resnet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. The transformer aggregator gave the largest gains.
