Because this was a clean one-factor change, the initial observation is that the transformer aggregator, as configured here, performed much worse than avgpool. A drop this large, below even the single-profile result, suggests the transformer may have failed to train well (e.g., optimization, hyperparameter, data-size, or implementation issues) rather than revealing a basic limit of learned aggregation. This is a single run without a variance estimate, so it is untested whether a tuned transformer would recover or exceed avgpool, how this aggregator behaves with other encoders (e.g., ViT-L), RNA-only, or multimodal settings, and whether its failure shares a cause with the unexplained multimodal degradation. For now, avgpool remains the better-supported aggregator for multiprofile runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is clearly the best result so far (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It beats single-profile image-only (0.632), all RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532), all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519) and the transformer aggregator (0.494). The image encoder has not been varied at all, so it is unknown whether ResNet50 is a good choice or a bottleneck. 2) Test: config_014 keeps the best setup fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This cleanly isolates the effect of the image representation within the strongest pipeline found so far. 3) Why now: it is both exploitation and exploration. It could raise the best accuracy, and it answers an important open design question with a single-factor comparison. Its result will also guide later runs. If ViT-L helps, ViT-L variants of the single-profile and multimodal configurations become higher priority. If it does not, ResNet50 stays the reference encoder, and the remaining budget can go to diagnosing multimodal fusion under multiprofile avgpool (e.g., config_018).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best prior setup fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_007 at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether the image representation was a bottleneck. It reached validation accuracy 0.411 and F1 0.378, far below ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool and single-profile ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607). This is now the lowest result so far, below the RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532), all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519), and the transformer-aggregator run (0.494). Because this was a clean one-factor change, the initial observation is that ViT-L, as configured in this pipeline, performed much worse than ResNet50, so ResNet50 remains the reference image encoder. A drop this large for a typically strong encoder suggests possible feature-extraction, preprocessing or resolution mismatch, normalization, or downstream-training issues rather than a basic limit of ViT-L representations. This single run has no variance estimate. It remains untested whether a corrected or tuned ViT-L pipeline would recover, and whether this failure shares a cause with the unexplained multimodal and transformer-aggregator degradations. This lowers the priority of ViT-L variants of other configurations until the encoder pipeline is checked.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It improved on single-profile image-only (0.632 / 0.607) in a clean one-factor change. Profile setting has only been tested for images, so it is unknown whether the multiprofile gain is general or image-specific. Among RNA encoders, scVI-n200 is slightly the strongest (0.532 / 0.516 vs PCA 0.520 / 0.479), though that gap is small. Multimodal runs consistently fall to or below RNA-only levels. The transformer aggregator and ViT-L both performed poorly, so neither is a good choice for a clean test. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile avgpool, relative to scVI RNA-only (config_004). It shows whether multiprofile avgpool also helps the RNA modality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean, low-risk test of whether profile setting matters broadly, using the aggregator that has worked. It also provides the RNA-only multiprofile reference needed to interpret later multiprofile multimodal runs (e.g., config_030 or config_031). Given that fusion appears to track or degrade toward the RNA side, that reference is needed before spending budget on multimodal multiprofile configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the scVI-n200 RNA-only setup (llm_summary_006, 0.532 acc / 0.516 F1) and changed only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, to test whether the multiprofile gain seen for image-only ResNet50 also applies to RNA. It reached validation accuracy 0.721 and F1 0.681, a large improvement over single-profile scVI RNA-only and now the best result so far, above multiprofile image-only ResNet50 avgpool (0.688 / 0.659). Because this was a clean one-factor change and both modalities improved under the same change, the initial observation is that multiprofile input with avgpool helps beyond the image modality and is not image-specific, though profile setting and aggregation were introduced together and cannot be separated. The gain here (about +0.19 accuracy) is much larger than for images (about +0.06), which is notable and worth confirming. Each result is a single run with no variance estimate, so the small RNA-vs-image multiprofile gap (about 0.033) may not be meaningful. It remains untested whether multiprofile multimodal fusion (e.g., scVI + ResNet50 avgpool) would beat either single modality or still show the unexplained fusion degradation, and whether the PCA RNA encoder gains similarly. This run now serves as the RNA-only multiprofile reference for those comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matter. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest reference point. Every more complex choice can be compared against it with one change at a time: a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), adding images, moving to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, or adding fusion. 3. Spending the first experiment on this baseline gives a lower bound for accuracy and F1. It also keeps later comparisons interpretable, so we do not have to start with a complex multimodal model whose result could not be attributed to any single design decision.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first reference point with the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA-2000 RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 (primary metric), with a validation F1 of 0.5727 as supporting evidence. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only a baseline and does not show whether modality, encoder type, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. Future single-change comparisons against this setup, such as a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), adding images, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, or fusion, are needed to judge the impact of each design choice, and variance across runs or seeds is also still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727). We do not yet know the effect of any design choice. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor, the profile setting. It moves from singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the same RNA-only PCA-2000 setup. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. 3) Why now: Profile setting cuts across every modality and encoder in the search space, so this result informs a large share of the remaining configurations. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity aggregation, which gives a clean read on the multiprofile effect before testing transformer aggregation, other encoders, images, or fusion. A gain here would point the search toward multiprofile variants; no gain would steer the budget toward encoder or modality changes.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from the llm_summary_001 baseline and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, using no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6390 (+0.048, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6197 (+0.047) as supporting evidence. This suggests that multiprofile input with simple mean pooling may help in the RNA-only PCA setting. However, multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so their separate contributions cannot be told apart, and each configuration was evaluated only once, so run-to-run or seed variance is unknown and the gain may be partly noise. It also remains untested whether the benefit carries over to learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or fused modalities, or a more expressive aggregator such as a transformer, so multiprofile variants are a promising direction rather than an established improvement.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool (config_001 to config_002) raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.639, and F1 rose by a similar amount. That makes multiprofile the most promising direction so far. However, each setup was run only once, and the aggregation method has not been varied. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether a more expressive aggregator adds value beyond simple mean pooling. It also checks whether the multiprofile gain holds up under a different aggregator. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest evidence while changing exactly one design choice, so the result is easy to interpret. The avgpool-versus-transformer choice recurs in every multiprofile configuration (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal), so resolving it early informs many later experiments. Encoder and modality questions can follow once aggregation is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6390 to 0.6530 (+0.014, primary metric; +0.062 over the single-profile baseline llm_summary_001), and validation F1 rose from 0.6197 to 0.6283 (+0.009) as supporting evidence. Because only aggregation differed, this is a direct comparison, and it suggests transformer aggregation may give a modest benefit over mean pooling in this setting. Each configuration was run only once and seed or run-to-run variance is unknown, so this small gain may fall within noise; it also remains untested whether the transformer advantage holds with learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only, or multimodal fused configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA-2000 series suggests multiprofile input helps (+0.048 accuracy). Transformer aggregation adds a smaller gain (+0.014), with F1 moving the same way. Each result comes from a single run, so the aggregation gain may be noise. The image modality, the defining question of multimodal profiling, has not been tested at all. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer; config_003). It only adds ResNet50 image features with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing against config_003 directly tests whether adding images improves accuracy and F1 beyond RNA alone. Concat is the minimal fusion choice, so weighted fusion can be compared in a later experiment. 3) Whether to use images at all is the largest open design decision and determines which half of the remaining search space deserves budget. Swapping the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) would only refine a single axis within the modality already tested. Building on the strongest known configuration also keeps this a reasonable exploitation step while it serves as an exploration step.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only configuration fixed (llm_summary_003: PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion, the first test of the image modality. Validation accuracy dropped sharply from 0.6530 to 0.5399 (-0.113, primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.6283 to 0.5245 (-0.104) as supporting evidence. This multimodal result is also below the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.5907), so in this setup, adding images through plain concatenation clearly hurt rather than helped. Because the image encoder and concat fusion had to be introduced together, the evidence cannot tell whether the image features carry little useful signal or whether the fusion itself is the problem (for example, imbalance between the two feature sets). The result comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, and untested options include weighted fusion, an image-only configuration, and other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), so the value of the image modality remains open rather than ruled out.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input helped RNA-only PCA (0.591 to 0.639), and transformer aggregation added a modest gain (0.653). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_020) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.540, with F1 falling similarly. Because the image encoder and fusion were introduced together, we cannot tell whether the image features lack signal or plain concatenation is the problem, for example the image features swamping the RNA features. 2. Test: config_021 is identical to config_020 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This single-change comparison isolates the effect of fusion. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.653, concat was the bottleneck and multimodal fusion remains viable. If it stays well below the RNA-only result, the ResNet50 image features themselves are probably unhelpful or harmful here. 3. Why now: Multimodal settings make up most of the remaining search space. Learning whether fusion choice can rescue the image modality decides whether those configurations deserve budget, so this experiment is worth more than an incremental RNA-encoder test. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image-only checks remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the multimodal llm_summary_004 configuration (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) but changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted, which isolates the effect of fusion choice. Validation accuracy recovered from 0.5399 to 0.6501 (+0.110, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.5245 to 0.6275 (+0.103) as supporting evidence. This suggests concat fusion, not the presence of image features alone, was responsible for the earlier drop. However, the result is essentially tied with the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_003: 0.6530 accuracy, 0.6283 F1; -0.003 accuracy here), so there is no evidence yet that ResNet50 images add useful signal. Weighted fusion may simply be down-weighting the image branch, but the learned weights were not inspected, image-only performance is untested, and each configuration was run once with unknown seed variance. Multimodal configurations therefore remain viable but unproven, and natural next steps are an image-only check, inspecting the fusion weights, and trying learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) under weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input with transformer aggregation is the best RNA-only setup so far (0.653 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images hurt badly with concat fusion (0.540). With weighted fusion it only tied RNA-only (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). So it is still unclear whether the ResNet50 image features carry any useful signal, or whether weighted fusion is simply down-weighting the image branch. 2. What this tests: an image-only model with the same multiprofile transformer setup, swapping only the modality relative to config_003. This isolates how much predictive signal the image branch carries by itself. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: About half the remaining configurations are multimodal. If images alone perform near chance, effort should shift to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and image fusion can be deprioritized. If images are reasonably strong, the tie suggests the fusion is under-using them, which justifies trying ViT-L and other fusion variants. Either outcome sharply narrows the search, so it is a better use of budget than further multimodal guesses.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 was the first image-only test. It used the multiprofile transformer setup from llm_summary_003 (ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA, no fusion), so modality was the only change. Validation accuracy was 0.5793 (primary metric), with F1 0.5631 as supporting evidence. That is clearly below the RNA-only counterpart (0.6530 accuracy, -0.074; F1 -0.065), slightly below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.5907), and above the concat multimodal model (0.5399), which suggests ResNet50 images carry some predictive signal but less than PCA RNA features in this setup. Because the image-only model outscored the concat model that also had RNA, the evidence is consistent with concat fusion actively interfering rather than images being useless. However, the number of classes and the chance level are not given, so how much image signal exists beyond chance is unclear. It also remains unresolved whether the weighted-fusion tie (llm_summary_005) reflects down-weighting of images or images being redundant with RNA, since fusion weights were not inspected. Every result comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, and stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) are untested.

selection_reason: 1) Existing evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. RNA-only PCA multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_003) scored 0.653 accuracy, versus 0.579 for image-only. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 images only tied that result (0.650), and concat fusion hurt it. Multiprofile and transformer aggregation look beneficial. The biggest untested design choice is the RNA representation, because every run with RNA so far used PCA-2000. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This directly shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation improves on PCA. 3) Why now: since RNA drives performance and image gains are unproven, the RNA encoder is the dimension most likely to raise the ceiling. A single-change comparison against config_003 is clean. The result also decides which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal weighted-fusion runs, which is more informative than further image or fusion variants built on PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.6530 to 0.4106 (-0.242, primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.6283 to 0.3785 (-0.250) as supporting evidence. This is the lowest result so far, below the image-only run (0.5793) and the concat multimodal run (0.5399), and because only the encoder changed, it suggests that scGPT embeddings as used here are much worse than PCA-2000 in this pipeline, so PCA remains the better RNA encoder to carry into weighted-fusion runs for now. It remains unclear whether the drop reflects scGPT's representation itself or how it was applied (for example, frozen versus fine-tuned embeddings, gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, or aggregator hyperparameters tuned for PCA); the result also comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, chance level is not given, and scVI is still untested, so learned RNA encoders are not ruled out in general.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. The best result is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (0.6530 accuracy / 0.6283 F1). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 images only tied it (0.6501), and image-only scored lower (0.5793). So the RNA representation appears to drive performance. Among RNA encoders, scGPT dropped accuracy sharply (0.4106), while scVI is still untested. It is unclear whether learned RNA encoders fail in general or only scGPT as applied here. 2) Test: config_006 keeps config_003 fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. This directly isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. It shows whether a compact learned latent space can beat or match PCA, and whether the scGPT result reflects learned encoders broadly. 3) Value: the RNA encoder is the choice with the largest observed effect, and the result decides which encoder to carry into the many remaining multimodal and weighted-fusion configurations. Resolving it now, with one clean comparison, avoids spending budget on scVI multimodal runs that would confound encoder and fusion effects. Testing ViT-L images is a reasonable later step, but images currently add little.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI with a 200-dimensional latent. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6530 to 0.7150 (+0.062, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.6283 to 0.6872 (+0.059) as supporting evidence. This is the best result so far, well above the weighted-fusion multimodal run (0.6501) and far above scGPT (0.4106). Because only the encoder changed, it suggests scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this pipeline, and that the poor scGPT result does not mean learned RNA encoders fail in general, which makes scVI the leading encoder to carry into weighted-fusion multimodal runs. It remains uncertain whether the gain comes from scVI's learned latent space itself or from factors such as its much lower dimensionality interacting with transformer hyperparameters originally used with PCA. All results are single runs with unknown seed variance, chance level is not given, and it is untested whether ResNet50 or stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) add signal on top of scVI under weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: scVI-200 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (config_006) is the clear leader at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. That is +0.062 over PCA-2000 in an otherwise identical setup. Separately, weighted fusion recovered from the large concat drop, but it only tied PCA RNA-only (0.6501 vs 0.6530). The image-only ResNet50 run (0.5793) shows images carry some signal, so whether they add value on top of RNA is still unresolved. 2. Test: config_033 changes one factor from the best configuration, adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion while keeping scVI, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation fixed. It asks whether images add complementary signal to a stronger RNA representation, or whether the PCA tie reflects image features being redundant or down-weighted. 3. Why now: this is a single-variable extension of the best model, so it exploits the strongest evidence while answering the key open question of whether multimodality is worth pursuing. If it clearly beats 0.715, it justifies testing ViT-L images next. If it ties or falls short, the budget can shift toward refining the RNA-only scVI setup, such as aggregation and profile ablations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the best configuration (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion, testing whether images add complementary signal on top of the stronger RNA representation. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.7150 to 0.5420 (-0.173, primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.6872 to 0.4833 (-0.204) as supporting evidence. This result is below the PCA-2000 weighted-fusion run (0.6501), below image-only ResNet50 (0.5793), and close to the failed PCA concat run (0.5399), so in this setup adding images to scVI clearly hurt, and the run gives no support for moving on to ViT-L images. It suggests the budget should favor refining RNA-only scVI, but it is unclear why weighted fusion tied with PCA yet degraded with scVI: possible explanations include scale or dimensionality imbalance between the 200-d scVI latent and ResNet50 features, fusion-weight behavior (weights were not inspected), or hyperparameters tuned for other setups. The result is also a single run with unknown seed variance, so it does not rule out multimodality in general.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation is clearly the best configuration so far (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). Adding ResNet50 images to scVI hurt badly (0.542), so the RNA-only scVI direction deserves exploitation. Within that direction, the aggregation choice is the least settled. Transformer beat avgpool by only +0.014 accuracy with PCA in a single run, which may be noise, and that comparison has never been made with scVI. scVI's much smaller 200-d latent could change how the two aggregators behave. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the aggregation (transformer to avgpool) on the best scVI multiprofile setup. It isolates whether transformer aggregation actually helps, or whether simpler mean pooling performs as well or better with the stronger encoder. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it is a single-variable comparison in the most promising region of the search space. It has a real chance of matching or beating the current best, and either outcome sharpens the aggregation conclusion. Testing the single-profile scVI setup (config_004) would ask about profile setting, which already had the more robust effect (+0.048 with PCA). Further image or multimodal runs currently have weak support.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration fixed (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 RNA-only, multiprofile, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, to test whether the small transformer advantage seen with PCA (+0.014, llm_summary_002 vs 003) also holds with scVI. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.7150 to 0.5729 (-0.142, primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.6872 to 0.5730 (-0.114) as supporting evidence. The result is also below PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.6390) and even the single-profile PCA baseline (0.5907). Because only aggregation changed, this suggests transformer aggregation matters much more with scVI than with PCA, and that scVI's advantage over PCA depends on the aggregator, so scVI plus transformer remains the configuration to build on. It is unclear why mean pooling hurts scVI so much. Possible explanations include mean pooling washing out information in the compact 200-d latent, or hyperparameters suited to other setups, but neither has been tested. All results come from single runs with unknown seed variance, and the single-profile scVI setting is still untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, most interpretable baseline. Many later experiments can be compared against it by changing one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (config_004 for scVI, config_007 for scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (config_002 for multiprofile avgpool), the modality (config_010 for image-only), and adding fusion (config_016 for multimodal). 3) With a limited budget, a cheap, low-variance reference point is the most efficient first experiment. It sets a performance floor and avoids confounding several design choices, so it should be run before testing more complex multimodal or multiprofile models.
experiment_summary: This first experiment (llm_summary_001) established a baseline using an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.480, which gives an initial reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons (e.g., scVI or scGPT RNA encoders, multiprofile avgpool, image-only, multimodal fusion). Because no other configurations have been evaluated, it is unknown whether this performance is strong or weak relative to alternatives, and no conclusions can yet be drawn about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. Run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized, so small future differences from this baseline should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. We do not yet know how much the image modality contributes, and that is the largest open question because it determines whether the many multimodal and image configurations are worth testing. 2) Test: config_010 is the image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model, with no aggregation or fusion. Against config_001 it changes only the modality, so it directly measures how informative images are compared with RNA. 3) Why now: knowing the strength of the image modality alone sets the reference point for later fusion experiments. If images are weak, the search can focus on RNA encoders and profile settings. If they are comparable or stronger, multimodal fusion becomes a more promising direction. This is the most useful uncertainty to reduce with the next experiment. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI or scGPT) or adding multiprofile pooling are natural follow-ups after that.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.516), slightly above the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.519, F1 0.480). This is an initial sign that images alone are at least comparable to RNA alone, with a somewhat larger margin on F1. Because modality and encoder changed together (PCA vs ResNet50), the comparison reflects these specific encoders rather than the modalities in general. The roughly 1.3-point accuracy gap is small and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so it remains uncertain whether either modality is truly stronger. The result does make multimodal fusion and alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) reasonable next comparisons.

selection_reason: Evidence: the two single-profile baselines are close. RNA-only PCA reached 0.519 accuracy (F1 0.480) and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.532 (F1 0.516). This suggests the two modalities are roughly comparable, though variance is uncharacterized. The biggest open question is whether combining them adds complementary signal. Test: config_016 is single-profile multimodal with concat fusion, using exactly the PCA and ResNet50 encoders already tested. It therefore isolates the effect of fusion against both unimodal references, with no confound from encoder, profile setting or aggregation. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference point for testing weighted fusion later. Why now: whether to fuse is a top-level decision for the rest of the search. A clear gain over 0.532 would point the budget toward multimodal extensions such as aggregation, weighted fusion and stronger encoders. No gain would point toward refining unimodal encoders and profile settings instead.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested a single-profile multimodal model that concatenates the same PCA (n=2000) RNA and ResNet50 image encoders used in the two unimodal baselines, with no aggregation, so fusion is the only change relative to those references. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1 0.479), nearly identical to RNA-only (0.519, F1 0.480) and below image-only (0.532, F1 0.516). This is an initial sign that simple concat fusion adds no complementary signal here, and the near-exact match to RNA-only might hint that the fused model leans on RNA features, though that is a hypothesis the current evidence does not test. Because run-to-run variance is uncharacterized and only one fusion method was tried, it is unclear whether the shortfall versus image-only is real, or whether other fusion schemes (e.g., weighted fusion, feature normalization or balancing) or other encoders would let fusion help. For now, this result does not support prioritizing multimodal concat over refining unimodal encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: all three runs are single-profile. Image-only ResNet50 is slightly best (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). RNA-only PCA (0.519) and concat fusion (0.520) are nearly tied, and fusion gave no benefit. The profile-setting and aggregation axis is completely untested, even though it applies to every model type. 2) This run changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, on the current best configuration (config_010). That isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregation as the reference before trying transformer aggregation. 3) It explores an important unmeasured design axis while building on the strongest result so far. A clear gain would point the rest of the search toward multiprofile settings across modalities. No gain would let us drop many multiprofile configurations. That makes it more informative than tweaking fusion, which has already shown no benefit, or swapping encoders right now.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested the best configuration so far (image-only, ResNet50 from llm_summary_002) with one change: single-profile was switched to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.523 (F1 0.508), slightly below the single-profile image-only result (0.532, F1 0.516). This is an initial sign that combining profiles by simple average pooling does not help this image-only setup, but the roughly 0.9-point drop is small and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so it may be noise rather than a real decline. The result is specific to this configuration. It is unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer) or multiprofile settings with RNA-only or multimodal models would behave differently, so it is premature to drop the multiprofile axis entirely.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). It is ahead of RNA-only PCA (0.519) and PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion (0.520), and multiprofile avgpool did not help (0.523). All gaps are about 1 point with unknown run-to-run variance. The encoder axis is completely unexplored for both modalities. 2) This experiment changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps the best setup otherwise: image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion. It isolates whether representation quality, which may matter more than profile or fusion choices, can improve the strongest modality. 3) It exploits the current best direction while answering a key design question with a single controlled change. The answer also guides later multimodal choices: whether to pair RNA with ViT-L or ResNet50, and whether a stronger image encoder lets fusion add value. Testing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is a close alternative and a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion, from llm_summary_002) and made one change, replacing the ResNet50 image encoder with an ImageNet ViT-L encoder. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.208 (F1 0.172), compared with 0.532 (F1 0.516) for ResNet50 and about 0.52 for every other configuration tested. This drop of about 32 points is far larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen so far, so it is unlikely to be run-to-run noise, and because the encoder was the only setting changed, it indicates that this ViT-L setup performs much worse here than ResNet50. It is still unclear whether the cause is ViT-L's representations being poorly suited to these cell images, or an implementation or optimization problem specific to this run (e.g., preprocessing, input resolution, feature extraction, or training instability), so the result should be checked or debugged before ViT-L is ruled out, and ResNet50 remains the safer image encoder for multimodal follow-ups and RNA-encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Every working configuration so far sits near 0.52-0.53 accuracy, with image-only ResNet50 single-profile slightly best (0.532, F1 0.516). The ViT-L run collapsed to 0.208, so ResNet50 is the safer image encoder. RNA has only been tested with PCA, and concat fusion with PCA RNA matched RNA-only almost exactly. That leaves open whether PCA is a weak RNA representation that holds back both RNA-only and multimodal models. RNA encoder choice affects most of the remaining search space (scVI and scGPT appear in about two-thirds of the untested configurations), yet it is entirely unexplored. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI (n=200) relative to the config_001 baseline, keeping RNA-only, single-profile, and no aggregation or fusion. This isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: A clear scVI gain would point to better multimodal follow-ups, such as config_028 or config_029 with scVI and ResNet50. Another result near 0.52 would suggest that RNA representation is not the bottleneck and shift priority toward fusion type (e.g., config_017 weighted) or transformer aggregation. This one-factor change reduces uncertainty on a high-leverage design axis more than further tuning of the already-mapped image or concat-fusion settings.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the RNA-only, single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 and made one change, replacing the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder with scVI (n=200). Validation accuracy dropped to 0.427 (F1 0.417), about 9 points below PCA (0.519, F1 0.480) and the roughly 0.52-0.53 range of all other working configurations. This is several times larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen so far, so it is unlikely to be noise alone, and it is an initial sign that this scVI setup is a weaker RNA representation than PCA here, which offers no support for the hypothesis that PCA is the bottleneck. It remains unclear whether the drop comes from scVI itself or from this particular setup (e.g., the much smaller latent size of 200 vs 2000 PCA components, scVI training or preprocessing choices), and scGPT is still untested. Multimodal follow-ups using scVI (e.g., config_028/029) therefore look less promising for now, and fusion type (e.g., weighted fusion) or aggregation choices may be the better next axes to test.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The working configurations cluster around 0.52-0.53 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 is best (0.532, F1 0.516). Concat fusion of PCA and ResNet50 (config_016) matched RNA-only (0.520, F1 0.479) and fell slightly below image-only. That suggests either the modalities are not complementary, or naive concat lets the fused model lean on the weaker RNA features. Only one fusion method has been tried, so this is the main open question about multimodal value. 2) Test: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 (single-profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, no aggregation) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. If weighted fusion reaches or exceeds image-only, the problem was how the modalities were combined. If it stays near 0.52, that is stronger evidence that the RNA signal adds little and that unimodal image refinements or other RNA encoders such as scGPT deserve priority. 3) Why now: It is a clean one-factor test of the fusion axis, built on the best-supported encoders. It avoids the failed ViT-L and the weaker scVI, and its result tells us whether the remaining multimodal configurations are worth budget.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the multimodal concat configuration from llm_summary_003 (single-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell to 0.435 (F1 0.423), about 8.5 points below concat (0.520, F1 0.479) and about 10 points below image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516). That gap is much larger than the roughly 1-point differences seen among working configurations, and fusion was the only setting changed, so this weighted-fusion setup appears to perform worse than concat here and gives no support to the hypothesis that the way modalities were combined was what held fusion below image-only. It remains unclear whether the drop reflects weighted fusion itself or this particular implementation or optimization (e.g., weight initialization or learning, feature scale imbalance between PCA and ResNet50 features, training instability), and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized. Across two fusion methods, multimodal models have not beaten image-only, which weakly suggests that unimodal image refinements or untested RNA encoders such as scGPT deserve priority over further PCA+ResNet50 fusion variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Among working setups, ResNet50 image-only single-profile is best (0.532 acc, 0.516 F1). PCA RNA-only (0.519) and PCA+ResNet50 concat (0.520) are close behind. scVI (0.427), weighted fusion (0.435) and ViT-L (0.208) all fell clearly short. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, and many remaining multimodal configurations (040-051) depend on it. 2) Test: Swap PCA for scGPT in the RNA-only single-profile baseline (config_001), with everything else unchanged. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA. That would show whether the RNA side is the bottleneck that kept fusion from beating image-only. 3) Why now: It resolves the largest remaining uncertainty on the encoder axis with a clean one-factor change. If scGPT beats PCA, scGPT+ResNet50 fusion and multiprofile follow-ups become worth testing. If it does not, those 12+ configurations can be deprioritized in favor of refining image-only models, such as transformer aggregation in config_012.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only, single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 and made one change, replacing the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder with scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.586 (F1 0.574), about 6.7 points above PCA (0.519, F1 0.480) and about 5.4 points above the previous best, image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516), so it is now the best configuration tested. Because the encoder was the only setting changed, and the gain is several times larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen among working configurations, this is an initial sign that scGPT gives a stronger RNA representation than PCA here, and it is consistent with the hypothesis that the RNA representation limited the earlier PCA-based fusion. That hypothesis is not yet tested, since run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, scGPT has been run only once, and it is unknown whether scGPT's advantage carries over to multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (concat or weighted) or to multiprofile settings, so scGPT+ResNet50 fusion and scGPT multiprofile follow-ups are now the most informative next experiments.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only is the best result so far (0.586 acc, F1 0.574). It beats PCA (0.519) and image-only ResNet50 (0.532) by margins well above the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations. Concat fusion of PCA with ResNet50 (0.520) matched PCA RNA-only and did not beat image-only. Weighted fusion did clearly worse (0.435). It is still untested whether fusion failed because the PCA representation was weak. 2) This experiment keeps the previously tested single-profile, ResNet50, concat fusion setup and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. Two comparisons follow: against config_016 it isolates the RNA encoder's effect inside fusion, and against scGPT RNA-only (config_007) it shows whether adding ResNet50 image features adds complementary signal on top of the strongest RNA representation. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it can produce a new best configuration and also answer the main open question, whether multimodality helps at all. It uses concat, the better-behaved fusion method, and avoids confounding the result with multiprofile or aggregation changes. Those changes have shown no benefit so far and can be tested afterwards with config_008/009.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the single-profile concat fusion setup from llm_summary_003 (ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 (F1 0.455), about 7.9 points below scGPT RNA-only (0.586, F1 0.574) and also below image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516). Against PCA+ResNet50 concat (0.520, F1 0.479), it was about 1.3 points lower, which is near the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations. Because adding ResNet50 features through concat was the only change from scGPT RNA-only, and the drop is far larger than that noise, this is an initial sign that this concat fusion degrades rather than complements the strongest RNA representation. It also shows that the stronger RNA encoder did not rescue fusion, so it gives no support to the hypothesis that weak PCA features caused the earlier fusion shortfall. It remains unclear whether the cause is concat fusion itself or this implementation or optimization (e.g., feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between scGPT and ResNet50 features, lack of normalization, or training dynamics). Each configuration has also been run only once. Across three fusion runs, no multimodal model has beaten its best unimodal component, so scGPT RNA-only remains the best configuration, and diagnosing or normalizing the fusion pipeline may matter more than further encoder swaps within it.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT RNA-only single-profile (config_007) is the clear best so far, at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Three fusion attempts have not beaten their best unimodal component. Multiprofile has been tested only once, on image-only ResNet50 with avgpool, where it gave a small drop (0.532 to 0.523) that is within likely noise. So it is still unknown whether multiprofile helps RNA models, and in particular the strongest RNA encoder. 2) What this tests: config_008 changes only the profile setting of the best configuration, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates the profile and aggregation effect on scGPT RNA and checks whether the earlier image-only avgpool result carries over to RNA. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest finding (scGPT) with one logical extension and could raise the best score. It also resolves an important, under-tested design axis. Avgpool is the simplest baseline aggregation, so it should come before the learned transformer variant (config_009). A gain would justify testing transformer aggregation next. A loss would strengthen the case that single-profile scGPT is the configuration to refine.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration, scGPT RNA-only single-profile (llm_summary_008: accuracy 0.586, F1 0.574), and changed only the profile setting, switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.579 (F1 0.563), about 0.6 points lower in accuracy and 1.1 points lower in F1. That gap is within the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations, so it does not show a real decline, and scGPT single-profile remains the nominal best. Together with the similarly small drop for image-only ResNet50 (0.532 to 0.523), this is an initial, weak sign that avgpool multiprofile aggregation does not help in either modality, though neither drop clearly exceeds noise. Multiprofile and avgpool were changed together, so their effects cannot be separated. Each configuration has been run only once, and it remains untested whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer) or multiprofile in multimodal settings would behave differently, so the multiprofile axis is not ruled out, but it currently offers no evidence of gains over single-profile scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-complexity baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later comparisons can build on one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only performance, and the added value of multimodal fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a simple anchor makes every later experiment interpretable as a single-factor change. It also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win, so it is the most informative first experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678, with a validation F1 of 0.646. Because no other experiments have been completed, this result is a reference point only. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Later single-factor comparisons are needed to find which design choices matter, and run-to-run variability around this baseline is still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: only one result exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.678, F1 0.646). We know nothing yet about which design factors matter. 2. Test: config_002 changes a single factor, single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), and keeps the PCA RNA encoder. This isolates whether pooling several profiles per sample helps accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: profile setting affects every model family (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal), so learning its effect early will shape how much of the remaining budget goes to multiprofile versus single-profile configurations. Avgpool is the cleanest first test before trying transformer aggregation. Testing encoder or modality would be equally clean, but the profile effect has the broadest bearing on the rest of the search.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) setup from baseline llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with simple average pooling (no image encoder or fusion). Validation accuracy fell from 0.678 to 0.653 (about -0.025), and validation F1 fell from 0.646 to 0.628 (about -0.018). This suggests that average-pooled multiprofile input did not help this RNA-only PCA model and may have hurt it. However, this is a single pair of runs with unknown run-to-run variability, and the effect cannot be attributed to multiprofile input in general rather than to avgpool aggregation specifically. It also remains unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer), other RNA encoders, or image-only and multimodal models would respond differently to multiprofile input.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Single-profile (0.678 accuracy) did better than avgpool multiprofile (0.653). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though most of the remaining search space (image-only and the 36 multimodal configurations) depends on how useful image features are. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 baseline measures how much signal images carry by themselves. It uses the simplest setting, with no aggregation or fusion, so it is directly comparable to the RNA-only single-profile baseline (config_001). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If images are weak, the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If images are competitive or complementary, multimodal fusion becomes a priority. Follow-ups that refine RNA (such as transformer aggregation in config_003 or scVI in config_004) answer narrower questions and can come after this broader uncertainty is reduced.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the first image-only baseline: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 and a validation F1 of 0.610, about 0.059 accuracy and 0.036 F1 below the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.678 / 0.646). This suggests images carry real but weaker standalone signal than RNA in this setup, though the comparison changes both modality and encoder (PCA vs. ResNet50), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. It is still unknown whether image features are complementary to RNA in multimodal fusion, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would change the picture, and how large run-to-run variability is, given that each setting is a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline is the best so far (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Average-pooled multiprofile input lowered RNA-only performance by about 0.025 accuracy. The image-only ResNet50 single-profile model is weaker (0.619 / 0.610) but carries real signal. The main open question is whether that image signal adds to RNA or is redundant with it. 2. Test: config_016 joins the two already-tested single-profile components (PCA RNA and ResNet50 image) with simple concat fusion. Both parent baselines are known, so any change can be attributed to adding the image modality, without confounding from a new encoder, aggregation or fusion method. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the search space, so whether images help on top of RNA is the most important design question to settle early. A gain would justify exploring fusion types, image encoders and aggregation. No gain would point the budget toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and learned aggregation instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested the first multimodal configuration. It combined the two known single-profile components, a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and a ResNet50 image encoder, with simple concat fusion and no aggregation, to see whether image signal adds to RNA. Validation accuracy was 0.224 and validation F1 was 0.184. That is far below both unimodal parents: RNA-only llm_summary_001 reached 0.678 / 0.646 and image-only llm_summary_003 reached 0.619 / 0.610. A collapse this large, to well below the weaker single modality, looks more like a failure of this particular run or setup (for example, feature-scale mismatch between PCA and ResNet50 embeddings, optimization instability, or an implementation or pipeline issue) than evidence that images are merely redundant with RNA. It should therefore not yet be read as showing that multimodal fusion or concat fusion inherently hurts. This is a single run with unknown variability, and the cause has not been diagnosed. Whether image features are complementary to RNA remains unresolved, so verifying or rerunning this configuration (or trying a normalized or alternative fusion) is advisable before using it to redirect the budget away from multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA single-profile is the best so far (0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1), and image-only ResNet50 trails it (0.619 / 0.610). The first multimodal run (config_016, PCA+ResNet50, concat) collapsed to 0.224 / 0.184, far below either unimodal parent. That pattern points to a fusion or setup failure, such as feature-scale mismatch, rather than to images being redundant. It is currently the largest unresolved question in the study. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 (single-profile, PCA, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to at least unimodal-level performance, the collapse was specific to concat fusion, and multimodal models remain viable. If it also collapses, the problem likely lies in combining these encoders or in the multimodal pipeline itself. 3) Why now: the multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Diagnosing this failure with a clean single-factor change tells us whether to keep investing budget in multimodal models or shift it toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT). That makes it more valuable than an incremental unimodal test.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the collapsed multimodal setup from llm_summary_004 (single-profile, PCA 2000-component RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy recovered from 0.224 to 0.635 and F1 from 0.184 to 0.618. That is above the image-only baseline (llm_summary_003: 0.619 / 0.610) but still below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.678 / 0.646). In this single-factor comparison the concat collapse did not recur with weighted fusion, so multimodal models look viable, but adding images has not yet beaten RNA alone. Each setting is a single run with unknown variability, and the concat failure was never diagnosed (e.g., feature-scale mismatch, instability, or a pipeline bug), so the recovery cannot be firmly attributed to weighted fusion. It also remains open whether normalized concat, other fusion methods, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or multiprofile input would let multimodal models exceed the RNA-only baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) is the best result so far. Single-profile setups have beaten avgpool multiprofile. Multimodal models have not yet exceeded RNA alone (weighted fusion 0.635; concat collapsed). The RNA encoder, which drives the strongest modality, has never been varied, so it is the largest untested design choice for the current best direction. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, in the RNA-only single-profile baseline. This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the answer feeds directly into which RNA encoder to carry into later multiprofile and multimodal runs, which is better than spending runs on fusion or aggregation variants built on a possibly suboptimal encoder. It is also a low-risk, interpretable comparison against a known reference. The scGPT single-profile run (config_007) is the natural follow-up to finish the encoder comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the RNA-only single-profile setup of the best baseline (llm_summary_001) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.678 to 0.435 (about -0.24) and F1 from 0.646 to 0.423, which also puts it below image-only ResNet50 (0.619) and weighted multimodal fusion (0.635). In this single-factor comparison, the scVI-200 configuration as run was much worse than PCA-2000, so PCA remains the reference RNA encoder for later runs. However, this is one run with unknown variability, and the drop cannot be attributed to learned latents in general. It may instead reflect this scVI setup, such as latent size, scVI training or convergence, input preprocessing, or a pipeline issue, so whether a better-tuned scVI or another encoder (e.g., scGPT, config_007) could match or beat PCA remains unresolved.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (config_001: 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) is still the best run. scVI-200 did much worse (0.435). Whether the RNA encoder choice favors PCA in general, or only PCA over this scVI setup, is unresolved. The third encoder, scGPT, is untested. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT, keeping the best RNA-only single-profile setup. This completes the single-factor RNA encoder comparison and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding can match or beat PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: RNA is the strongest modality so far, and the RNA encoder choice applies to roughly a third of the remaining multimodal and multiprofile configurations (all scGPT variants). Settling it now lets later aggregation and fusion experiments build on the best RNA representation. If scGPT also falls short, PCA is confirmed as the RNA backbone and many scGPT configurations can be deprioritized. This experiment is cleaner and more decision-relevant than adding further multiprofile or multimodal factors at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the RNA-only single-profile setup of the best baseline (llm_summary_001) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (2000 components) to scGPT embeddings, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. This completes the single-factor RNA encoder comparison. Validation accuracy was 0.537 and F1 was 0.518. That is well below PCA-2000 (0.678 / 0.646) and above scVI-200 (0.435 / 0.423), and it also trails image-only ResNet50 (0.619) and weighted multimodal fusion (0.635). In this comparison, both learned encoders as run fell short of PCA, so PCA remains the reference RNA backbone, and scGPT-based configurations look like reasonable candidates for deprioritization. However, each setting is a single run with unknown variability. The gap cannot be attributed to pretrained foundation-model embeddings in general, since it may reflect this scGPT setup (e.g., checkpoint, embedding extraction, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary matching, or the downstream head). It also remains untested whether scGPT would behave differently in multiprofile or multimodal settings.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 is still the best result (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) lowered accuracy to 0.653, but that comparison cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself hurts or only simple average pooling does. Learned transformer aggregation has not been tested at all, and it appears in about half of the remaining configurations.
2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect on the strongest backbone. If transformer aggregation recovers or beats 0.678, multiprofile stays a live direction across unimodal and multimodal settings. If it also falls short, that is stronger evidence to focus the budget on single-profile models.
3. Why it is the best use of the budget: it resolves an open design question that affects many downstream configurations. It also has a realistic chance of exceeding the current best, since it builds on the strongest encoder. It is a cleaner and more broadly useful comparison than another encoder or fusion variant right now. The image-encoder question (ViT-L, config_013) is a good candidate for the following experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, to test whether learned aggregation could make multiprofile input competitive with the single-profile best (llm_summary_001: 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.227 and F1 to 0.191, far below both avgpool multiprofile (0.653 / 0.628) and every unimodal baseline. The result is strikingly close to the concat-fusion collapse in llm_summary_004 (0.224 / 0.184), so it looks more like a training or setup failure (e.g., optimization instability, lack of normalization or tuning for the transformer, degenerate predictions, or a pipeline issue) than evidence that transformer aggregation or multiprofile input is inherently harmful. This is a single undiagnosed run with unknown variability, so the multiprofile question is still open; avgpool remains the only working multiprofile aggregation, and the transformer configuration should be verified or rerun before the budget is moved away from transformer-aggregated configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA encoders have now been compared head to head, and PCA-2000 is best as run (0.678). Multiprofile avgpool slightly underperformed single-profile. Both concat fusion and transformer aggregation collapsed to about 0.22, which looks like a setup failure rather than a verdict on those methods. Weighted multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (0.635) sits between image-only and RNA-only. The image encoder is the one major design factor not yet tested at all: ImageNet ViT-L has never been run, and ResNet50 image-only reached 0.619. 2. What this tests: config_013 is the clean single-factor counterpart to config_010. It changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ViT-L, in the simple single-profile image-only setting, which avoids the unstable fusion and aggregation components. This shows whether a stronger image representation raises standalone image signal enough to make images more useful to RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use: The result decides which image encoder to carry into later weighted-fusion multimodal runs (e.g., config_023 vs. config_017). Those runs are the most plausible route to beating the RNA-only baseline. Testing the encoder in isolation first avoids confounding it with fusion or aggregation, and roughly half of the remaining configurations depend on this choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only single-profile setup of llm_summary_003 and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.619 to 0.519 (about -0.10) and F1 from 0.610 to 0.480. That puts it below RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.678 / 0.646) and weighted multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (0.635 / 0.618), and it is also below scGPT RNA-only (0.537), though it does not show the ~0.22 collapse seen with concat fusion or transformer aggregation. In this single-factor comparison, ViT-L as run gave weaker standalone image signal than ResNet50, so ResNet50 is the better-supported image encoder to carry into later weighted-fusion multimodal runs (e.g., favoring the ResNet50 counterpart over ViT-L configurations such as config_023 vs. config_017). However, this is one run with unknown run-to-run variability, and the drop cannot be attributed to ViT architectures or larger pretrained image models in general. It may reflect this ViT-L setup (e.g., input resolution or preprocessing, feature extraction layer or pooling, embedding dimensionality, or downstream head tuning). Whether ViT-L features could still add complementary signal to RNA in weighted fusion remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input has only been tested in the RNA modality. With PCA-2000, avgpool gave a small drop (0.678 to 0.653), and transformer aggregation collapsed to 0.227, which looks like a training failure. ResNet50 is the best image encoder so far (0.619 image-only), and weighted fusion with PCA reaches 0.635. That is still below RNA alone, so it is open whether any multiprofile or multimodal direction can beat the RNA baseline. Whether multiprofile aggregation helps or hurts depends on modality is untested. Image features may benefit from pooling over several profiles even if RNA PCA features do not. 2. What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting relative to config_010 (image-only ResNet50, single-profile to multiprofile avgpool). It uses avgpool because that aggregation has trained stably so far, and it avoids the collapse-prone transformer and concat components. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor test of whether the multiprofile effect is modality-specific. That bears directly on the large untested block of multiprofile multimodal configurations, such as config_019 and config_021. If multiprofile helps images, config_019 becomes a well-motivated exploit. If it hurts again, multiprofile can reasonably be deprioritized across modalities, with the caveat that each comparison is a single run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the image-only ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_003 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. The goal was to test whether the multiprofile effect seen in RNA depends on modality. Validation accuracy fell from 0.619 to 0.485 (about -0.13) and F1 from 0.610 to 0.464. In the RNA-only PCA-2000 pair, the same change gave a much smaller drop (0.678 to 0.653, llm_summary_002), so avgpool multiprofile input did not help in either modality tested and was clearly harmful here. The result is well above the ~0.22 collapses seen with concat fusion and transformer aggregation, so it does not look like a training failure, and it weakens the motivation for multiprofile multimodal configurations such as config_019 and config_021. However, each comparison is a single run with unknown variability, and the effect cannot be separated from avgpool itself, since transformer aggregation has never trained stably. It also remains untested whether other aggregations, normalization, or multimodal weighted fusion would change how multiprofile input behaves.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion strategy matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration and serves as a baseline. Later experiments can each change one choice against it: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), and the modality (image-only, multimodal). 3. Starting with a simple, low-variance reference uses the limited budget well, because the gain from added complexity can then be measured directly rather than assumed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile configuration using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.3316 (primary) and validation F1 0.3150 (supporting). The similar F1 suggests performance is roughly even across classes rather than driven by a few, though this is tentative. No other experiments have been run, so it is unknown whether this level is good or poor for the task, or whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only, or multimodal fusion would do better. Future experiments that change one choice at a time against this baseline would be needed to attribute any gain to a specific design choice; with a single run, variance across seeds is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. RNA-only, single-profile PCA reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. We do not yet know which design dimension drives performance. Most of the remaining space (36 of 50 configs) is multiprofile, so the value of multiprofile input is a large open question. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Encoder (PCA) and modality (RNA-only) stay fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregator rather than a transformer, so any gain is not confounded with aggregator complexity. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: this one-factor comparison against the baseline directly informs whether to prioritize the multiprofile part of the space, including later transformer and multimodal variants. If it gives no gain, we can redirect budget toward encoder choice (scVI, scGPT) or image modality instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only configuration with a PCA (n=2000) encoder, changing only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation (no image encoder or fusion). It reached validation accuracy 0.5203 (primary) and F1 0.4982 (supporting), up from the single-profile baseline's 0.3316 / 0.3150. Because this is a one-factor change, the roughly 0.19 accuracy gain is attributable to multiprofile input with avgpool in this setting, and it supports prioritizing the multiprofile part of the space. It remains uncertain whether the gain holds across seeds (each configuration has only one run), whether it transfers to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or multimodal settings, and whether more complex aggregators such as transformers would add further benefit over avgpool.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA (0.520 vs 0.332 accuracy, with F1 following the same pattern). That makes multiprofile/avgpool the current anchor. Nothing yet tells us whether the image modality adds value, even though most of the remaining search space (36 of 49 configurations) is multimodal. Question: config_018 keeps the best configuration (PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). Comparing it with config_002 isolates whether adding image features improves on RNA alone. Why now: the answer decides whether the budget should go to the large multimodal region or to refining RNA-only choices such as encoder and aggregator. It is also a reasonable exploit, since it extends the strongest configuration so far. A single run should be read cautiously, but a clear gain or loss here will narrow the search more than tuning the aggregator or encoder first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the best configuration so far fixed (PCA n2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and changed one thing: it added a ResNet50 image branch fused by simple concatenation, so it is a direct comparison with llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy was 0.5200 (primary), essentially identical to the RNA-only 0.5203, and validation F1 was somewhat lower (0.4791 vs 0.4982). This suggests that adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion gave no accuracy gain over RNA alone in this setting, and may slightly worsen class balance, though the F1 gap is small. It remains uncertain whether this holds across seeds (one run each), and whether the image modality could add value with other fusion methods, image encoders, aggregators, or RNA encoders. Concat alone should not be taken as evidence that the whole multimodal region lacks benefit.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Switching from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool gave the largest effect so far (0.332 to 0.520 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave no accuracy gain (0.520) and slightly lower F1 (0.479 vs 0.498). So the multiprofile setting is the clearest lever. How to aggregate across profiles is still untested. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. 3. Why now: This exploits the strongest finding with a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation also applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings, so the result will guide many later choices. Other questions, such as RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and whether images carry standalone signal, are left for later experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup fixed (PCA n2000 encoder, multiprofile input, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer, making it a direct one-factor comparison with llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy rose to 0.5729 (primary) from 0.5203, and validation F1 rose to 0.5730 from 0.4982. The F1 is now on par with accuracy, which tentatively suggests more even performance across classes. Within this configuration, the roughly 0.05 accuracy gain is attributable to transformer aggregation, making it the new best setting so far. It remains uncertain whether the gain holds across seeds (one run per configuration), and whether it transfers to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), to image-only settings, or to multimodal settings, where transformer aggregation might also change the null result seen with ResNet50 and concat fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input (+0.19 accuracy over single-profile) and transformer aggregation (+0.05 over avgpool) both helped clearly. The best result so far is config_003 (PCA n2000, multiprofile, transformer), at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave no gain. Every run so far used the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the effect of the RNA representation is completely unknown. Since RNA appears to carry most of the signal, that choice may matter a lot. 2) What this tests: config_006 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, while keeping the best multiprofile and transformer setup. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest setup found so far while exploring an untested design factor that affects every downstream RNA-only and multimodal configuration. The result will show whether the remaining budget should focus on PCA or shift to a learned encoder before spending more runs on fusion or image variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best setup so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. This makes it a direct one-factor comparison with llm_summary_004. Validation accuracy fell to 0.4348 (primary) from 0.5729, and validation F1 fell to 0.4234 (supporting) from 0.5730, which suggests that in this configuration the scVI n200 representation performs clearly worse than PCA n2000. PCA n2000 therefore remains the preferred RNA encoder for now. It remains uncertain whether the roughly 0.14 accuracy gap holds across seeds (one run each), whether it reflects scVI itself or its lower dimensionality or training setup (n200 vs n2000 is confounded within the encoder change), whether scVI would compare differently under avgpool, single-profile, or multimodal settings, and how other untested encoders such as scGPT would perform.
